# Review and issue record

**N-E refusal growth and pre-consent outcomes, 2026-11-11 (review pending):**
Missing folder paths, a busy maintenance request and known file/read-policy
preconditions now share the existing counted, bounded refusal summaries and
receipt aliases. Folder path count is checked before its handler; arbitrary
entered selectors keep their exact records. A concurrent call rechecks the ID
after refresh, so its busy refusal cannot erase another call's running intent.
Initial, explicitly typed confirmation-constructor refusals are not executed.
Approved or previously entered handlers retain their original ID and outcome;
effects followed by a policy failure remain unknown and never replay.

After successful execution and audit, completed/received/awaiting-native guards
retain audit routing and native target identities, rather than the whole consent
snapshot. Full commands, IDs, results and delivery remain. This reduces visible
receipt metadata; it does not change invocation arguments or deduplication.
Pending, cancelled and uncertain guards are preserved, including an audit failure
after execution. The real delivery consumer still rejects a replacement native
identity after restart. The representative guard falls from 1,733 to 122 bytes.
Ordinary commands and results still grow with executed IDs. They cannot be
discarded under the refusal rule: changing their retention or replay contract
requires a separate decision. The 32MiB hard limit still retains existing data
and refuses new intent before its handler; no unlimited-history claim is made.
Path-based file-read membership (N-B) is unchanged and still awaits the person.
**Native quota failure input, 2026-11-11 (independent review pending):**
Claude can finish an exhausted-credit request before its StopFailure hook.
An error without the API Error prefix previously prevented the late confirmed
failure from enabling a new explicit chat input. Tool permission boundaries
also revoke reply-sharing authority; recovery now uses the separately observed
started root without restoring that authority or automatic continuation.
Completed-root input is consumed once and revoked by later control boundaries,
disconnect, observation gaps and rebinding. The shared workspace readiness guard
is unchanged. A native synthetic credit error receives a localized manual
recovery notice only when its processed text retains that fact.
The sandboxed real-Claude loopback journey covers plain, tool, background-command,
child and native-terminal input, with fixed replies, stable native identity,
one-time tool execution and no automatic recovery request. Event-order,
redaction and revocation regressions cover the boundaries; Codex's completed
failure still returns to ordinary idle input. This is not a real billing reset
or permission-mode qualification. Independent code and wording review is required.

**Mod readiness file visibility, 2026-11-11 (incremental review pending):**
The integration run exposed a gap in the new timeout test: the shell creates
and truncates child-ready before writing its PID, so existence alone could
return an empty string. Readiness now requires a complete numeric line; the
before-output marker likewise requires its complete ready line. Controlled
real-file reads expose creation, partial content and the completed line: both
old helpers fail, both repaired cases pass. Holding the actual sandbox script
after file creation reproduces the PID-zero failure; the repaired test waits
for its completed write and then passes with real process-group termination.
Both timeout cases now check no completion and no group signal at 599ms,
followed by exactly one real group SIGKILL at 600ms. A private loader that moves
only the deadline to 599ms makes both tests fail. The full mod-check file passes
13/13. Production code and all time limits are unchanged. This corrects the
earlier readiness proof, without claiming that synthetic file scheduling
reproduces the precise historical load. Formal independent review is pending.

**Mod timeout test ordering, 2026-11-11 (author verification pending):**
The process-group timeout test treated a 600ms spawn deadline as proof that the
sandbox's shell had created a child and printed its PID. Holding the fake program
before that print reproduces the same empty note and null-match failure without
load. Production collection already waits for close and drains both pipes; no
production output-loss fix is justified by that evidence. The test now advances
only its deadline clock after a fixture-owned readiness file proves the PID was
written, then checks the real sandbox, SIGKILL, complete output and group exit.
A second ordering expires before output and requires an incomplete, empty note.
An independent wall-clock startup watchdog reports missing readiness explicitly;
finally aborts and awaits the exact run before removing its scratch directory.
The production timeout, sandbox profile and record rules are unchanged. PID is
matched as one complete line among diagnostics rather than the entire note.

**PTY stop during startup, 2026-11-11 (independent review pending):**
The display restart test failed again after its unrelated test-only stop bound
was widened. The host published started immediately after the parent returned
from PTY fork, before the child necessarily established its session. A stop or
input EOF in that gap called killpg(childPid), got ESRCH, and was silently lost.
An owned-child readiness pipe now gates started and queued commands. Child
setup failure closes the pipe and still reaches waitpid; it cannot hang waiting
for an acknowledgement. SIGTERM policy, default stop time and confirmed-exit
criteria are unchanged; stream EOF alone still does not prove native exit.

Controlled standard-library fork scheduling reproduces all three failures:
stop at started, queued stop, and input EOF. Each old run reports missing group,
then actual native output, then SIGALRM from its test safety alarm instead of
the requested SIGTERM. After the fix each is reaped by SIGTERM. Existing ignored
termination and native-display activity tests remain in the affected group.
This proves a production race with the observed symptom; the historical flaky
log has no group identity and cannot uniquely establish that occurrence's cause.


**S2 bounded refusal summaries, 2026-11-11 (delta review pending):**
confirmation-limit and originating-session-unavailable now retain one counted
summary per native actor, reason and minute, with at most 128 recent summaries
in the operation file and 128 summary events per space, at most 32 per stable
NAW session across native replacements. Global overflow removes the oldest row
from the largest remaining share, so a busy session cannot consume every slot.
They retain method names,
counts and timing, never request arguments or a full consent snapshot. Space
counters include only requests audited in that space; duplicate or older audit
deliveries do not change a newer count. Other history and legacy records remain.

Review rejected the unpublished retry-prefix candidate: one transient refusal
changed every later invoke and blocked implicit foreign snapshots. The correction
uses option B: no operation-ID prefix rule. Reusing a compacted, proven
not-executed ID is a new request through current admission and any required human
confirmation. The tool description and refusal hint explain this for invoke and
snapshot. Ordinary send, viewState and queue intake keep their unique-ID protocol.
Existing ordinary and legacy per-ID records retain their exact command binding,
including executed, uncertain, cancelled and pending operations across restart.
An already approved operation is never compacted after a later confirmation
refusal: effects may have occurred, so its original intent, decision and unknown
outcome remain durable and cannot replay. Counterexamples reproduce one effect
followed by a quota refusal and verify retention and no second effect.
Recent original refused IDs resolve to their aggregate receipt, with at most
512 aliases globally and 128 per NAW session, while the referenced summary
remains. Aliases bind provider, session and native identity; they are metadata
for receipt lookup only, never invocation replay records. An actual normal
operation with that ID takes precedence and removes the alias. Evicted aliases
return no receipt; old candidates did not store original IDs, so those cannot
be reconstructed. Stored summary hints now agree with immediate replies and
the tool description, including on loading an earlier candidate file.
No model, provider permission or human-window behavior changes.

This bounds those two refusal classes, not all ordinary operation history. At
32 MiB a write fails before replacing the existing file. A new intent then does
not run; a handler that already ran before its final save failed has an unknown
result and cannot be replayed. Pickup cannot expose a read body without saving
consumption first. Failed summary saves roll back their counters and perform no
new action. Legacy history is not deleted to create space. The real 32 MiB probe
and counter/replay regressions require incremental independent review. Nonblocking
follow-ups remain: growth of other ordinary refusal classes and typed, compact
not-executed results for file preconditions that currently report unconfirmed.

New background file selectors without explicit paths return not-executed with

hosted file operations validate path cardinality and the owned export token before

reset keeps its path-free confirmation. Space-file imports require paths, while
file-ID reads keep the existing member and one-use rules. Missing/consumed export
tokens ask no futile question. Human windows and the undecided path-read policy

receipts and duplicate binding. Only typed errors thrown by the maintenance
confirmation callback qualify, before any handler has run. Handler errors and
resumptions after possible earlier effects stay unconfirmed; a resumable handler
records that boundary in its existing pending-row save. Both providers have
sixteen pre-confirmation counterexamples;
valid paths still ask before file metadata, reset and space-file reading work.

Non-maintenance background consent fingerprints now project sessions through
RoomState.apply, as admission, actor checks and maintenance fingerprints already
do. A real standalone target archive does not change backend state or membership;
the old raw-session fingerprint therefore allowed its pending stop to execute.
Both providers reproduce that failure and now reject the stale consent before
the target RPC. The no-profile connection-update fallback remains unchanged:
all five production callers pass RoomState, so only the isolated test helper uses
that fallback. Backend migration safety still examines all backend sessions.

**S2 shared confirmation admission, 2026-11-11 (delta review pending):**

Missing, replaced, archived and context-pending callers receive no new card or

**S2 requester admission, 2026-11-11 (delta review pending):**
the pending-count filter must not exempt an ineligible requester from its own

Hosted `terminalSnapshot`, `observe` and `terminal` refuse a secretary before

The pending-confirmation bound counts only actors in the refreshed consent

**S2 consent follow-ups and space files, 2026-11-10 (delta review pending):**
the person approved retaining a cancelled implicit conversation-read receipt
until its selected target or consent fingerprint changes. Navigating away

them follows the same rule as renaming another session. Confirmation includes

Display escaping additionally covers Default_Ignorable_Code_Point and U+2800;
the actual Electron runtime supports that Unicode property. Execution keeps the
original text. Session archive plans save the following neighbour; restore
inserts before it even if the number of earlier active members changes. Legacy

The person's later space-file decision applies to `spaceFiles(roomId, fileId)`:

The approved body uses the same ephemeral one-use cache as conversation and

Conversation, terminal and image read values no longer enter the durable operation

An approved foreign read has one frozen, in-memory copy in a shared bounded cache

Regression work also found native approval text in navigation consent guards.

## Queued terminal questions retain their reply group (T-138, 2026-11-09)

On exact Claude 2.1.321 and 2.1.322, a question entered while Claude works
raises `UserPromptSubmit` with the previous question's id. Its later reply
has a new classic prompt id, distinct from the engine turn id, display turn
id and accepted message UUID. Treating the nearest answer as its reply would
misplace late output from an older turn.

The native journal records the accepted user UUID and its new classic
`promptId` together. That exact UUID connects the display to the existing,
limited queued-turn recognition, which still requires the first queued
composer prompt and its exact accepted text. Unknown, ambiguous, child,
foreign-session and stale-observer identities stay unlinked. The bridge
does not independently prove the older queued-turn recognition rule.

Only the authenticated current root can request the unique UUID from its
already observed journal path. Reads require an owned regular file with the
exact session filename, reject final symlinks, and inspect at most 256 KiB
per read. Native may flush the user row after drawing begins: this one
metadata request permits five reads with 25 ms gaps, rechecking the
lease and observer before each. No history or prose is returned. A bounded
miss remains a separate display turn rather than retagging published text.
Overlapping display callbacks also re-read the pinned link after the lookup:
the first published namespace wins even if a later lookup obtains a UUID.
Overlapping chunks share one in-flight lookup, preserving their text order
and avoiding duplicate journal requests; live lookups are not evicted.
When the identified reply is drawn after its own completed footer, native
record insertion keeps it before that footer, within its question's group.
It does not move interrupted boundaries or narration, or attach old output
to a newer question.

A separate reading-only capability permits one queued `-q` input trigger
on these two versions when whole turn records are unavailable. This bit
itself does not enable shell records, ordinary input triggers, narration,
abort or whole turn records; the combined-gates main independently qualifies
whole turn records and narration on both versions. Both negotiation modes
have regression coverage. Display aliases do not enter the prompt authority
map or certify a shared final reply. Earlier unprovable saved rows are not
backfilled.

The original base and the later combined-gates main reproduce the defect.
Two actual native composer trials with loopback canned responses verify
the fixed question/reply turn identity on 321 and 322; each uses two local
responses and zero paid inference. These are native producer checks, not
physical iTerm acceptance or daily-app installation. Related tests cover
delayed journal writes, replaced observers, duplicate/foreign identities,
pinned old output, missing proof and capability boundaries. Independent
review applies to this source delivery; merge, installation and daily-use
acceptance remain separate.

**Decision notifications, 2026-11-09 (B1; independent review PASS_SCOPED):**
Queue outcomes that ask for a decision or fail now notify once per persisted event,
with localized bounded text, and clicking reveals that exact space record after a
workspace renderer is ready. Other waits stay silent. Notification failures cannot
undo the record or trigger retries; active objects and remembered ids are bounded.
Owner: B1 author. Initial reproduction: 13 of 14 new checks failed on the prior code.
Review counterexamples reproduced four failures: a recorded name equal to a session
id, non-LF line separators, a flattened-reply fallback, and a different loading
window being foregrounded. All four were fixed; 125 related checks pass without skips.
Chinese and English isolated source GUI trials verify deduplication, exact record
focus, retained unsent drafts, failure notices and unchanged clipboard counts using
synthetic provider transports and captured notifications. Final Chinese trial passed
again after the fixes. Independent review closed all five findings (the fifth
clarified that zero model calls follow from fixture construction).
Scope excludes real OS banners, lock-screen previews, cold-start old notifications
and the signed installed app; those remain installation acceptance. A future direct
caller of the notification callback must retain the first-line question contract.

## New sessions retain the selected project directory (B2, 2026-11-09)

New sessions previously defaulted to another empty automatic directory. The
desktop now remembers successful human creation choices in one private record
across backends: the last selected worktree repository, then the last selected
ordinary directory. A repository defaults to a fresh isolated worktree using the
existing preview and creation path. Its tracked project instructions come from
checkout; NAW writes no instruction files and adds no native directory flags.
Uncommitted source changes are not part of that checkout.

Only main's stored repository or the person's explicit folder selection can
authorize a preview. Defaults loading blocks creation and stale responses cannot
overwrite later selections. Failed, background and automatic-directory creates
do not change the preference; a save failure retains the created session.

Rotation records can save the successor path and exact worktree plan before
creation and recover by nonce even when the prepared path is canonicalized.
Legacy creating records first adopt any already-created old-directory successor.
A pending create rejected or completed as the GUI closes leaves that recovery
receipt intact, rather than recording a shutdown failure or advancing its phase.
Migration applies only to NAW's shared directory or direct automatic UUID child;
handoffs list at most twenty old-directory names, including hidden entries,
without reading their contents or removing anything. Malformed plans are ignored.
Unattended directory migration remains disabled until native first-directory
trust is qualified; the isolated synthetic test override cannot enable it in an
ordinary app launch. Saved plans still resume when that gate is off. Source and
synthetic checks do not prove native rule loading, daily acceptance or installation.
Before enabling migration, native trust remains unqualified. A missing saved
repository or failed preview currently fails the rotation and retains the old
session; there is no implicit fallback to an empty directory. Interrupted planning
keeps its temporary choices local until the complete plan can be saved together.

**Space task queues and session rotation, 2026-11-08 (independent review, first round CHANGES_NEEDED):**
the person asked that NAW itself send each idle space member its next queued item, and
that day-old sessions hand over to a new session to free memory. Findings reproduced and
fixed: (1) an interrupted or silent turn was settled as done and the next item followed;
now a turn with no reply, a later human message or a changed control revision holds the
member as "needs your decision". (2) dispatch used the person's input path, so it counted
as a takeover, paused unrelated collaborations and recorded NAW's text as the person's;
the backend now has its own `dispatch` input (capability `queueDispatchV1`) that takes no
control, pauses only that member's handoff, is refused while the person has a draft or
automatic messages are off, and records `origin: naw-dispatch`. (3) dispatch could take a
session out of the person's terminal view or another window; it no longer claims, and a
session the person touched in the last two minutes is skipped. (4) rotation could stop the
old session while the person used it; the old session is rechecked before the handoff and
before it is stopped, a failed rotation stops only the unused new session and returns the
work, a restart adopts an already created session, and the rotation file must be private
and well formed. Also: refusals before sending return the item to the queue (at most five
times), every call has a timeout, and unchanged state is not reread every tick. Checks:
`app/tests/queue-dispatch.test.cjs` and `app/tests/workspace-queue-dispatch.test.cjs`;

inference). Not verified: Codex rotation with a real Codex app-server, and the memory
saving of rotating a long-lived session (a fresh native process starts near 300 MB).

queue items (the person decides whether they may), resolving a decision is recorded, a

being updated, and space handoff rows are not read as the person. Round 3
(APPROVE_WITH_NOTES) notes fixed: the new member takes work as soon as its handoff is
confirmed, the old session waits at most 30 minutes for running collaborations and is then

The author and independent reviewer have separate roles. The reviewer reads the
actual change, callers and complete evidence, then checks the original feedback
and plausible counterexamples. The maintainer verifies those findings and owns
the final delivery decision. Small changes need one short review; complex fixes
are reviewed again when new evidence is available. No automatic model-test loop
or standing background agent chat is required.

Issues move through **reported → reproduced → fixing → awaiting review → closed**.
An untested case remains **unverified**. A code change, mock or skipped test alone
does not close a native-user-experience issue. Reopen the same item when evidence
contradicts it; keep the former result's scope and date.

Before a commit or artifact handoff, review the affected rows and record the
actual verification. High-risk issues relevant to that delivery cannot be closed
by a summary or an author-only approval. Unrelated findings stay scoped to their
next trigger; they do not justify expanding the current task.

### Native snapshot scroll regions, origin cursor and erased pending rows (T-77)

Read-only terminal views lost scroll regions (DECSTBM) and origin mode (DECOM)
when rebuilt from a snapshot, so later output scrolled or landed on the wrong
rows. Default snapshots now restore each buffer's region, the origin-relative
cursor, a pending-wrap cursor (by reprinting the last glyph with absolute
styles) and uniformly background-erased pending rows. Three content fix-ups
support this: a forced wrap for blank-led wrapped rows, an ECH so the first
replay scroll does not inherit the previous row's background, and keeping
trailing background-erased rows. Explicit serialize options and
non-reconstructable pending rows keep the previous bytes.

A fresh read-only reviewer first required changes: the glyph reprint used
relative SGR, and SGR 22 dropped bold and dim on the cell and pen, a regression
from the previous bytes. It was fixed with absolute styles. A pre-existing
one-column error for the inactive normal buffer in origin mode was also fixed,
and the whole-call legacy guard gained a failing control. The delta review
passed. Known gaps shared with the previous bytes: an origin-mode cursor outside
the region is restored at the region bottom (source row 4, restored 3, stock 0);
the alternate screen's first cells assume a default pen (foreground 1 against
the source's default); the saved-cursor slot is not reproduced. Not verified:
browser rendering, graphemes and combining reprints, charsets, underline style
and colour, and the installed app.

### Full-width punctuation drift in terminal rows (T-77)

The user reported terminal display problems with Chinese text. Ordinary CJK
glyphs leave a gap inside their two cells, as in the user's iTerm2; that is not
a defect. The lane's independent reviewer found a NAW-only defect the author had
missed: after each full-width punctuation mark the rest of the row moved right
by about 0.8 of a cell, so punctuation-heavy rows lost their last glyphs at the
right edge. Chromium's default text-spacing-trim compresses adjacent full-width
punctuation, and xterm measured those marks at half width. The fix sets
text-spacing-trim to space-all on the terminal; the delta review passed.
Follow-ups: a per-step drift check for long rows, and code-point column mapping
for captured input. Not verified: the installed app; input methods, VoiceOver
and selection, reasoned from source only; the shipped 13px default, covered only
by the probe; more than one green GUI run per checkout; and the right-edge cut
reported earlier, pending an installed check.

### A prompt typed while Claude works can wake peers, and its turn settles (T-138, wake half)

Claude 2, 11-02. Review: a fresh lane session over four rounds (CHANGES, then CHANGES (narrow), then PASS, then a delta for the stale-origin item, which passed).

**Trigger.** On Claude Code 2.1.316 and 2.1.317, a prompt the person types while Claude works raises `UserPromptSubmit` once, at enqueue, with the running prompt's id. Measured by a read-only probe that records ids and text hashes only (`t138-probe-20261102/`).
- **Path A (no mid-turn point).** The prompt later starts its own turn, whose `turn.start` text is exactly that prompt. The turn's classic events (PostToolUse, Stop, MessageDisplay) carry a new prompt id that no `UserPromptSubmit` announced.
- **Path B (a tool call in the running turn).** The prompt joins that turn as a `queued_command` delivery.
- **`!` turns.** Their `turn.start` text is the command output, they raise no `UserPromptSubmit`, and their Stop is also unannounced.
- **Esc.** Esc runs the queued prompt as its own turn at once.

**Findings.**
- **T-138.** The queued prompt's own turn could not wake a peer; its link was ambiguous.
- **F1 (reviewer).** After such a turn, or a `!` turn, ran a tool, NAW showed 正在工作 for good. The adapter drops a Stop whose id was never announced. The symptom was measured. That it predates the change (any tool in a queued turn on HEAD) is inferred from the source.
- **F2.** Clearing on interrupt would refuse the prompt the engine runs right after Esc, as measured. Kept.
- **F3.** A `!` turn can't match: its text is the output.
- **F4.** Entries are tied to the prompt id.
- **F5.** The line admits composer input only. At `UserPromptSubmit` entry, exactly one foreign submission must be in flight and its origin must be composer. In-flight submissions are tracked as a set, because a saved-and-restored origin went stale when submissions interleaved (round 3, low).
- **Round 2, finding 1.** A native permission ask clears `rootTurn`, so settling now uses the started turn instead.

**Fix.**
- **`register.js`.** A bounded line of composer prompts typed during a root turn. A new root turn after idle, with no newer prompt and not NAW's own, is that prompt's turn only by exact text equality with the first entry; on any mismatch the line is dropped. A `queued_command` delivery or an idle prompt clears it.
- **`adapters.cjs`.** An unannounced Stop, plus the started root turn's own completed `turn` block (either order, with no prompt announced since that turn started and nothing pending), settles the session to idle with an untagged empty `complete`.
- The background computation is shared in `emitBackground()`.

**Evidence.**
- **Unit tests:** 2203/2203 in the lane's final round, 2221/2221 on main. Mutations fail exactly their tests:
  - no-unambiguous;
  - no-text-match;
  - no-delivery-clear;
  - no-settle;
  - no-announced-check;
  - origin read after await;
  - the round-4 stale saved origin, which fails exactly the new interleaving test on both versions.

  The permission tests fail on the round-2 adapter.
- **Real CLI** (source app, local fixed replies, 0 paid, fake pbcopy):
  - **Red, 2.1.317:** with no-unambiguous, the wake is refused. With no-settle, S ends `working`.
  - **Green, 2.1.317 and 2.1.316:** B is woken (`submitted`). S is idle after the queued turn and at the end. A later `!` turn is still refused.
  - The red runs and the 2.1.316 run used round 3, which differs only in how submissions in flight are tracked; the final bytes ran on 2.1.317 in the lane and once on main.

**Open.**
- **Display half:** the queued prompt's own row collides with the running prompt's row id (`adapters.cjs:992`, `workspace.cjs:566`; inferred). The new prompt id seen in classic events is the lead.
- **T-141 (F6):** a queued `UserPromptSubmit` may re-capture T1's wake authority (inferred).
- **Not covered:**
  - a `!` turn whose tool actually runs (same adapter path, no test);
  - ↑ recall of a queued message (unmeasured);
  - a prompt typed, or blocked by a hook, while the queued turn runs. The adapter counts it as announced, so the queued turn's own Stop doesn't settle. If that prompt carries T1's id and no later turn starts, S stays `working` (round 3, low, unmeasured).
- **Deliberate narrowing:** queued Remote Control (`bridge`) prompts are not admitted.
- **Integration review (inferred, low):** an unannounced Stop is credited to whichever root turn has started when it arrives; if it arrives after the next turn started, that turn settles once with the earlier turn's background counts and again at its own Stop. Nothing is shared. The settle is not limited by Claude version, though it was measured only on 2.1.316 and 2.1.317.


### Agent wakes appear in the collaboration space's shared record (T-137, item 1)

The person asked how agent-to-agent messages are tracked and asked that they
leave a record in the collaboration space. Before this change a wake left a row
only in the sender's own conversation. Now the sender's backend also writes one
system row into each space the sender and recipient share, or into the sender's
own spaces when they share none. The row stores the sender's and recipient's ids
and names and the wake's id inside its wake reference, and the full message as
its text; when shown, its delivery status, and its text while the sender's row
exists, are read from the sender's row, names follow renames, and the member
filter finds it. It has no top-level session id, final reply or share tag, which
keeps it off the handoff path, and no other reader passes space rows to an
agent. It is saved with the space's records and stays after the sender's own
records are removed, then showing that the sender's record is gone; clearing the
space's shared records removes it on every backend. Claude 2's lane reviewer
asked for changes once and then passed it.

Open, all low: a name in a wake row is not a filter shortcut, though the member
menu works; if a finished wake's sender record is removed before a merge is
confirmed, the merge fails safely with the generic error; the combined view of
two backends is tested only for the default space; code later added between the
row push and the save could let an unsaved wake be sent; the status lookup for
wake rows runs on every snapshot and its cost is not measured. The person's
choice for wakes with no shared space is T-143, and the daily check across
backends is still to do. The lane's first GUI round ran against a stale UI
bundle; its final rounds rebuilt it, and every main GUI batch from alpha.158 on
has a log of rebuilding the bundle before running; packaging always rebuilds it.

comes from the message text; control, zero-width and bidirectional characters
are removed from the claimed name.

Open, low: a claimed name can imitate the process-match marker; some invisible

### Cross-session messages are listed in the space's shared record (T-137, item 2b)

When a Claude Code cross-session message reaches a session, the recipient's
backend now writes a row 「sender（未核实） → recipient」 with the message into the
space's shared record: into a space both share when the sender is a session on
the same backend, otherwise into the recipient's spaces. The row is never passed
to an agent, an unparsed message keeps its original text, the stored name keeps
the unverified mark in merged copies, a repeated prompt id adds no second row,
and clearing the space's shared records removes it. The rule for where the row
goes is part of the person's choice in T-143.

Claude 2's lane reviewer asked for changes once and then passed it. Lane
evidence: the full suite passed 2,234 checks on the alpha.168 base; mutations
for the narrowing and the duplicate guard fail their tests; on real 2.1.317 and
2.1.316 with local replies and a message sent by hand, Receiver B's 共同工作 record
showed 「Claude 2（未核实） → Receiver B」 with the message, it stayed under B's
filter, and the item 2a checks still passed; with the write removed no row
appeared. The red run and the 2.1.316 run used the previous patch, which differs
in a name and a text. Not exercised: the sender filter with a NAW session as
sender, held messages and senders on another backend. The integration reviewer
noted that with no shared space the row goes into all of the recipient's spaces
and that a space merge selects such rows by default; this stays open in T-143
until the person answers. Not verified: a peer prompt that carries the running
turn's prompt id gets neither a session row nor a space row, though it is still
classified as a peer message and still voids wakes.


### Each grid column's terminal height can be changed (T-135, 180f110; first 6845505)

**Source.** User feedback 2026-11-02 (board T-135, screenshot under feedback): in a space grid each column's terminal is about five lines and cannot be made taller; columns should be adjustable one by one, with a way to make them all the same height, and no complex logic.

**Change.**
- A line above each column's terminal (a labelled separator) changes that column's height by dragging, or with ArrowUp/ArrowDown (16px), Home and End.
- While the person changes it: at least 64px, at most what leaves the conversation 80px and the column's input whole (in a window too small for that, the old 112px stays possible).
- On release or a key the height is kept per session with the window's view (the 200 most recently changed), and the native terminal is fitted once.
- The column ⋯ menu offers 「所有列都用这个终端高度」 while the column shows its terminal.
- A redraw or a smaller window lowers a tall height to what fits (not below 112px) without a native resize; the terminal scrolls in its box with the cursor in view.

**Review.** A fresh read-only reviewer in the author lane, three rounds.
- **Round 1, CHANGES:**
  - High: the box changed but the native terminal was never fitted, so a taller terminal showed no more lines; the first GUI check measured only the box.
  - Medium: no upper limit on redraw, so a tall height after a window shrink could cut off the input.
  - Medium: the menu path skipped the 200-entry cap, which could make every later view save fail.
  - Two Medium-Lows on stale and interrupted drags, and an inaccurate toast.
  - All fixed, with a GUI check that one release causes one native resize and the rows fill the box.
- **Round 2, PASS** with five Lows. Taken: ArrowUp could shorten the terminal in a very small window; a drag left set after leaving the room.
- **Round 3, PASS** on that delta.

**Evidence.**
- Full suite: 2198/0.
- Hidden synthetic GUI, 0 model:
  - column-terminal 8/8: a drag of 112→192px moved the terminal's rows from 102 to 187px with one native resize; the smaller window lowered it to 154px with the input whole and no native resize.
  - column-input 17/17 (including 850×600).
  - grid-follow 7/7 and reading-turns 8/8 (at r5).

**Open.**
- L2: a redraw that changes the box height scrolls the terminal to its bottom. Trigger: a person reading scrollback when the window size changes.
- L3: only a window resize redraws; a hand-resized shared composer can cut off a column's input until the next render. Trigger: if reported, watch `.collaboration-readers` with a ResizeObserver.
- L4: the one-time resize permission can stay set when no fit runs (same as the existing activation path).
- Not tested: after scrolling the conversation to the latest by hand, making the terminal taller before any redraw can leave the last lines below the bottom until the next redraw (the same as a window resize today).
- Integration review, low: removing a session's records does not drop its saved terminal height, and the window sends its own copy back on the next save.
- Integration: the new separator made test-collaboration-overview.cjs's column-width locator match two elements; main narrowed it to the vertical separator.
- Replayed onto main 1af6800 as 180f110 (only a test-file insertion point differs); the same reviewer passed it in a fourth round.
- Not verified:
  - a state update during a drag (code reading only);
  - four terminal columns at once;
  - a real trackpad;
  - a screen reader;
  - the daily app.

### A staged wake is withdrawn when an input boundary interrupts its turn (T-141)

When an agent staged a wake in a turn and, before that turn ended, the person
typed another prompt, a cross-session message arrived or a native permission ask
came up before the wake was staged, the boundary cleared the turn record, so the
turn never reported its end and the wake stayed 已登记，尚未投递 for good. The adapter
now reports that turn's end once with a boundary status, and the wake is
withdrawn with the note 发送方这一轮中途有新的输入或权限确认；自动消息未投递. A turn that already reported
its end is not reported again.

On its own this mitigates T-141 rather than fixing it: a person's input in the
middle of a turn still gives that turn back its wake authority (the native start
capture in the workspace), and only this boundary end stops the wake from being
delivered. The display half of T-138 narrows that to a prompt identical to the
running one, or a turn whose first text the adapter no longer has: after a
backend restart, after 64 newer prompt ids, or when the first hook event was
lost. Wakes staged after a boundary that came before staging, such as a
cross-session message, a task notification or the native approval of the call
itself, are now withdrawn instead of hanging; none of them was delivered before.
By NAW's own rules those should be deliverable, so on Claude they remain an open
limitation, not a regression. A permission ask after staging was already
withdrawn. Claude 2's lane reviewer passed it in one round. Its concern that a
second, boundary end after an end already reported could cancel a capacity
recovery just scheduled on 2.1.310 to 2.1.312 is closed by the post-review
additions; a boundary end still cancels capacity like any end that is not a
failure, and capacity is off on 2.1.316 and 2.1.317. The addition that stops a
failure end from being followed by a boundary end has no unit test and was
checked by reading the source.

Lane evidence: the full suite passed 2,238 checks; with the boundary end or its
guard removed the tests fail; on real 2.1.317 and 2.1.316 with local replies,
the wake stayed 已登记 before the fix and was withdrawn with the note after it,
without waking the recipient. Open, low: the withdrawal note can appear when the
turn record was cleared for another reason, such as a reconnect, a rebind, a
context end or a failure for another prompt, though a pause normally withdraws
the wake first in those cases; a completed turn whose display record is
incomplete still reports no end; a real run with a boundary before staging or
with a permission ask was not measured.


### A prompt typed while Claude works has its own row (T-138, display half)

On Claude Code 2.1.316 and 2.1.317 a prompt the person typed while a turn ran
had no row in NAW's conversation view: the adapter gave it the running prompt's
row id, and the workspace skips a row whose id already exists. Its row now gets
its own id, derived from the running prompt's id and a short hash of its text,
and when the prompt runs as its own turn it stands after the first turn's reply,
at the head of that turn, as in the native terminal; if the running turn takes
it in, the row stays where it was typed, which is not measured. Its time is when
it was typed. The prompt's own later turn is linked only when its text matches.

The wake rule becomes stricter: after the person types a different prompt in the
middle of a turn, a wake that turn tries to stage is refused when it is staged,
instead of being staged and withdrawn at the turn's end; only an identical
prompt still gives the turn its wake authority back, which the T-141 boundary
end then withdraws. Cross-session messages, task notifications and blocked
prompts that carry the running prompt's id now also each get a row instead of
being dropped, and such a cross-session message is then also copied into the
recipient's spaces under the alpha.169 rule; this is inferred from the source
and not measured, and the space copy was not part of the lane review. Claude 2's
lane reviewer passed it in one round: ids can only disagree in ways that leave a
row unlinked or missing as before, apart from a 32-bit hash collision.

Lane evidence: the full suite passed 2,243 checks; six mutations fail their
tests; with the unchanged T-138 runner on real 2.1.317 the row was missing
before the change, and with the change a frozen checker found exactly one row,
after the first reply and heading its own turn, on 2.1.317 and 2.1.316. The
integration reviewer also noted that a row already linked to a turn now leaves
an entry in the capped list of rows waiting to be linked, which can never link
anything. Open, low: after a backend restart in the middle of a turn the typed
prompt still loses its row, as before; the second turn's reply still starts its
own reading group, which predates this change.

### A message can be queued while Claude works (T-133, item 1)

On Claude Code 2.1.316 and 2.1.317 NAW disabled its send button while Claude
worked, so the person could only type into the native terminal. Sending is now
allowed from the session chat and from a space while a turn runs: the message
waits until that turn ends, runs as its own turn, and its reply is attached to
it, in the space record too; in the session chat it stands after the previous
turn's reply, as in the native terminal. Clicking 停止 while a message is queued
no longer reports 原生中断结果未确认: the stop no longer waits for a queued message that
has not started its own turn. 停止 stops only the running turn: the queued message
then runs at once as its own turn, as Esc does in the native terminal; NAW
cannot withdraw it.

Claude 2's lane reviewer asked for changes once: the probe it asked for showed
the false 未确认 report after 停止, which was then fixed, and the second round
passed. Three test assertions it suggested, one case per run, an exact request
count and the shared row's delivery state, were added afterwards and checked
only by real runs. Kept under the existing rules: queueing in the session chat
stops a shared reply in progress, and after queueing from a space and clicking
停止, the queued message's reply stays in the session and is not shared, because
the stop withdraws that sharing grant.

Lane evidence: the full suite passed 2,247 checks; four mutations fail their
tests; native probes on real 2.1.316 and 2.1.317 measured how native handles the
queued message. Before the change, the frozen runner (private and shared) and
the script's queue mode (private) failed at the disabled send on 2.1.317;
nothing was run before the change on 2.1.316. After it, both passed in private
and shared form on both versions, and the default flow passed on 2.1.317. Open,
low: stopping a turn that something other than a NAW message started during the
wait, such as a prompt typed in the terminal, still reports unconfirmed; the row
move follows a receipt that travels on a different channel from the rows, though
every measured order was right; stopping a queued turn before its receipt
arrives could leave the session needing input, not reachable at human speed; 停止
while queued on 2.1.316 and 2.1.312 was not run. Item 2, which would show
prompts typed in the native terminal, and their images, from the plugin's own
input records, stays off until it is aligned with T-99. The integration reviewer
added, all low or recorded only: the plugin's pending submission spans the whole
wait, so a prompt typed or arriving during it leaves NAW's reply unattributed
and turns off turn heading and typed-prompt linking for turns that start then;
the stop fix still depends on arrival order, and the conservative unconfirmed
report returns if the queued prompt's events land before the abort completes,
though all five measured runs were in the right order; the row move also applies
to 2.1.308 to 2.1.312, unmeasured; a wake staged after a queue from a space in
the same running turn can still be delivered, as the existing rule says; the
private queue check covers row order but not turn linkage; and a held question
does not block queueing, though the queued message cannot answer it and native
handling while the question hook blocks is not measured.

### An image in a prompt typed in the Claude terminal is shown (T-133, item 2)

On Claude Code 2.1.316 and 2.1.317, when the person pasted a screenshot into a
prompt in the Claude terminal or dragged an image file in, NAW's conversation
showed only the text and [Image #1]. By the lane's account, a read-only probe
showed that the plugin's prompt block holds the image while the hook NAW used
sees only text. The plugin now sends that block's image pixels to NAW, keyed by
the prompt id and a tag of the text, and the workspace attaches them to that
prompt's row, including a prompt typed while Claude works; a row that has not
arrived yet is waited for within a limit. As agreed with Claude 3 under T-99,
the prompt row keeps its source, the two native prompt-input switches stay off
on 2.1.316 and 2.1.317, and turn linking and machine-input classification are
unchanged; 2.1.312 is unchanged and shows no second copy. The image is stored in
the local native image cache, as privacy.md now says.

Claude 2's lane reviewer asked for changes once, for the privacy note and for a
plugin reload that could attach an image to the wrong row; with rows found by
prompt id and text tag, the second round passed, and afterwards only a comment
changed. Lane evidence: the full suite passed 2,256 checks; six mutations fail
their tests; the native blocks script's new prompt-image mode types a prompt in
NAW's native terminal and pastes an image path through the terminal's own input,
without touching the clipboard, and failed before the change at the row with its
image on 2.1.317; nothing was run before the change on 2.1.316. After it, it
passed on real 2.1.317 and 2.1.316, and the default flow passed on 2.1.317;
re-picked onto main as 1749707 with identical changed lines, it passed 2,270
checks and the same runs. Open, low, an image can be lost but not misplaced: a
queued image prompt taken into the running turn, a NAW send with the same text
that runs first, a frame lost to a gap, and a plugin reload between the prompt
and its block. An image never goes to a prompt with different text or to another
session. The same text typed twice in one turn has one row, so the second one's
image shows on that row, and a different image that row already showed is then
marked as changed. Not run: an image prompt typed while Claude works, several
images in one prompt, images over 1 MB, and an image pasted from the clipboard;
the runs pasted a file path so the clipboard stayed untouched. The integration
reviewer also noted, from the source only: removing a session's records deletes
its prompt images as T-140 does for tool images; pasted screenshots now count
toward the 64 MB per-session cache, after which later images show as
unavailable; and images still waiting for their row are limited by count, at
most 8 prompts of 17 images in backend memory, not by time.

### A new session can join or create a collaboration space (T-115)

The person asked on 10-31 whether starting a session could join an existing
collaboration space or create one. Codex 2 proposed an optional 协作空间 field with
three choices, independent by default, join an existing space, or create a space
and join it; that proposal (A) was adopted on 10-31 under the board's 20-minute
rule rather than chosen by the person. Claude 2 implemented it on current main,
using Codex 2's uncommitted work only as a reference because it rested on a
translation layer main does not have and mixed in other wording. The steps run
in order, validation, the session, the new space if any, then the join; if a
step fails, what succeeded is kept, the dialog names the unfinished step and the
button becomes 仅继续加入, which only does what remains and never recreates the
session or space. A session or space that was written although its reply was
lost is adopted only when exactly one new one appears; the space-name adoption
was in Claude 2's first version and the lane review extended it to sessions; it
departs from the adopted proposal, which said a lost reply is never resolved by
guessing from a name or folder. The integration reviewer flagged the departure:
a session created at the same moment in the same folder, or a same-named space
from another window, could be adopted, and such a space is joined without a
further click. It is now part of the person's open question on the row. Closing
the dialog midway keeps what was created and stops the remaining steps. It works
with the automatic folder, a chosen folder, a Git working copy and skipping
permission prompts.

Claude 2's lane reviewer asked for changes once: a failure of the session
creation itself could create a second session, and no test covered it, and the
regression runs predated the final renderer; both were fixed, and the second
round passed. Lane evidence: the new create space choice GUI script ran the
whole journey with eleven checks passing, the unit suite passed 2,286 checks and
the session directory script passed; dialog lifecycle and navigation fail on
clean main as well (T-159). The integration reviewer also found, non-blocking:
when the session is created but the two state reads right after it both fail,
the session is not adopted and a retry creates a second one; after the dialog is
closed, or when the space was archived or the session is on an old backend, the
next-step text still suggests 仅继续加入; and in the adopted Git-copy case the
preview still asks to reselect the repository. Not covered, though sound in the
source: a lost join reply, and a lost space reply followed by a failed re-read.
Open for the person: with a space chosen, continuing an existing session or
taking over a Claude session cannot be combined yet; the dialog says to continue
first and then join from the session menu. The recommended A keeps that; B would
add it now; A applies under the 20-minute rule unless the person answers.

### Short empty polls of running commands

- Trigger/severity: P2 cost. In one weekly usage window, about 15% of the development agents' tool calls were empty waits of one second or less on a command that was still running. Each wait is a full model call over the whole context, and the team exhausted its weekly allowance in about three and a half days.
- Owner/status: Claude, rule-only change approved by the person: one sentence in the shared project rules (Test costs and instances) asks for one long wait that returns when the command exits, instead of repeated short polls. No product code or native settings changed. Agents apply it after rereading the rules at a safe checkpoint.
- Evidence/recheck: counts come from the agents' own local session records, with no model calls. Across four development agents, 121 waits of at least five seconds were measured. All 57 that saw the command exit returned at exit, before the full yield. The other 64 waited the full yield while the command was still running, and none of them received new output, so returning on output remains unverified. The measurements are from Codex sessions; the Claude side of the rule is untested. An independent read-only review approved the sentence and found no conflict with the existing polling-prompt and single-background-command rules. Reasoning effort and context length were also observed as large cost factors; they are native settings and were not changed.

## Codex startup refused before the new socket listens (T-156) — 2026-11-09

A full parallel run once failed `codex-host-recovery` with a raw `ECONNREFUSED` on the test's own `codex.sock`; single runs passed. Source finding: `startCodex` waited only for the socket file, which appears at `bind()`, before `listen()`. A server paused between the two refuses the first connection, so Codex startup failed. ## B3 fallback to the last qualified Claude version, checkpoint 2 (2026-11-10)

Dispatch B3: 「自动判不了时临时绑上一个已核验的版本，并说明怎么自动解除」; design decision 4: 「把会话钉在旧版本，只在自动核验判不了时临时回退」. Claude has no automatic comparison yet, so every new Claude version cannot be judged; this checkpoint builds the fallback for Claude. The Codex fallback is not built (one shared app-server serves every Codex session, so it needs its own design); B3 stays open for it.

When the launcher is a link into the vendor's `versions` folder and its version is not on the mod's qualified list, a session NAW starts uses the newest qualified version still installed beside it (`app/claude-pin.cjs`). A new session always may. A resumed one only when NAW's own launch record and the newest `version` in the end of the session's own transcript are both not newer than the fallback; a transcript NAW cannot find, or one naming no version, keeps the launcher, as does a fork picked in the native picker. This goes beyond the spec's "only new or rotated sessions": a session already on the fallback stays on it across a restart when nothing newer has run it. Running sessions are untouched; an exact program the person selected, or another install layout, is used as it is. The fallback lasts at most seven days per fallback version, counted in the persistent data directory, and ends by itself when a NAW update qualifies the new version, the vendor removes the fallback version (NAW returns to the launcher, never to a still older version), or the time passes. The session status names the version in use, the new version and the last day; the hover text says the session does not get the new version's features and fixes. A record that cannot be trusted means no fallback. A test keeps the host's list equal to the mod's managed native-blocks list. Automatic Codex decisions also moved to the data directory.

Author-run: unit tests cover each rule with fake programs; full suite 4114/0. One real-CLI trial under the loopback fixture (real Claude 2.1.322, launcher pointing at a failing unqualified stub): the session started with 2.1.322, bound as usual and showed the notice; no request reached the fixture. The first attempt failed only on the script's handling of the native trust prompt and is kept. The trial covers a new session only; resume, expiry and restart are covered by unit tests. A synthetic print-mode turn confirmed that transcript entries written by 2.1.322 carry `version`.

Independent read-only review (one session, three rounds): CHANGES (the clock was stored in the per-start socket folder and restarted with the service; removal of the fallback version moved NAW further down; a session resumed elsewhere by a newer version could be reopened by the older one), CHANGES (a transcript missing at the computed path counted as no outside writer), then PASS on `678bc1e`. Open: whether the seven days should run per fallback version (built) or per episode; the details are in the hover text only; a real-CLI resume is unverified.
## Reboot recovery when a lock PID is reused (2026-11-10)

Owner: service lifecycle author. Severity: startup unavailable. Base: `6a92546`.
After a reboot, a persisted PID can belong to a root helper or the newly launched
GUI. Previously both service locks treated that PID as their live owner and
refused startup. The two numeric-self-PID cold-boot reproductions fail on
`dbe02b7`, the main revision when reproduction began, and pass with this repair.
Later rebases brought the candidate to `6a92546`.

New locks record PID, process start time, role, canonical data directory and an
ownership token. Start time is read under a fixed locale and timezone. Numeric
legacy records use the live command and data directory; an unreadable or
ambiguous owner remains protected. Startup, service shutdown waiting and backend
switch waiting use the same birth identity. A release checks the file identity
and complete record before removing it. Both runtime and application payloads
include the helper, and fixture cleanup reads both record formats.

Author-run: both lock kinds recover with an actual unrelated root process whose
liveness probe returns EPERM. A real test-owned daemon paused with SIGSTOP stays
protected for both lock kinds and both old/new formats, retaining its record,
connection and process identity. Each kind of numeric lock naming the actual
GUI process also boots through normal main/service startup in a hidden isolated
source GUI. Both trials have zero sessions, dispatches and model calls, and their
owned processes and profiles are released. These GUI trials ran at `b6c430a`;
the final rebase to `6a92546` retains the later packaging entries. The full suite
passes 4306/4306 with no failures or skips at concurrency two. The UI build also
passes. An earlier full run caught a missing packaging entry and an unbuilt UI;
the repaired payload tests and subsequent full suites pass.

Independent read-only review approves the lock implementation with no blocker.
The source, real-process counterexamples and full-suite totals were inspected;
the tests remain author-run. This is a local candidate, not an installation or a
completed rollout. Product tests made no paid model requests. The daily
application and native parents were not stopped or restarted.

Legacy startup locks naming a GUI/Node process without a provable data directory
remain conservative, including a helper of the newly launched GUI. Such a
number-only record can still report that the service is connecting; new records
use process birth identity. Releases predating this lock format cannot read a
JSON lock left by an unclean exit, so rolling back to those releases can also
refuse startup. Recovery requires a compatible version or explicit operator
verification of a stale lock; the old release must not blindly remove it.
A moved/deleted recorded directory keeps the lock held while its PID is alive.
The change does not claim to make comparison plus unlink atomic against
arbitrary same-user writers, or to solve the separate memory investigation.
## Full-state pushes to a slow page exhausted memory (2026-11-10)

The person's machine panicked: the compressor's segments were full and the watchdog timed out. Before it, compressed memory that no process owned had grown from 4 GB to 38 GB in about forty minutes while nine sessions produced output, and quitting only the app's window released it; the next evening it grew from 3 GB to 25 GB in ten minutes and the same quit released it again while every backend kept running.

Source finding: each backend broadcasts its complete state after a change, and the main process forwarded every such event, with every session's messages, to the page with no bound.

Runtime evidence from a minimal Electron program outside this repository's code, measured as system anonymous memory plus compressor contents next to the program's own processes: a main process sends a 10 MB object every 35 ms for 12 s to a page that is alive but needs 250 ms per object. In three flood runs the system total rose 2.3 to 2.8 GB while the program's processes accounted for at most 0.26 GB and about 2.5 GB was unacknowledged, and it fell by 2.3 to 2.6 GB when the program quit. In three runs with one object in transit and the newest kept, at most 10 MB was unacknowledged and the change at quit was between a rise of 0.42 GB and a fall of 0.45 GB. The machine's own drift during a run was up to 1.8 GB, and readings a few seconds after quit moved by up to 0.9 GB either way, so only the size of the release at quit separates the two modes. An earlier run that sampled only compressed memory showed no release and is not comparable; a run before that never started the program. That the daily page was slow enough for this to be the cause of the 38 GB is inferred from the matching signature (memory that no process owns, released by quitting only the window), not measured in the daily app. In another agent's attempt a page that was fully stopped did not reproduce growth, and polling the backends from outside did not either.

Owner: the integrator, at the person's request. The repair bounds the push in `app/state-push.cjs`: once a window's page reports ready, one snapshot is in transit and only the newest later one waits; the page acknowledges after handling it. A page that has not reported ready, reloads or loses its process is sent state as before and is never held; a background window loads no document and is therefore never bounded. Independent review approved the first commit with notes; these were taken afterwards and re-reviewed: a snapshot counts as in transit only once its send returned, so a send that throws cannot hold the window; a second ready report keeps the bound; the reconnect refresh, the one other complete state sent to the page, discards an older waiting snapshot so nothing older arrives after it; a background window is not wired to a bound it could never arm. Declined: narrowing the load event that removes the bound, which is the same event that already resets the page's ready flag. Known and accepted: the page can miss a state that lasts less than one render (the 35 ms coalescing in the backend already allowed that), and one extra snapshot can be in transit for a moment at a reconnect. In an actual hidden window with a synthetic provider, 80 changes produced against a slowed page led to 26 numbered sends, all handled, and the last state rendered. Renderer-heap retention fixed earlier is a separate, smaller effect. Not covered: incremental state instead of full snapshots, and sending messages only for sessions on screen. Daily acceptance after install is the unowned-memory reading over a working day.

## Sends to background windows were the larger source of the unowned memory (2026-11-10)

The bound in the previous section was installed and did not hold: with seven sessions working, memory that no process owned rose from 4.5 GB to 16.9 GB in three minutes, and quitting only the window released it again. A four second sample of the main process during the rise showed its main thread idle about 61% of the time and handling backend socket reads about 37%; within those, roughly 200 of 3265 samples were serialising values for sends to a window, which the sample cannot attribute to a particular window. After the window was reopened the figure stayed near 4 GB for nine minutes, so the growth comes in episodes.

Source finding: workspace control creates one hidden window per agent session that has used it and keeps it until the app quits. That window owns the agent's connection and dialogs and never loads a document, yet the client wiring forwarded every state change, terminal chunk and progress line to it, and the broadcasts to all windows included it. Runtime evidence in the same minimal Electron program as before: 297 sends of 10 MB to a hidden window with no document raised system anonymous memory plus compressor contents by 2.3 GB while the program's processes accounted for 0.07 GB, there was no release beyond the machine's noise during an eight second hold (0.47 GB against noise of up to 0.9 GB), and 2.1 GB came back when the program quit. Observed in the daily app: the growth comes in episodes, does not drain, and ends with the window process. Inferred, not yet observed: that an episode starts when agent sessions first use workspace control after a window restart and scales with the number of background windows; the readings now record the number of backend connections of the window's main process, twelve per background window, so the next episode can confirm or refute this.

Owner: the integrator. Repair: one function, `sendToPage`, sends to a window's page and refuses a background window; the state push refuses it as well; the client wiring does not compute a display state for it. The remaining direct sends go to windows that always have a page. Correction to the previous section: the unbounded push to a slow ready page is real and now bounded, but it was not the main cause of the exhaustion, and the claim that it was is withdrawn. Not covered: each background connection still receives every backend's complete state over its sockets, which costs processing time in the main process but is owned memory, and the number of background windows grows with each distinct actor view until the app quits; daily acceptance is still the unowned-memory reading over a working day.

## B11 loopback fixture rollout: native-tools and native-retained-codex — 2026-11-10

**Nested sandbox (fact for every real-CLI script on the fixture).** On this macOS a process inside any restricting sandbox cannot start another one: `sandbox-exec: sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted`. Only an outer profile with no deny rule lets an inner one apply. Probed with the fixture's own policy as the outer profile, each of its rule groups alone, a stricter inner profile, and Codex 0.167.0's `codex sandbox macos` (exit 71). So inside the loopback fixture Codex cannot use its own seatbelt, and a change or command that Codex runs through it fails. A command that asks for escalation is different: probed on Codex 0.167.0 with its read-only sandbox, it asked (`item/commandExecution/requestApproval`), and once approved in the TUI it ran, wrote the file and returned its content. On the current host that pending command left no tool row in the shared record.

**native-tools** has two journeys, one per run. What was tried on Codex 0.167.0 inside the fixture: with Codex's read-only sandbox and `on-request`, the file change asks for approval but the approved change is not applied ("Failed to write file"); with Codex's sandbox off and `on-request`, the tools run and nothing asks. With `approval_policy = "untrusted"` in the config, Codex's backend did not start (one run); with `unless-trusted`, Codex reported an invalid configuration. `on-failure` and the granular policy load without an error and were not tried as a journey. The script keeps the file-change permission rather than a command permission, because its sharing rule is about the diff the person is asked about.
- Default: Codex's sandbox off in the script's private config. The fixed apply_patch and cat really run; the results reach the solo and shared readers and the native model input; the reply is published once. The fixture sandbox does not limit file writes: the writes are bounded by the fixed responses (two tool calls, both in the session folder, which is checked to be inside the owned base).
- `NAW_TOOLS_APPROVAL=1`: Codex's read-only sandbox. A real native file permission is asked, shown in the GUI, approved in the same-screen TUI. The shared diff freezes: the later reply stays private, and the frozen row stays exactly as it was when the person was asked, so the later failed write does not reach it. The run checks from the tool output returned to the model that the answer was an approval (Codex attempted the write). The applied file is not checked: the write fails inside the fixture.
- Both journeys then check the same things: the TUI shows the result, a reload and a service stop/resume add nothing to the shared record and send nothing, and the tool history is still there. In the approval journey the frozen diff and the private reply are checked again after the reload and after the recovery.
- The header label checked in the approval journey is now the interface-language text (等待确认); the old raw state name is no longer shown.
Both pass on real Codex 0.167.0 with two `/v1/responses` requests each and no credential violation.

**native-retained-codex** is ported to the fixture but was not run to the end, and the committed script stops at its version check on any Codex but 0.163.0. The observations below come from one local run with that check relaxed: the retained alpha.2 host started with Codex 0.167.0 inside the sandbox, ran its terminal task and attached its history with the same native id and pid, then met a product gate: a retained host's Codex replies are shared to a space on Codex 0.163.0 only (`app/legacy-codex.cjs` `sharedReplyAvailable`). 0.163.0 is not installed. The script keeps the exact 0.163.0 check, with that reason. Its tool step now uses one command with escalation that writes and reads the file, because a sandboxed apply_patch cannot run inside the fixture. Unverified until 0.163.0 is available: the whole flow after the gate, and in particular the check that a shared tool row is frozen when the permission is asked (before, the applied patch row satisfied it; a pending command may leave no shared row).

Not done in this batch: native-addressed and native-concurrent (real Claude and real Codex in one run: two fixtures, and a per-version decision for each assertion), native-retained-claude (needs Claude 2.1.302; 2.1.319, 321 and 322 are installed), native-history-existing (imports a history produced by test-native-codex-context.cjs, which is not ported, and reuses that script's unsandboxed shim and fixed port).

## B6 step 1, checkpoint A: the space records a delivery line and an emptied queue (2026-11-10)

Requested outcome: NAW notices by itself, without a model, when a member delivers and when a space has nothing left to send, so that this no longer depends on someone reading replies and the board. This checkpoint only records. A reply holding one whole line `READY <branch> <commit>` has the line validated and kept on the queue item; the space record gets one entry when the item becomes done, or when the person marks a waiting item handled. A queue that runs dry gets one entry from the write that took its last queued or sent item away. Both are saved in the same write as the queue change, before that write's own entry, so the decision notification still names the last entry.

Independent review, two rounds in one session, found nothing blocking. Reproduced and fixed from its notes: a queue that was already dry before this build got one stray entry when the person marked an old waiting item handled, because the first version asked only whether anything was left to send; an item added by an older build could leave a round unrecorded, because the round was raised when items were added; a stored line with a key from a later build would have made the queue unreadable; the entry's kind had the same name as the butler ledger's `queue-empty`, which is defined differently. The entry is now written only by the write that empties the queue, the space counts entries instead of additions, extra keys on a stored line are tolerated, and the kind is `queue-dry`. Two tests added for these fail on the first version.

## B6 step 1, checkpoint B: a space records a member that stays stuck (2026-11-10)

Requested outcome: when a member's interrupt does not take effect, or a native prompt waits for the person, the space shows it after five minutes and shows when it ended, without a model and without anyone watching from outside. On 2026-11-09 a sub-agent held an interrupted turn for 45 minutes; the session's status line said why, its space said nothing. The backend now remembers when such a wait began, sends state once more after five minutes if it is still on, and marks the session; the desktop writes one entry per mark in each space the session is a member of and one more when the mark is gone. Records only: nothing is stopped, answered, sent or notified.

Independent review, four rounds in one session. The first two asked for changes, all in how the backend decides that a session is waiting; each was reproduced by a test that fails on the earlier version. First round: the timer read the clock again when it fired and could decide, one millisecond short, that nothing was due, after which nothing asked again; a Claude prompt was never seen, because Claude reports it as a state and not as a request object, and the tests and the GUI fixture had used the path only Codex uses; a tool notice replaced the interrupt notice the rule depended on, so a wait was either never marked or ended in the record while the turn was still running. Second round: counting the approval state itself was too loose, because without the bridge that state lasts until the next hook, and an approved command running for five minutes would have been recorded as waiting. As built: the timer firing is what makes a wait due; a confirmation wait lasts exactly while a prompt is open (a Codex request that blocks, on a connected backend in a running turn; a prompt the Claude bridge reports; or more requests than can be shown); an interrupt wait follows the turn it was sent to, and for a session without a native turn identity ends at the native interrupt, a completion, or when the session stops working. What holds an interrupt is read when the mark is made, not from the status line. A space that is busy gets its entry at the next state; a sub-agent's name is cut to one line of 80 characters.

Owner: the author of this checkpoint. Evidence: 20 unit tests in `app/tests/stuck-records.test.cjs`; full unit checks 4532 pass, 0 fail; in a hidden window with synthetic members and no model, the stuck scenario passes in Chinese and English and the full queue journey still passes on the final version (the earlier checkpoint's scenario and the decision notification passed on the version before the last, which differs only in the Codex condition and the wording). Known limits: a Claude session without the bridge is never marked for a prompt; a bridge that registers again in the middle of a turn drops an interrupt wait tied to that turn; a prompt replayed after a gap, or belonging to another turn, is not counted; a session in no space gets no entry; a session deleted while marked never gets its end; a backend started before this change sends no mark. The GUI fixture sets the prompt on the synthetic runtime directly, so the GUI runs prove the desktop path and the unit tests prove the backend rule. Not done here: the version-gate case, and any use of these entries by the butler.

Measured with Claude alone in a plain terminal, inside the same sandbox policy, without NAW (five trials, no Enter, no model request): a key sent at about 55 ms selected Yes and was undone at about 153 ms (2 of 2); a key sent at 300 ms or 1.5 s stayed (3 of 3). After that pause one press was enough at every startup: 24 in runs 8, 11 to 18 and 20 to 28 (run 14's from its saved notes; there is no run 19).

**Not run:** Claude 2.1.309 to 311 (not installed). What ended the second Claude session of run 4 within 165 ms is not proven; an Enter landing after Claude's redraw fits it.
