## B3 option B: the mod's tests run in the background for an unqualified Claude version (2026-11-10)

The person, asked how Claude's side of B3 should go (A: keep the fallback and the manual qualification; B: also run `plugin test` automatically in the background and write the result into the verification record; C: let NAW quietly start a session of the new version offline): 「同意」 to the recommended A+B, recorded as 「Claude 侧走 A+B（回退＋人工核验＋后台自动跑 plugin test 写进核验记录），C 不做；Codex 回退先不做」. It serves the vision's approach, using every agent well through one entrance: a vendor update should cost the person as little of NAW's Claude support as possible, and the manual qualification that ends the fallback starts from a fact instead of from nothing.

When the launcher is a link into the vendor's `versions` folder and that version is not on the qualified list, NAW runs `claude plugin test` once with that version's own file, on a private copy of the mod's three files and four test files (`app/claude-mod-check.cjs`, called when a Claude session starts). The run is under `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`: no network or local socket, no keychain service, no write outside the run's own folder, no read of `~/.claude` or `~/.claude.json`; seven fixed environment variables with a private home and configuration directory; no input; the whole process group is ended after 60 seconds or when NAW closes. No session starts and no model is called. If the sandbox program is missing, or refuses the profile or the program, nothing runs. The record (counts, failed test names, the engine's message, or why the run did not happen) is `claude-mod-check.json` in the data directory, one per version, tied to a hash of the mod and its tests: a run that ended with an exit code is kept until a NAW update changes them; anything else is tried again after the next start. It decides nothing: the qualified list, the fallback and its clock are untouched, and an exact program the person selected or a dedicated butler service is not checked. The four test files travel in the package and are copied beside the mod in the daemon's runtime copy, so the folder a session loads is the same three files as before.

Limits. A pass means only that the engine calls those 40 tests reach still exist in that version; which of the mod's engine calls and events they reach is not measured. The record is a private file: the interface does not show it, and the service's log line is discarded in daily use. A configuration folder the person keeps outside `~/.claude` is readable by the run (nothing read can leave). If the service is killed during the one or two seconds of the run, nothing stops the sandboxed program.

Author-run, zero model calls: the module against the real Claude 2.1.319, 2.1.321 and 2.1.322 programs, 40 pass / 0 fail each in about a second; against a scratch copy of the mod with one engine call renamed, 3 pass / 37 fail with the engine's "is not a function" message kept. Unit tests use fake programs under the real sandbox; 21 single-line mutations of the module, the wiring and the runtime copy each make them fail (the first set let two through: a redundant condition, removed, and the once-per-start guard, now tested). Full suite 4619/0. The real-CLI trial (`scripts/test-native-claude-pin.cjs`: real Electron, normal service bootstrap, real Claude 2.1.322 under the loopback fixture, launcher at an unqualified stub that is the real program only for `plugin test`) passed on the final product head: the session ran the fallback, and the background check, from the copied runtime, recorded 40 pass / 0 fail; no request reached the fixture and no prompt was sent.

Found on the way, not caused by this change: four of the first five trial runs stopped at the native trust question, one of them with the background check removed. The retained service screen of one run shows the arrow key had been written to the native terminal and the choice had not moved; a question that has just appeared can drop a key. The trial now presses again only while the screen still shows the other choice, at most three times, and confirms only once Yes is shown selected; on a failure it keeps the service's own screen. Why the native program drops the key is not established.

Independent read-only review (one session, two rounds; the CLI reported the model as claude-opus-5-5): PASS on `19f7faf` (`2cd04b5` after the rebase onto `51fafd6`) with notes, taken: the sandbox allowed writes outside the home folder and reads of the Claude configuration (both now denied); a refusal by the sandbox itself was stored as a finished run (now retried); a comment and the guide said the result was logged; the final head had no passing trial (rerun). Then PASS on `413624d` (`932fb03` after the rebase) with notes, taken in a commit that changes only comments, the guide's wording and one test's readiness check: the guide names the two protected paths and the crash case, the close test waits for the program itself, and the mutation run was repeated on the commit. Not verified: the sandbox's message when a profile fails to apply; the read denial for the account's real home (testing it would read the real configuration).

## A backend's own program locations no longer leave it silently unable to run a provider (2026-11-10)

The person: 「为啥不把 agent 更新到最新」. The integrator found the command-line tools current, but the backend that took new sessions after an update kept its own `runtime-locations.json` naming a Claude and a Codex version the vendors had since removed; it reported both providers unavailable, the interface showed nothing, and Settings edits only the shared file. Dispatch: such an entry must be dropped or reported visibly when a backend restarts on a new runtime; "the backend predicted to become active can run both providers" must be a hard check before an update; a page on whether backends should pin versions at all; counter-case tests for an entry naming a missing file, an existing older version, and no entry. It serves the vision's "用好所有 agent": the agents a person reaches through NAW should be the current ones, and never unreachable without a word.

Built. When a backend starts, an entry of its own file whose program no longer exists is dropped (`backendLocations` in `app/runtime-locations.cjs`, called from `startService`), and the last twenty repairs are kept beside the file. A file left with no entry is no override, so the shared Settings file applies again. An entry whose program exists is kept. The shared file is never changed; a file that cannot be rewritten is used as it is; a file that cannot be read still stops the start and names itself, as before. A backend now resolves its programs on every initial state as well as before each session (`programAvailabilityV1`), so `available` is current. When the active backend cannot run Claude Code, Codex or Python 3, the combined snapshot carries `programWarning` and the alert line shows it in both languages; a change in Settings refreshes it at once. It is deliberately not part of `storageWarning`, which holds back image sends. `scripts/check-backend-programs.cjs` answers, read-only, whether a given backend could run all three after a start: its `ok` is the field for the update operator before an update, and `available.*` with the capability is the one after.

Limits. A running backend is not repaired: an own entry whose program disappears while it runs stays until its next start, and the alert's advice to look in Settings does not help in that one case. Own entries naming an existing older version are kept; whether to drop them too is with the person. The check assumes the PATH of an app opened from the Finder, and that the backend's folder is writable (a backend whose folder is not cannot start at all).

Author-run, no native program started and no model called: unit tests with fake programs, including a real start of NAW's own backend service with gone entries (both providers available afterwards, the file emptied, the repair recorded, and a program removed and restored while it runs seen at the next initial state); 22 single-line mutations each caught; full suite 4652/0. One hidden GUI run on real Electron: with a Settings selection for Codex that is gone, the alert shows the Chinese text, the English text after switching language, and goes when the selection is set back to automatic discovery; the same run with the Settings refresh removed fails at that last step. Two earlier suite runs are kept: one never finished (the new start test removed its folder before closing its backend), one had seven failures in existing tests whose fake hosts and source harness lacked the new call.

Independent read-only review (one session, two rounds; the CLI reported the model as claude-opus-5-5): CHANGES, then PASS on `58a3b16` (`4a66fdc` after the rebase onto `5033176`). Taken: a repair that could not be written stopped the start; the record was overwritten and written in place; the private conclusion page said Settings always clears the alert. Withdrawn by the reviewer after reading the earlier source: that an unreadable own file newly stops a start (it always did; now tested at the service start). Noted, not changed: resolving on every initial state lets an initial request change the resolved programs between a session's check and the shared Codex server's start, which matters only if the program changes in that window; the read-only check can pass for a backend whose folder is not writable.

The report now distinguishes the two named, unprobed Mach denials from complete DNS/keychain isolation, installed utility modules from mounted plugins, and the FIONREAD mechanism control from a GUI launchd positive control. Additional actual-run checks isolate the provider rejection, reject old payload/source references, and require ESRCH for owned host/MCP processes after cleanup. The fixture's README records the limits and reproducible command; private evidence stays outside Git.

## B6 integration handoff, checkpoint H1: the backlog record — 2026-11-10

**What this is.** `app/integrator-handoff.cjs` is the record NAW will keep about delivered work (a member's READY line) until the person's designated integrator has dealt with it. It is a source checkpoint: nothing in the app or its scripts loads it yet. It sends no message, merges nothing, takes no lock, starts no timer and calls no model; every effect is returned as data for a later caller.

**What it decides.**
- A delivery is stored once, by its key, also after its record was trimmed. Names and task text are labels: cleaned and shortened, never a reason to refuse the delivery.
- A newer delivery of a branch replaces an older one of the same space that is still waiting or held. An older one that is inside the open handoff is left to that handoff; if it leaves the handoff without an outcome (the send was refused, or it is held), it is void and is not handed again. Other spaces are not touched: the same branch name there may be another repository.
- A delivery is deliverable or held. A held one carries its reason and comes back only when the person retries it, retries its reason, or exactly that condition changes. No tick, restart, new delivery or other event brings it back.
- One handoff is open at a time, with at most 40 deliveries, oldest first. Deciding and recording are one step: a handoff opens only for the integrator and main head observed in that step, and its id includes how many handoffs were opened before, so an old decision cannot be replayed. It opens only when that session can take a message now by the same rule as a queue dispatch.
- With no integrator, or with the designated session gone from a complete session list, the person is to be asked once. A handoff that opens ends that question and releases what was held because that session was gone, so a later loss is asked about again.
- The handoff is recorded as sent before anything is sent. A refusal before sending is not a handoff; after the queue's limit of refusals in a row the deliveries are held for the person.
- Reasons are of two kinds. A standing condition (reviews off, the daily review amount used up, a lock held by an owner, no integrator, a full backlog) is asked about once for as long as it lasts; a retry puts deliveries back but does not end it; only the condition changing does. A later day releases what the review amount held, once per day, and keeps the unanswered question open. Every other reason is an event (an unverified merge, a missing record, an unconfirmed or refused send, no result line, an invalid checkpoint, a conflict, a task returned too often, another hold): it is over when nothing is held under it any more, by a retry or by a newer delivery, and the next failure of that kind is told again.
- Telling the person about a reason is recorded in three steps (pending, started, done). One not yet started is still due after a restart. One started but never confirmed is left unknown, is not sent again and can be listed in a report: after a crash at that moment the person may get no notice, never two.
- The handoff message starts with its own marker, not the queue's. It lists each delivery with its labels in quotes and says they are not instructions; it says whether reviews are off, on or used up for the day and what to answer in each case; it names the reasons a HELD line may use, `stale-commit` for a RETURNED line, and the full lock command with the handoff id.
- An unreadable or unsafe record stops everything and is left as it is. A save that fails stops the backlog too; the record on disk is then the last saved one (tested for a failure before anything is written; if only the final folder sync failed, the new record is already in place). A change that would make the record larger than the next start accepts is refused and nothing is written. A full backlog refuses a new delivery instead of dropping one, and the person is told once for as long as it stays full. A newer delivery of a branch already waiting still gets in, because it replaces one; that leaves the backlog as full as it was and does not end the condition. Only real room does, and filling up again after that is a new occurrence. The refused delivery itself is not kept here (it stays recorded in its space). Finished outcomes beyond the last 200 are trimmed by when they ended, and their keys are remembered.

**Checks.** Twenty-four unit tests on synthetic records, no model. Thirty-three deliberate breakages of the module each turned tests red. The full unit suite passes with the new files.

**Independent review, first round: not passed.** Two blocking findings, both fixed and tested: an older delivery could be handed again after a newer one of its branch had arrived (it stayed inside the open handoff and came back from a refused send or a hold); and a handoff decision could be replayed, because opening took a plan from outside and checked only its shape. Other findings fixed: the message asked for a review without saying reviews are off by default and gave no reason names; a reason could stay open with nothing under it and silence the next real occurrence; a save could write a record the next start refuses; a bad name lost the whole delivery; a handoff naming one delivery twice loaded; a long lock owner could not be cleared; missing tests, including a failed save.

**Independent review, second round: passed.** Both blocking findings closed. Four further points fixed afterwards and tested: opening a handoff ended the missing-integrator question without releasing what was held under it; a task returned too often never ended as a reason; a retry could end the full-backlog condition and so notify twice; and the test of that condition ending did not test it. Also taken: only a later calendar day counts as a new day; labels cannot carry NAW's own markers; the lock owner in the command is quoted.

**Independent review, third round: not passed, one finding from the fix above.** Letting a replacing delivery into a full backlog also ended the full-backlog condition, so the next refusal told the person a second time although the backlog had been full throughout. Fixed: only a delivery that found real room ends it. Also from that round: outcomes are trimmed by when they ended, not by when their deliveries arrived, and a day that does not exist is refused.

**Not in this checkpoint.** Settling a handoff from the integrator's reply, checking a MERGED line against git and registering an installable main commit (H2); until then a sent handoff that is never confirmed keeps the one place taken. Sending the message, space records, the person's actions, notifications, the integrator's designation record and watching the lock's release records connect the module to shared files and come after H2, each with its own claim. The repository rule that members end a delivery with a READY line is not written yet either.

**Left open, with what would trigger work.** One process must own the record: two instances on one file would overwrite each other, which the connection has to rule out. Open standing conditions are not capped in number (many different lock owners or integrators that never clear): the size check then refuses changes rather than writing a bad record. A delivery refused by a full backlog is not fed back automatically. Deliveries carry no repository: which repository a READY belongs to is decided when the module is connected.

**For the connection later.** Only the code that just saw a send refused may report the refusal; an unconfirmed send found after a restart is not one. The queue's `replyAfter` counts a user row as the person's unless it carries an automatic origin or one of two markers; the handoff message must be sent so that its own row counts as automatic, or every handoff would look like the person intervened.

## A session opened under a creation grant can receive work (B5 prerequisite, 2026-11-11)

Requested outcome: a session an agent opens under the person's creation grant should not sit unused. Until now it was created within the grant's quota and then left alone: in no space, so no queued work could reach it. A grant may now name one space, chosen by the person. The backend, whose quota gate and caller check are unchanged, lists a session created under such a grant until the desktop has placed it; the desktop joins it to that space, writes one entry there and saves the result. Ordinary dispatch then sends it queued work. The opener's task is still not delivered or queued, as the tool's description and the person's consent text say; only the person or the secretary adds queue items. A grant without a space joins, records and sends nothing, as before. Three things differ even then, in data only: the result of `workspace_open` and the operator row built from it always carry `space` and `placement`, both empty; the policy carries an empty list of placements; and each state event in a person's window runs the placement step, which finds nothing listed and does nothing.

Independent review, five rounds in one session; the first asked for changes. Blocking: the placement still went ahead when the person revoked the grant, or turned the interface off, after the session was created but before it was placed. A placement is now offered only while the grant is in force (not revoked, not expired, the interface on for everyone and for this initiator, the initiator present), and the desktop asks the journal that owns the action before every attempt. The first version also queued the task when the opener was the secretary; the review pointed out that this contradicted the unchanged tool description and consent text, and since a secretary can already queue an item for a member itself, that path was removed. From the notes: an agent's context is refused, before any confirmation is shown, for a grant that names a space and for both placement calls, and only a person's window runs the step; archiving is checked on the desktop, which owns that list; a session the person has already put elsewhere is left there; the join carries the placement it acted on, so a move made in between fails it and is not undone; a session already in the space is not joined twice; retries are seconds apart with one timer each, not one per state event, and after the last one the space gets a visible entry that the session could not join; a result is saved truthfully even if the grant ended in the middle of the join.

Owner: the author of this change. Evidence: 18 unit tests in `app/tests/open-placement.test.cjs` with a real backend journal and space store and the function from the main process (the join itself replaced by a recorder), all failing on the unchanged code; full unit checks pass with no failures; in a hidden window with synthetic members and no model, a session opened within quota joined the named space through the real join and was sent the waiting queue item within seconds, a second open over quota created nothing, and repeating the same action repeated nothing, in Chinese and English; the stuck scenario, the full queue journey and the operator interface script still pass. The field on the grant form by which the person chooses the space is the next section; what is for the person to decide is listed there. Known: the error text an agent receives says "only you", meaning the person; if saving a refusal such as "space unavailable" itself fails, the last attempt saves it as a refused join; an entry that says the session could not join stays if the person later drags it in. Not covered: the steward's own identity and quota, archiving within quota, and telling the person when a new session has not received work after ten minutes.

## The person chooses, in the grant form, the space new sessions join (B5 prerequisite, second step, 2026-11-11)

Status: built and independently reviewed; agreed by the person on 2026-11-11. This step was the first question left to the person, whether the grant form should offer the space new sessions join. The integrator recommended merging it, and the person answered that the recommendations could be followed (「其他的貌似可以按你推荐的来」).

Requested outcome: the person, and nobody else, chooses the space a grant names. The grant form in the pending-authorization card now lists the person's open spaces, the same list the sidebar shows, and starts at "None (create only, as before)". With none chosen, the consent sentence and the request that saves the grant are what they were. With a space chosen the person ticks under a different sentence, which names the space and says that the sessions created join it as members and are sent the work queued there; choosing or changing the space clears the tick, since it is a different consent. A space that was archived or removed after it was chosen is not saved: the person chooses again. A saved grant's summary names the space and says when it is archived or gone. The row of a created session says what the desktop did with it: joining, joined, or not joined and why.

A second independent review of the first step, asked for by the integrator in a separate read-only session, found nothing blocking and four notes, all done here. The saved journal is checked for the shape of a grant's space (a space id) and of a placement result (exactly the fields the journal writes, for a created session, into the space its grant names); a journal that fails disables the interface, as any other invalid record does. The operator row shows the placement result. The record of the first step no longer says "exactly as before" and lists what differs in data. The retry count of a placement that is no longer listed is dropped.

Independent review of this step, three rounds in the session that reviewed the first step; no blocking finding in any round. The first confirmed that no path saves a grant with a space unless the tick was made under the sentence naming it (changing the choice, a language switch, a redraw, a rename, an archived or missing space), that the default request is unchanged, and that nothing here lets an agent choose or influence the space; from its notes, the consent sentence now says the sessions join "as members", and an archived space is marked as archived in the summary. The second confirmed that the new journal checks cannot refuse a journal this code writes; its one note, that dropping a retry count the moment it is unlisted could restart the tries when one of the person's windows briefly lacks a backend another window lists, is done: a count is dropped only a minute after its last delay. The third round confirmed that change.

Owner: the author of this change. Evidence: unit tests on the form, the summary and the row (`app/tests/operator-ui.test.cjs`) and on the saved-record checks and the retry counts (`app/tests/open-placement.test.cjs`); the two for the journal and the counts fail on the first step's code; full unit checks pass with no failures; in a hidden window with a synthetic backend and no model, the person's path through the real form in Chinese and English: the select starts at none under the old sentence, choosing the space clears the tick and the sentence names it, the form does not submit without the tick, and after it exactly one session is created, joined to the chosen space and recorded there, the row says it has joined, and a second open over quota creates nothing; the older operator journeys and the open scenario still pass in both languages.

For the person to decide, with what the reviews asked to be said. First, whether this field should exist; without it the first step stays unused. If it exists: when the opener is the person's secretary, the secretary can add queue items in that space for the session it has just opened, which is the secretary's existing power but together with this field lets one agent both open a session and give it work; once placed, the new session could in principle report what it saw in the space to an opener outside it, which is unlikely because neither the task nor the ids it would need are delivered to it; and when the person has already put the new session elsewhere, the named space still gets an entry with the session's and the opener's names although the session is not a member. Second, whether an opener's task should enter the queue, which would also change the tool's description and the consent text.

Known: two spaces with the same name look the same in the select, as they do in the sidebar. The card is drawn again only when its own record changes, so a space created while the form is open is not offered until then. The older labels of this card that kept the earlier language after a switch are fixed separately (the section on the operator card's language below); the new field, sentence and lines follow the language from the start.

## B6 integration handoff, checkpoint H2: settling a handoff — 2026-11-10

**What this adds.** `app/integrator-handoff.cjs` can now settle the open handoff from the integrator's reply, and `app/integrator-git.cjs` answers the questions about git that this needs. Both are still not connected: nothing in the app or its scripts loads them, and a test says so. The handoff module still runs no program; it asks git through a reader the caller passes in. The reader only reads (rev-parse, merge-base, rev-list, log, patch-id). It runs git without the person's configuration, with the worktree helper's switches and a few of its own, so a repository's hooks, diff and text drivers, file monitor, signature program and grafts take no part, and a change of a submodule is read as its two commit ids without running git inside the submodule; test repositories that set up each of these show it. The reader does not judge the repository it is pointed at (its includes, alternates or linked metadata): choosing and checking the repository belongs to the step that connects it. Two existing files changed by one export line each: `app/queue-dispatch.cjs` (`startsWithDecision`, `UNCONFIRMED_SEND_MS`) and `app/git-worktree.cjs` (`controls`, `gitEnvironment`).

**When a handoff settles.** By the queue's own times and fall-backs: a send never confirmed fails after the queue's wait and is not sent again; an integrator that was replaced or revoked, or whose session is gone from a complete list, fails the handoff; a designation that could not be read is not a revocation and decides nothing; while the integrator works or has not been idle long enough nothing happens; no record of a reply fails it; the person typing after the handoff, or taking control, makes it wait; an empty reply makes it wait. Otherwise the integrator's answer is its last message that reads like one: it has a line that begins like a result, or it asks the person to decide. An answer whose lines cannot be read is still the answer; its deliveries then have no result. The first line of the answer decides between done and a decision for the person, and its lines are read. A closing remark after the answer loses nothing, and a line from an earlier message, written while the integrator still worked, is not mixed in.

**What the reply's lines do.** One line per delivery, named by the delivery's own commit. Backticks, asterisks, a list mark or a number in front, a colon after the first word, extra spaces and one final full stop are tolerated; a quoted line is not read; the last line about a delivery counts. A line that begins like a result but cannot be read, or whose commit names none or several deliveries, is counted as ignored.
- MERGED counts only if git confirms three things and every test passed: the named commit is on main now; it was not on main when the handoff began; and every commit the delivery holds relative to that earlier main is among what was merged up to the named commit, as the same commit (a fast-forward) or as a commit with the same change (a cherry-pick). So the named commit must be one that holds the whole delivery. The verdicts carry the handoff and the main head they were made for, and a verdict counts only for the commit its line names. Otherwise the delivery is held as an unverified merge and is not handed again by itself. A MERGED line that cannot be read is still a claim and is never taken as merged.
- RETURNED is recorded with its reason and reported as a suggestion to redo the work; nothing is added to any queue. After more than two returns of one branch of a space the person is asked once instead.
- HELD keeps the delivery under the named reason. The reason is the first word of what the integrator wrote, so a comment after it does not change it; the whole text is kept as a note. The standing conditions (reviews off, the daily amount used up, a lock held by an owner) and an invalid checkpoint do not keep the handoff's place: the handoff is done and later deliveries go on. A conflict line in a reply that does not ask the person is held under that handoff's own conflict. Any other reason is kept as "held for another reason".
- A delivery without a line is handed once more by itself, then held.
- When the reply asks the person to decide, the handoff always waits and keeps the one place until the person resolves it, whatever its lines say, and the question is kept. Deliveries with lines get their outcome; those without a line, and those the integrator held for the conflict itself, stay inside the handoff, with what it wrote about the conflict kept as a note. The question is kept in the queue's short form. The person ends it with "handoff dealt with", or with a retry on its reason in the list of open questions, which is the same retry: what is inside may be handed again. Without a retry it stays held.
- A failed handoff holds all its deliveries under the failure.
- Waiting without a reply tells the person once, because it holds the only place. The person's own typing is recorded but not announced to them.
- A delivery inside a handoff cannot be held or retried from outside it; it leaves through the settlement, a refused send, or the person resolving the handoff. A result that the reply reader could not have produced is refused and nothing is recorded.

**Installable main.** A settlement in which at least one merge was verified registers one question: the main head that now holds it may be installed. It is keyed by that commit, so the same head never registers twice; an older question that is still open is closed, because main has moved on. This reads the spec's "once per main commit" as once per batch's resulting main head, not once per MERGED line. The question ends only with the person's answer; so does the question about a branch returned too often.

**Independent review, round 1 (not passed, then changed).** One blocking finding: a retry on the reason a waiting handoff waits on, or a hold of a delivery inside it, could leave the one place taken with no question open. Both are closed: the retry now ends the handoff as "handoff dealt with" does, and a hold of a delivery inside a handoff is refused. Six further findings were changed as described above: the verdicts are tied to their handoff and to the named commit; numbered and listed lines, comments after a reason, and lines in an earlier message are read; a reply that asks the person always waits; the reader no longer runs a repository's signature program, no longer takes a branch named like a short commit id for that commit, and takes a change's id from the bytes of its patch; the named commit must hold the delivery; an unread designation is not a revocation.

**Independent review, round 2 (passed, with one more finding, then changed).** The reviewer found the blocking finding closed and reasoned that a submodule shown as a diff would still run that submodule's own programs; a real superproject with such a submodule confirmed it, and the reader now reads a submodule change as its two commit ids. From its notes: a grafts file no longer changes what the reader answers; the answer is one message, as described above, instead of every message after the handoff; a colon after the first word is read; the text of a conflict line kept inside a waiting handoff is kept; the "not connected" test now scans the app's subfolders and the scripts. A third, short round passed and asked for one more change, made: a final answer whose lines cannot be read is still the answer, so an earlier line cannot stand in for it.

**Checks.** Fifty-five unit tests for the backlog, the settlement and the reader. The three questions to git are tested with fixed answers for each way they can fail, and against a real temporary repository: a fast-forward, a cherry-pick onto a main that moved, and a fast-forwarded branch that holds a merge commit are verified; a partial merge, a commit already on main at the start, a commit not on main, an unknown commit, a new main commit that does not hold the delivery, a delivery with nothing to merge and a different change under the same file name are not. One test takes the real reader through the verdicts and the settlement together. Thirty-three deliberate breakages of the first version, twenty-eight of the first round's changes and nine of the later rounds' each turned tests red. The full unit suite passes on the delivered head; the count is in the delivery note.

**Not in this checkpoint.** Everything that connects the module: sending the handoff, writing space records, notifications, the person's actions (retry, handoff resolved, answer), the integrator's designation record, the lock's release records, and choosing and checking which repository and main branch the reader looks at. The mapping of reasons and questions into the steward's ledger is also later.

**Left open.**
- A delivery handed a second time after the person's retry does not get another automatic re-hand when it has no line again.
- A delivery whose branch holds a merge commit is verified only when it was fast-forwarded; cherry-picked, the merge commit has no single change to find again and the delivery ends as an unverified merge. So does a delivery that was already on main when the handoff began.
- A change that was merged and reverted again during the handoff still verifies.
- The install question names the main head the checks were made for, which may also hold commits from outside the batch.
- Result lines spread over several messages are not put together: only the last message that has one is read, and a delivery named only in an earlier message is handed once more. If that delivery was in fact merged, the second handoff begins with it already on main, so it then ends as an unverified merge and the person is told. A decision asked in an earlier message is dropped when a later message answers with result lines, as the last message decides for a queue item; conflict lines in that answer still tell the person once.
- A lock owner's label is read up to a bracket or a comma. A branch or tag named like a short commit id makes that short id unusable; the full id still works.
- If the integrator's session is rotated during a handoff, the handoff fails as "integrator missing" for the old session; the connection must treat the successor as designated.

## B6 integration handoff, checkpoint H3: the person designates the integrator — 2026-11-11

**What this adds.** A private record, `integrator.json` in the app's data folder, names the one session the person designated as integrator (`app/integrator-role.cjs`). It is written like the queue secretary's record: one session with its native id, readable by the owner only, saved atomically, and after a session rotation it follows the written rotation log to the successor by the secretary's own rule. A record or log that cannot be trusted is an error, never "nobody designated". The record names a session and nothing else: it grants no tool, no queue power and no permission, and nothing is sent to the integrator yet. The handoff backlog and the git reader are still not connected.

**Who may set it.** Only the person. The entry in the main process (`integrator`) refuses any call that comes from an agent's background operation, in its own first line, because the general background gate is a fixed table that has no row for this method. The person's call designates a session, replaces the earlier one, or clears the designation with `null`. A session is accepted only when it has a native id and is not archived, ended, in the background or still waiting for its native context, and only when it is in no collaboration space: a member of a space is sent queue work, which an integrator must not get. Whether a session is archived is read from the desktop's own record, because the backend's list does not say. Every window is told after a change. The app's state carries the designation; if the record cannot be read, the storage warning says so.

**Where the person finds it.** In a session's own menu in the sidebar and in the header menu of the selected session: "Use as integrator (merges delivered work)" on a session outside every space, "Revoke integrator" on the designated one, wherever it is by then. A space member, an archived session and a session without a native id are not offered the action; the terminal's own menu does not carry it; a disconnected menu shows it disabled. A revoke from a menu opened before the designation moved does nothing, so it cannot revoke the session designated since; the header menu ignores any action once the designation changed, and a row menu closes when its actions change.

**Checks.**
- Unit: the record (six tests), the real `register` wrapper and the real entry taken from `main.cjs` (five tests: the person designates, replaces and revokes; an agent can do neither, whoever it is and whatever it names; a space member or an unusable session is refused and the earlier choice stays, among them a session archived the real way, which the backend's list does not mark; a failed save is reported and nothing is announced; the wiring), and the two menus (three tests). Thirty deliberate breakages each turned tests red.
- Real window, zero model: `scripts/test-sidebar.cjs` designates a session from its menu, sees both windows' state and menus follow, replaces it with another, revokes it, designates again and finds the designation after a reload and a whole-app reopen; the record on disk is private. `scripts/test-session-menu.cjs` shows a space member is not offered the action, an ended session is refused in words with nothing saved, and the header menu carries the action.
- The packaging list names the new module; the packaging guard test would otherwise fail.

**Independent review (passed, with one finding, then changed).** The refusal of an archived session never fired in the real app: the entry asked the backend's list, which does not mark archived sessions, and the test's fake backend marked them. The entry now reads the desktop's record, and the test archives a session the real way. The secretary's entry has the same line and the same gap from before this checkpoint; it is recorded for its owner, not changed here. The reviewer also confirmed that an agent's read of the state does not carry the new field (the background projection is an allow-list), and that the only way an agent's action arrives as the person's is computer use in the person's own window, which holds for every person-only action.

**Left open.**
- A session that is a member only of an archived space is refused until it is taken out of that space.
- A session that is designated and afterwards put into a space keeps the designation, and its menu still offers the revoke. The step that connects the backlog must not hand anything to an integrator that is inside a space, and must tell the person once.
- Nothing shows who the integrator is except that session's own menu. A visible mark is for the step that shows handoffs in the space record.
- The record is read on every state snapshot, as the secretary's is.

## B6 integration handoff, checkpoint H4: handing out — 2026-11-11

**What this adds.** `app/integrator-engine.cjs` carries out the steps between the handoff record and the app: it takes in the deliveries NAW recorded in spaces, and when the session the person designated as integrator can take a message it opens one handoff and sends it. Everything it touches is passed in (the record, who is designated, a fresh look at the sessions, main's head, the send), so it calls no model, runs no program, merges nothing and takes no lock. It is not connected: nothing in the app or its scripts loads it, and a test says so. Settling a handoff from the engine and telling the person are the next checkpoint.

**Taking deliveries in.** A delivery is the READY fact NAW writes into a space when a queue item is done. The engine takes a fact only from the space that recorded it and only in the shape NAW writes; anything else is passed over and counted. The first intake sets the record's starting line, once: a delivery recorded before it was dealt with by hand and is never handed out. A fact already known writes nothing. A delivery keeps the time it was recorded, so its age is its real age. A full backlog takes nothing in and tells the person once; the delivery is taken in on a later pass when there is room.

**Handing out.** One pass does this, in order.
- While a handoff is open, nothing.
- It reads who is designated. A designation that cannot be read decides nothing. Nobody designated, the designated session gone from a complete list, or the integrator found inside a space each ask the person once and hand out nothing; an integrator inside a space is a new condition in the record, over when the integrator takes a handoff.
- It asks the record whether a handoff would open, by the queue's own readiness rule and waits, without reading git or recording anything.
- Only if one would open, or if deliveries held because an integrator was gone may come back, it takes a fresh look. Everything from there is decided on that fresh view: a designated integrator whose session is present releases what was held for a missing integrator; main's head is read only if a handoff still opens; the decision and its record are one step. If the moment has passed, or the head cannot be read, no handoff is recorded.
- The handoff is recorded as sent before the message goes out, and the message goes out once. A tag confirms it, with the control revision of the session the message went to, so that the person taking control afterwards is noticed when the handoff settles. A refusal in which nothing was sent lets the deliveries wait again, and the fifth in a row holds them for the person; a refusal because the person left a prompt unsent in that session is not counted, as for a queue item, and the caller is told so that it leaves the session alone for a while. A send whose outcome is unknown is never repeated: the handoff stays unconfirmed and is later settled as such, also after a restart.

**Additions elsewhere.** The record gains its starting line, three read-only looks that copy nothing, and the uncounted refusal. The git reader can read the head of a local branch by its exact ref; a tag or another ref that only looks like the branch is not the branch. `app/queue-dispatch.cjs` exports one more name, the key of the unsent-prompt refusal.

**Independent review (passed, with two findings, then changed).** The control revision came only from the send's return value, so a send that returns just a tag would have switched off the later check for the person taking control; it now falls back to the session's own. The release of deliveries held for a missing integrator was decided on the older view, which could tell the person twice about one absence; it is now decided on the fresh look. From the notes: the caller is told when the person is at work in the integrator's session, so a handoff is not opened and refused on every pass; the caller can see that the record is unreadable; a starting line must be a real time; the branch is read by its exact ref; another native session under the integrator's id is treated as the integrator being gone, whatever its membership says.

**Checks.** Fourteen unit tests for the engine, one of them fed by the fact the real space record writes for a finished queue item; one more for the record's additions and one for the reader's. Thirty-eight deliberate breakages each turned tests red. The full unit suite passes on the delivered head; the count is in the delivery note.

**Left open.**
- The starting line compares times: a delivery recorded while the clock was set back before the line is passed over.
- Which repository and which branch "main" is are chosen by whoever connects the engine; here they are a function passed in. The send is passed in too: whoever connects it must make sure that an error the send can raise after the message reached the session never carries one of the queue's "not sent" keys.
- A question for the person, and the release just described, are recorded although the integrator cannot take a message at that moment; a handoff never is.
- An integrator that is put into a space while a handoff is open still has that handoff settled normally.
- Space records of a delivery being handed out, and the notices for the questions above, are written by the next checkpoint from the record's own state.

## B6 integration handoff, checkpoint H5: settling and telling through the engine — 2026-11-11

**What this adds.** The engine (`app/integrator-engine.cjs`) can now settle the open handoff and tell where things stand. It is still not connected. The space-record writer, the notice and the git reader are passed in, like everything else it touches.

**Settling.** The engine asks the record whether the open handoff can be settled now, by the rules of checkpoint H2. A settlement that needs no git (a failed handoff, no reply, the person's own typing, an answer without a readable merge line) is recorded at once. An answer that reports merges is checked first: main's head is read, git is asked through the reader, and because that takes a moment the answer is then read again on a fresh look and settled only if the record plans exactly the same; otherwise nothing is settled on that pass. If main's head cannot be read (nothing comes back, or something that is not a full commit id), the answer waits, for at most ten minutes from when that was first seen for this handoff; the first time is kept in the record, so a restart or a newly built engine does not begin the wait again. After that it is settled without git: its merges are held for the person under their own reason, "main could not be read", which is NAW's trouble with git and not a failed claim, instead of the one place staying taken in silence. A merge line that cannot be read stays an unverified claim either way.

**Telling the spaces.** Each delivery carries the label of what its space was last told (handed out in which handoff, waiting for the person, held for which reason, merged as which commit, returned). When the label a delivery should have differs, the engine has its space record written and then marks it. A crash in between writes the same record again, with the same key and label, so the writer can recognise the repeat. A space always ends up saying where the delivery stands now; a state that was passed through between two tellings (handed out, then merged before anything was told) is not told. The writer may answer at once or later and is waited for; if it fails, the records written so far are kept as written and the rest follow on a later pass, in order.

**Telling the person.** One notice per reason, in three steps kept in the record: not yet told, started, told. A notice that fails while being shown, or a crash between "started" and "told", leaves it started: it is not shown again and is reported as unknown. A notice says how many deliveries the reason concerns and where the first was delivered, never their text; for a handoff that waits it names the integrator's session, where its question can be read. The person's own typing in the integrator's session is recorded but not announced to them.

**One pass.** Take in, settle, hand out, tell, in that order, so the place a settled handoff leaves can be taken in the same pass. A record that cannot be read stops the pass and says so to the caller, together with what the pass had done by then. Any other failure in the first three steps still lets the telling happen, so a notice does not wait for an unrelated fault, and is then given to the caller with what was done.

**Independent review (passed, with three findings, then changed).** The space-record writer was not waited for, so a writer that fails later would have lost its record; it is awaited now. A head that came back as text but not as a commit id skipped the wait; only a full commit id counts as read. The ten-minute bound lived in the engine object, so a caller building a new engine on every pass would never have reached it; the first time is kept with the handoff in the record. From the notes: the distinct reason for an unreadable main; what a pass did before it stopped is given to the caller; the telling still happens when settling fails for another reason. The reviewer also confirmed the changes made after its review of checkpoint H4.

**Checks.** Eleven unit tests for these parts (twenty-five with the hand-out tests). Thirty-three deliberate breakages each turned tests red. The full unit suite passes on the delivered head; the count is in the delivery note.

**Left open.**
- A notice for a question (a main commit that may be installed, a branch returned too often) or for a waiting handoff with nothing left inside carries a count of zero; whoever connects the engine must word those notices by their reason, not as "nothing to do".
- A clock set back lengthens the wait for main's head by that much.
- Which space record is written for each label, and which notice, belong to the step that connects the engine.
- The record is written once more for each notice shown and for each batch of space records.

## B6 integration handoff, checkpoint H6a: the words — 2026-11-11

**What this adds.** The sentences a delivery's space and the person are given about an integration handoff, in Chinese and English, and the writer that puts a delivery's state into its space. Nothing is connected yet: no code path produces a handoff in the app, so none of these sentences can appear.

**Which sentence.** `app/integrator-words.cjs` only maps. Each reason has the sentence that fits what the person does next. The three troubles with the message itself are told apart: sent but never confirmed; refused several times before it was sent (automatic messages may be off); delivered, but the reply could not be read (look in the integrator's session). One delivery without a result line is "no result for it"; no answer at all is its own sentence, and its notice says why it matters: the waiting handoff holds the only place, so later deliveries wait. A space record has one sentence for handed out, merged, returned, fifteen for on hold and four for waiting for the person (one of them without a cause, for a reason that has no waiting sentence); it names the delivery by its task label, or by its branch when it has none. A reason from a later version still gets a sentence, showing the integrator's own words or the reason's name. A notice says how many deliveries a reason concerns; it is built from the record's notice information, which holds no task text. A waiting handoff with nothing left inside is worded as a question in the integrator's session, not as "0 deliveries". The person's own typing has no notice.

**Writing the space record.** `RoomState.recordHandoff` writes one record per delivery and state into the space that delivered it, with a key made of the delivery and its label; the same key again writes nothing, also after a restart, which is what the engine's telling relies on after a crash. A space that no longer exists has nothing to write to and does not hold up the records of other spaces; a space that is being updated refuses for now and is tried again.

**Independent review (passed, with three wording findings, then changed).** A reply that could not be read was worded as a message that was never delivered, which could lead the person to hand out work that is already merged; a refused send was worded as unconfirmed, although the next step is to turn automatic messages back on; the notice for no reply did not say that the handoff holds the only place. Each has its own sentence now. A waiting reason without a sentence no longer falls back to "met a conflict". The reviewer also confirmed that the renderer shows these records as ordinary system notices and that no other reader of space records takes them for its own kind.

**Checks.** Five unit tests: every reason kind of the record has a sentence group (the list is read from the record's own source); each sentence in both languages; the notices; the writer against a real space record, including the repeat, a second space, a missing space and a space being updated. Eighteen deliberate breakages each turned tests red. The packaging list names the new module. The full unit suite passes on the delivered head; the count is in the delivery note.

**Left open.**
- English notices put the count after a colon so that one and many read the same.
- Several notices say what happened but not yet what to do, because the person's actions (retry, open reviews) do not exist yet; they are to be reworded when those actions are added.
- The notice about a branch returned too often names the branch, not its space.
- A space that is being updated, or a spaces file that cannot be read, holds back the later records of that pass until it can be written again.
- A space record names the delivery's task label; it is written into that delivery's own space only.
- Which notification is raised, and what a click reveals, belong to the step that connects the engine.
### B2-TRUST-2 / 1: bounded directory-trust wait — 2026-11-11

Requirement: an ignored native trust prompt must not park the original queue and the sole rotation slot forever. The production main process forwards `NAW_QUEUE_DIRECTORY_TRUST_TIMEOUT_MS` independently from the still-closed migration gate. A positive decimal safe integer sets milliseconds; missing or invalid values use 600000. Ten minutes reuses the established `NEW_SESSION_READY_MS` startup budget rather than introducing a longer unmeasured human-response allowance. Configuration is read at main startup; it applies to the original persisted `trustWaitingAt` after restart.

At the deadline the waiting rotation enters the existing failed cleanup path. Only the unused successor is passed to the native stop API; queued ownership returns to the original, and the failed record no longer occupies an active rotation slot. The native stop contract may terminate or detach a connection. A rejected or unconfirmed stop produces an explicit decision notice instead of claiming the native process ended; shared services are never killed and no trust input is sent. Persisting failure before cleanup prevents another tick or restart from replaying this timeout. Space and OS notices are attempted once on that path; crash-time delivery remains best effort, and durable retention of the initial trust decision is the separate next item.

Author-run regressions use a synthetic successor, saved records and the actual dispatcher/RoomState. They cover the last millisecond and deadline, invalid configuration fallback, native readiness before expiry, restart without a fresh budget, ordinary queued dispatch and a different member obtaining the released rotation slot, plus stop refusal and the existing sixty-second RPC timeout. On the pre-change dispatcher the new group gives 1 pass and 19 failures; after the change it gives 20 passes with no failures or skips. The related five-file suite passes 162/162 with no skips. A real isolated Electron/main/service/Git GUI run uses a twelve-second configuration and synthetic native transport: all six checks pass, including the visible timeout, actual queued dispatch to the original member, and window restart with one failure event and one stopped successor. It reports zero native-provider processes, product-model calls, native inputs, renderer errors and clipboard accesses; owned cleanup is confirmed. The author's separate headless Claude reviewer approved this closed-gate source checkpoint after reading the raw red/green, related and GUI evidence. The complete rerun after restoring the lane's already-locked dependencies passes 5,128/5,128, with no failures, cancellations or skips. Production migration remains closed; no real adapter trust/state qualification is claimed by these tests.

The ten-minute default has costs: a sleeping machine or a late response may cross the saved deadline; the existing failed-rotation record prevents another automatic rotation during its seven-day retention, and the unused worktree is retained. Other members' rotation slots and the original member's ordinary dispatch are released. The explicit operator setting has no upper bound beyond a positive safe integer; short limits are observed on the existing dispatcher ticks rather than by a new timer.

Recovery limit, still a condition before opening migration: the pre-existing save-failure-first cleanup order can lose the subsequent stop call as well as notices if the application crashes between them. No restart replay is claimed. The next durable-receipt checkpoint must account for that timeout-cleanup boundary as well as initial decision deduplication.

The DSH client file is generated and ignored by Git. `scripts/build-ui.cjs` concatenates the primary locale catalogs; normal source start and packaging both rebuild it. The author rebuilt it, verified all four added locale keys in the output and reran the six-check GUI successfully. The first complete unit run had three missing-module failures in unchanged DSH privacy tests; the lane lacked dependencies already committed by its new base. Reusing exact locked versions from the existing main installation restored those tests to 4/4; The repair changed neither manifest nor lockfile; it used no network access or install scripts.

## B6 integration handoff, checkpoint H6b: connected, behind a closed switch — 2026-11-11

**What this adds.** The engine is connected to the queue dispatcher and the main process. The switch that builds it can be opened only by a verified isolated test run (`backgroundTest` and `NAW_TEST_INTEGRATION_HANDOFF=1`, the same way as the dispatcher's directory-migration test switch). In the daily app nothing is built and the engine's three modules are not even loaded: no handoff record is created, no delivery is taken in, nothing is sent, and the dispatcher runs exactly as before. It stays closed until the person's own actions for a held or waiting handoff exist (retry, "handoff dealt with", answering a question), because without them a held delivery would have no way back.

**The dispatcher.** `QueueDispatcher` takes one optional `integration`, a function that builds the engine for that dispatcher. With an engine, integration work that can move without the person counts as open work, so the passes keep going: a space record that changed since it was last looked through (it may hold a new delivery), a handoff awaiting its answer, a delivery for a designated integrator (also one held because an earlier integrator was gone), a space record or notice still owed. What waits for the person does not, so it keeps neither the passes nor a connection going: nobody designated, a waiting handoff, and a designated integrator whose last attempt stopped on something only the person can change (they were asked about it, automatic messages are off, that session is paused, its backend needs an update). Such a block ends when the person designates somebody else, or when any pass that runs for another reason finds it gone. At the end of each pass the engine makes one pass of its own, given the spaces' records as they are now (a delivery recorded earlier in the same pass is in them), the dispatcher's view of the sessions with its own idle and typing clocks, and a fresh look that reads the sessions again. A session list cannot say by itself that it is complete, so a designated session that is missing from it counts as gone only after it has been missing from every pass for ten minutes; coming back in between starts that again. A session that is in the list is the record's to judge: an archived integrator, or another native session under its id, is asked about at once. Reviews are stated as off in every handoff. An engine pass that fails keeps what its earlier steps recorded, and the next pass goes on from there; the failure is kept with the dispatcher and the person is told once per kind of failure in a run, so a different failure after a recovery is told too. A record that cannot be read stops the engine and the person is told once per run. In both cases the queue itself goes on, though an engine pass runs inside the dispatcher's pass and so can hold the next queue pass up for as long as it takes.

**The main process.** When the switch is open it builds the record, the engine and the git reader. The handoff message goes out through the dispatcher's own `send`: the same backend entry (which itself refuses when automatic messages are off or the person has left a prompt unsent there), the same check right before sending (`preflight`: the backend's support and a connection that is not being replaced) and the same "not sent" classification as a queue item, with the handoff's id where a queue item has its id. It does not go through a queue dispatch's own fresh readiness check and space-availability check; whether the integrator can take a message is judged by the handoff record on a fresh look (ready, settled, no recent typing, not engaged by NAW itself). git is read only in the repository the designated integrator works in (its session's working folder), whose main branch is "main". Space records are written by `RoomState.recordHandoff`; notices are system notifications worded by `integrator-words.cjs`. When the system cannot show a notification, the notice is kept as "may not have been shown" and is not repeated.

**Independent review (passed, with six findings; four changed, two listed below).** With the switch closed the reviewer found the daily app unchanged. ## The secretary's "archived" check reads the desktop's record — 2026-11-11

**What was wrong.** Two places in the main process refused an archived session by looking at `archived` on the backend's own session list: the entry that designates the queue secretary, and the check that lets the secretary add a queue item. The backend's list never marks a session as archived; only the desktop's space record does. So a session the person had archived could still be made secretary, and a secretary the person archived could still add to the queue. Found by the independent review of the integrator's entry (B6 H3), which had copied the same line.

**What changed.** Both places read the list after the space record has marked it (`roomState.apply`), as the other gates that depend on it do (the background actor check, the integrator's entry). Nothing else changed: the designation is still the person's alone, an agent's call is still refused in the entry, and an archived secretary keeps its recorded designation, which the person can revoke.

**Checks.** One unit test on the real entries and the real space record: a secretary is designated and adds an item; the person archives it the real way, and the backend's record still carries no "archived"; the archived secretary's next addition is refused and nothing is added; it cannot be designated again while archived; the person can revoke it and add items themselves; restored, it can be designated and add again. Reverting either line turns the test red. The full unit suite passes on the delivered head, and the real app boots and passes the session-menu journey.

**Independent review (passed).** The reviewer confirmed that for these two callers only the `archived` field differs from the backend's list, that nothing new can fail, and that a session being archived at that moment still counts as not archived until the archive finishes. It found two more places in the main process that read `archived` from the backend's own list and are not changed here: the fingerprint of an ordinary background command (archiving the target between an agent's request and its execution does not change the fingerprint), and the fallback that chooses which connection-update options are offered when no profile is passed.

## B6 integration handoff, checkpoint H7a: the person's own actions, as entries — 2026-11-11

**What this adds.** One entry in the main process, `handoff`, for the person's window only: retry one delivery that is on hold; retry everything under one reason; say that a waiting handoff is dealt with, with or without a retry; answer a question (a main commit that may be installed, a branch returned too often); and look at where things stand. It acts on the handoff record of the running engine. The switch that builds the engine is still closed in the daily app, so there the entry answers "integration handoffs are not enabled" and creates nothing. No screen uses the entry yet: the buttons and the list need a design the person has seen first.

**Whose it is.** The person's alone. An agent's call is refused in the entry's first line, whatever it names and whether or not the switch is open, because the general background gate is a fixed table with no row for this method. A retry counts only when it is exactly "true". After a change every window is told and the dispatcher looks again; looking changes and announces nothing.

**When it cannot be done.** An action that does not fit the record's state (a handoff someone already dealt with, a delivery that is no longer on hold, a reason or question that does not exist) is refused in words and nothing changes; the record itself marks these refusals. Any other refusal of the record is a fault of the record (it cannot be saved or read, or the change would have made it invalid or too large): it is said as that, never as "look again and retry", and its message is kept and shown in the overview.

**What the overview holds.** Counts; what is on hold, grouped by reason, each delivery with its space, branch, commit, task label and the integrator's note; the handoff that waits for the person with its reason, the integrator's question and the integrator's session; the open reasons with whether the person was told; and the notices that may not have been shown. It is for the person only, since it holds task labels of every space.

**Checks.** Six unit tests on the real `register` wrapper, the real entry and overview taken from `main.cjs`, and a real record: each action for the person; the overview; an agent refused for every action; the closed switch; actions that do not fit; the wiring and the words in both languages. Sixteen deliberate breakages each turned tests red. In the real app, called from the window of an isolated run: with the switch open the overview comes back and a stale action is refused in words; with the switch closed every call is refused as "not enabled" and no record exists. The full unit suite passes on the delivered head; the count is in the delivery note.

**Independent review (passed, with one finding, then changed).** Every refusal of the record was reported as a stale action unless the record was marked failed, so a broken invariant or a record that would be too large would have asked the person to retry something that can never work. Stale refusals are now marked by the record and only those are worded as stale. The reviewer confirmed that the gate is as strong as the integrator's entry, that every argument is checked by the record itself, and that the overview hands out only copies.

**Left open.**
- The screen: where the person sees what is on hold and presses retry. It needs a prototype the person, or a reviewer standing in for them, has looked at.
- After a retry the engine's memory of "only the person can change this" is not cleared by the entry; the next pass that runs for another reason looks again, which with a window open is within a minute.

A previous daemon can remove its lock between the launcher's existence check and
the lock reader's lstat/read. The reported startup then failed with ENOENT.
The shared reader now returns undefined only for ENOENT, null for a present
invalid record, and throws other I/O errors. Both ordinary bootstrap paths and
dedicated recovery/start use that distinction without a separate existence check.
Release treats absence as success and forgets its own held entry. Acquisition
still requires its newly written token to be present before claiming ownership.

Deterministic tests remove each of service.lock and services.lock immediately
before lstat and before reading the contents. All four actual isolated bootstrap
cases fail with ENOENT on the base and pass with the fix. Reader tests distinguish
invalid files, foreign ownership and permission errors; startup counterexamples
reject corrupt/nonregular/foreign/unreadable locks without allocating a runtime.
Real unresponsive daemon tests retain both old and versioned locks. Dedicated
recovery and startup use only a synthetic provider executable, with no inference.
The waitForShutdown and waitGone loops have absence checks without subsequent
reads; their socket/process identity safeguards remain unchanged. The separate
backend-switch serviceProcess pre-maintenance identity check reads the lock
directly and already fails closed if it disappears; that reader is unchanged.
The test-scratch ownership probe also reads directly and already catches ENOENT.
The separate desktop test-driver lock uses a different protocol and is outside
this repair.

The first independent review approved the product diff without code blockers,
conditional on a green full suite and the audit wording correction above (R1).
The first full run had one distinct failure: the existing service-reuse fixture
returned on socket close while its daemon still held the lock. The live-owner
guard correctly refused its second bootstrap. A deterministic fixture test fails
before the fix; cleanup now waits for both lock removal and owner exit before
rebooting or removing its owned profile. No production safeguard is relaxed.
The same independent reviewer approved the incremental fixture/doc diff with no
blockers and closed R1. Its final prerequisite is met: the full suite with test

### B2-TRUST-2 / 2: durable attempts and interrupted cleanup — 2026-11-11

The requested retention boundary exposed a second failure: saving a failed rotation before stopping its successor could abandon cleanup after a crash. This checkpoint keeps notice attempts and cleanup intent in the existing rotation record. Log, per-space and OS attempts are saved before the effect; clearing space history or trimming the log never makes an attempted or unknown effect pending again. Legacy waiting records suppress unknown log/space attempts and retain only the older OS flag's known-pending attempt. Legacy failures do not authorize another stop or notification. This is at-most-once notification attempt accounting, not exactly-once delivery.

Failure and cleanup intent share one save. Restart observes an ended, recoverable or disconnected successor instead of stopping it again; an interrupted attempt may retry once, with a hard limit of two attempts and the exact saved native, control, draft and placement revisions. A new backend capability rechecks unused ownership immediately before the adapter mutation, including after asynchronous observation. No native input, approval, interrupt, goal write or unguarded fallback is permitted. Automatic stop affects only its participant; cleanup departure skips an eager human-intervention pause and the backend atomically refuses departure if a space collaboration started meanwhile. Unsupported backends and changed or uncertain ownership stay unresolved.

Unresolved successors are excluded from queue planning, vacancy reporting and refreshed direct dispatch. The original member can continue queued work; cleanup does not occupy the single active-rotation slot. The failure record is retained beyond seven days until cleanup is observed complete, rather than forgetting a possibly live successor. Pending departures wait for unrelated space runs; uncertain departures are observed without blind replay. Readiness without an observed trust prompt is checked before expiry. A genuinely new visible prompt after readiness starts its own clock, receipt and notification. Malformed new receipt state fails closed instead of silently dropping quarantine.

Author-run baseline tests against the exact pre-change dispatcher and RoomState give 4 passes and 33 failures. Current durable-receipt, crash-boundary and isolation checks pass 45/45, with no skips. Guarded stop, existing maintenance and guarded membership checks pass 129/129, with no skips; the initial guarded-departure counterexamples fail 10/10 before repair. These are synthetic provider checks. The complete author-run suite passes 5,458/5,458 with no failures, cancellations or skips. An actual isolated Electron/main/service/Git run passes all eight checks: both waiting and timeout notices remain cleared after more than 1,000 later log rows and a real main-process restart; there is one synthetic successor stop and no extra successor or native input. It reports zero provider processes, product-model calls, renderer errors and clipboard reads/writes, with owned process/profile/socket/lease cleanup confirmed. Codex3's own separate headless Claude Fable 5.2 review session for this durable-receipt checkpoint returns APPROVE_WITH_NOTES, scoped to the unchanged source over the stated base with migration off. This records the author's review only; the integrator records its own subsequent review separately. Its initial invocation reached the eight-minute limit without a verdict; the same session then gave its bounded verdict from the evidence already read. Tool inventory was Read/Grep/Glob only, no MCP; HEAD, index and worktree stayed unchanged across both invocations. The reviewer read the GUI and regression logs; the author verified the actual full-suite output; the reviewer did not rerun it.

Production migration remains closed. Real trust-page state ordering, detection outside starting and actual Chat successor coverage remain B2-TRUST-2 items 3 and 4. Claude Chat creates a terminal; Codex Chat does not. No native qualification, installed daily-app acceptance or safe downgrade support is claimed by this checkpoint.

The reviewer leaves the following non-blocking conditions before migration can open. Unknown cleanup currently has no terminal resolution: a deleted row, changed native identity, missing proof or archived space can retain quarantine and prevent the original from auto-rotating indefinitely. It also keeps the existing three-second tick doing full passes and holding a service connection; define bounded passive observation and an explicit resolution. A later observed stopped state must not authorize removing a successor the person has since adopted: recheck unused control/draft/history before late departure.
