## B6 integration handoff: the whole journey in the real window — 2026-11-11

**What this adds.** One desktop script, `scripts/test-integration-handoff.cjs`, and no product change. It runs the real desktop app in a temporary profile with the handoff switch open for that run only: the real dispatcher, engine, handoff record, space record and workspace service, and the real git reader on a temporary repository. The provider transport is synthetic and system notifications are recorded by a stand-in instead of being shown, so there is no provider process, no model call and nothing reaches the OS. Git runs only in the folder the run's own profile gave the integrator's session; the script checks that before the first command.

**The journey.** The person queues one task for each of two members of a space; each gets its own and answers with a READY line for its branch. With nobody designated, nothing is handed out, and the person is told once that a delivery waits: the second delivery does not ask again. The person designates a session that is in no space; one handoff reaches it, naming both branches and commits and saying that reviews are off, and the space's shared record says for each delivery that it was handed out. The integrator cherry-picks the first delivery onto main in the repository, then answers MERGED for it and RETURNED, with a reason, for the second. The shared record then says the first was merged, with the new commit and the test count, and the second was returned, with the reason; the person is told that this main may be installed. The person answers that question. At the end: one handoff, sent once within the run; each member received its one task and never a handoff; two notices, neither carrying a task's text; one window and no page error. The designation and the answer are made through the window's entries, since no screen has buttons for them yet.

**Checks.** The script passes in the real app. Three copies changed on purpose each failed and were deleted: with the switch closed the person is never asked to designate anyone; when the integrator claims the merge without doing it, the space never says merged; when it claims the second delivery merged as well, that delivery is put on hold and not counted as merged. That NAW compares the answer with the repository rests on these two copies, not on a check inside the passing run. The full unit suite, which scans every script, passes with this one present.

**Independent review (passed).** The reviewer confirmed that each statement of the journey rests on a check that can fail, that git and file writes stay inside the run's own folders, and that nothing private is in the two files. It asked for the second member, which the condition in the H6b list names; that is added here. One point is not changed: when the script is interrupted by a signal while its teardown hangs, the shared GUI slot can stay taken, as in the other scripts that hold the slot themselves.

**Left open.**
- A delivery on hold, a retry, a lock held by someone else, a send that is refused or not confirmed and an integrator that never answers are covered by unit tests, not by this journey.
- The reader still reads main in the integrator's own folder; which repository counts is the person's decision (H6b list).
- The notices are read where the main process would show them; no real system notification is shown.
- The person sees "handed out", "merged" and "returned" only under the space's shared-record tab; the member overview, which opens first, says nothing about a handoff. After a return nothing queues the task again or tells the member outside that record. Both belong to the screen that still needs a prototype.

## B6 integration handoff: the second reviewer's four conditions — 2026-11-11

**Where they come from.** The integrator had a reviewer who had not seen the work check the connection (H6b) for one question: is daily queue dispatch unchanged while the switch is closed. It passed, and named four things that must hold before the switch is opened. All four are in code that runs only with the switch open.

**An engine that cannot be built.** The dispatcher built the engine in the middle of its own constructor. A fault there (a module that cannot be loaded, say) ended the constructor, and the main process then runs without any dispatcher: every queue stops, in silence. The engine is now built last, for a dispatcher that is complete, and a fault is caught: the dispatcher runs without an engine, keeps the fault and tells the person once. In the main process the person's own entry gets the handoff record only after the engine exists, so with no engine it changes nothing (it then answered "not enabled"; it now says that handoffs failed to start and why, see the section on the engine's faults).

**A record that cannot be read, a backlog that is full.** "Is there work" answered yes for every space whose record had not been looked through. With an unreadable record no space is ever looked through, and with a full backlog the space of the delivery that was left out is not marked, so the dispatcher went on making full passes and kept a connection open for nothing. Now an unreadable record is not work. A space whose delivery was left out is looked through again only when its record has changed since (it may hold a newer delivery of a branch that is inside, which still gets in) or when the backlog has room again; a space with nothing left out is marked as looked through even when it comes after the full one. The person is still told once about the unreadable record: by any pass that runs for queue work, or by the once-a-minute check through a window.

**A pass result that cannot be read.** Only the pass itself was guarded. What the dispatcher did with its result was not, and a result of the wrong shape, or a failure to tell the windows, was swallowed by the queue's loop. The whole step is guarded now and every such fault is kept and told once per kind, like a pass that throws.

**Who NAW itself is busy with.** The record refuses to hand out to an integrator that NAW itself is doing something with, but the dispatcher never said who that is, so the check could not fire. The view now names them by the queue planner's own rule: a session in a running space exchange, one a queue item was sent to whose answer is awaited, one in a session rotation that is not at rest, its unconfirmed successor, and a successor whose folder was not trusted until its cleanup is confirmed. The rule is a third copy beside the planner's and the vacancy list's, which are left untouched because they run in the daily app.

**Independent review (passed).** This is the author lane's own reviewer (headless session 980f8974, read-only tools); the integrator's reviewer checked the same commit separately. The reviewer confirmed that with the switch closed the dispatcher is unchanged, that nothing relied on the engine being built early, that no state exists where something can move and "is there work" says no (a space after the full one, room appearing with an unchanged record, a newer delivery arriving while full, a restart), and that the "engaged" rule is the queue's own. Its three remarks on these notes are taken in above and below.

**Checks.** Unit tests on the real dispatcher, engine, record and space record: an engine that cannot be built (the queue works, told once, the builder is given a complete dispatcher); a result without its list, no result at all and a failing announcement (each kept and told once, the queue goes on, what the pass did is kept); an integrator in a running exchange is handed nothing until it ends, and the view names each kind of engaged session; an unreadable record is not work, from the start and after passes, and is still told once; a full backlog with nothing new is not work, a changed space record is, room in the backlog is. Twenty-two deliberate breakages each turned tests red; one that only removes housekeeping stays green, as expected. The real-window journey passes on the changed code. The full unit suite passes on the delivered head; the count is in the delivery note.

**Left open.**
- With no engine the person's entry said "not enabled", not "failed to start", and the notice was the only place that said so. (Changed: see "the engine's faults in the person's overview".)
- The build fault is told through a system notification while the app starts. It is not exercised in the real app: nothing there can make the builder fail without a test-only fault.
- With no window open and no queue work, an unreadable record is told only when a window opens.
- An integrator that stays engaged until the person acts is handed nothing and nothing says why: a queue item sent to it that waits for the person, or a successor session whose folder was not trusted (the person is told about the trust question, not about the handoffs behind it). This joins the long-unready integrator in the list above.
- A fault of the dispatcher's own inside this step (reading the sessions again, telling the windows) is told as "the integration handoff step failed".
- Three copies of the "engaged" rule: to be made one when the planner is next changed.

Before migration opens, Codex3 owns the following conditions, combining the author's review notes and the integrator's subsequent source findings. They do not block this closed-gate delivery or authorize opening the gate.

1. **State corruption affects all dispatch.** Invalid durable receipt fields throw during dispatcher construction, silently disabling the entire dispatcher, not only migration. Separately, malformed JSON returns an empty rotation map: all saved successor quarantines are lost and those members can become eligible for queued work again. Preserve recoverable quarantine on both paths and provide an actionable explanation.
2. **One cleanup error blocks every space.** A persistent exception in `resumeTrustCleanup`, including a save failure, exits `advanceRotations` before ordinary rotations and `planDispatch`. The existing outer loop swallows and repeats the error. Isolate cleanup failures per record so other rotations and all other spaces' queued work can continue.
3. **Unknown cleanup has no terminal resolution.** A deleted row, changed identity, missing proof or archived space can keep the failure forever, prevent the original from auto-rotating, hold the dispatcher-owned connection and force full passes on every three-second tick. Legacy failed records become unknown immediately. Define an explicit resolution and bounded passive observation rather than a permanent resource cost.
4. **Adopted successors lose assigned work.** Every cleanup pass reassigns queued items from the successor to the original, including items the person assigned after adopting that successor. Preserve the person's later assignment and control decision.
5. **Inactive is insufficient authority for departure.** Native identity and an ended, recoverable or disconnected state do not prove that the successor is still unused. A person may have resumed, used and later ended that same thread; Codex disconnected describes this connection, not a stopped native thread. Recheck control, drafts and history before late departure and use an accurate completion condition.
6. **Flapping has no total bound.** Each readiness-to-prompt transition resets the wait, receipt and notice. Repeated flips can extend total waiting and notification count without limit. Add an overall bound and verify real prompt/state ordering before relying on a new-cycle deadline.
7. **Downgrade loses quarantine.** Older versions ignore the new quarantine fields, making the successor eligible again immediately; the failed record is cleared after seven days. Define downgrade handling before these states can occur in production.
8. **Real successor trust remains unqualified.** Codex Chat creates no terminal; Claude Chat does create one. Establish where their actual trust decision appears and whether the native state can leave starting while that page remains visible, allowing handoff text to be sent into it. Reliable detection or explicit unavailability is required; standalone first screens and injected prompts do not qualify ordinary Chat successors.

Notification delivery is an explicit tradeoff: attempts are **at most once**. A crash after saving attempted state but before emitting the notice permanently loses that notice; it is not retried and delivery is not guaranteed. Post-trust failures before confirmed handoff conservatively use guarded cleanup and may retain a quarantined successor. End-to-end departure through the dispatcher's scoped client also remains a runtime coverage gap: the GUI prompt precedes joining, and synthetic stop coverage does not qualify real adapters.

override public `recordPage` in a subclass or on the instance, returning a valid-
shaped fake receipt without a journal row or quota charge. The writable base
static directory predicate also allowed a host override to accept a wrong root.
These are blocking host-composition errors before activation; the B4 owner owns
this bounded repair.

The record implementation is now private. Business uses the base static record
entry, without dispatching instance/subclass overrides, and the base constructor
is frozen to fix both static entries. Public `recordPage` remains compatible.
This is a host API misuse guard, not protection from arbitrary same-process code.
Page/cursor/log schemas, callbacks, capacity, failed-write behavior and the fixed
64-page allowance are unchanged. Main, renderer and DSH integration are untouched.

New same-root subclass and own-method cases reproduce fake receipts before the
repair, then verify that the overrides are never called, all 64 real rows reach
the same person's readable journal, and page 65 is refused. Static assignment and
redefinition cannot authorize a wrong root or replace the record entry. The
bounded red run has 21 tests: 16 pass, 5 fail. Related strict credential-free
checks pass 131/131, with zero failures or skips; the empty-environment source UI
build exits zero (`audit-method-build.log` in the private lane). The complete
author-run suite passes 5,801/5,801, with zero failures, cancellations or skips
(`audit-method-full.log`). Fresh separate headless reviewerA4ABBAFF-DBE8-4D18-8DB1-CD950DDE0F57
returns APPROVE_SCOPED for the exact source delta. Its tools were Read/Grep/Glob
only, no MCP; HEAD, index and worktree matched the review snapshot. The reviewer
read author-run raw evidence and did not rerun tests. No provider/model call,
GUI or installed use is claimed here.

Consistency is not correctness: runtime acceptance must show a trusted actual
Main factory supplying its real `dataDir` and sole `butlerReadAudit`, also used
by the person reader. Pairing an audit and directory in the same wrong root is
not qualified. No production factory is added or proven by these synthetic
composition checks. Activation and the recording period remain closed.

Future factory acceptance must also establish the plain base instance, default
clock and unoverridden human reader, and the single Main-owned object reused
by both read paths. The module-local private-brand/physical-root checks do not
authenticate an arbitrary caller-supplied reference as Main's actual directory.

## Host-enforced whole-page admission (2026-11-11)

Old-host live Business/MCP/DSH fixtures reproduced input-boundary failures for
sequential over-reading, six same-step reads and a heavily escaped batch. The
host now admits each whole tool result only if the next projected wire request
fits with 64 KiB reserved, counting pending refusal envelopes and actual escaping.
It withholds an unfit result through the existing DSH post-execution policy,
then refuses further MCP reads in that batch. Cursor, authority and whole records
are preserved; the Business-approved page stays in the shared daily audit even
when not delivered. The new fixture passes the main process's trusted dataDir
and shared Audit. Rotation resets host admission, never the daily page count.

Ninety focused checks pass, including exact inclusive reservation, Unicode/JSON
escaping, pending parallel results, deferred context and unchanged hard ceilings.
Four live multipage scenarios pass, plus all ten prior host boundary scenarios.
The core over-reading case completes with all seven requests' usage in its ledger
and no blocked/unknown-cost notice. A new session can read again; its shared audit
still includes the withheld page. No real provider calls or credential values.
The normal fixed eight-request limit remains: an agent that keeps requesting
refused reads forever is not silently allowed more requests. Unbounded model
output and unsupported content remain hard refusals, not an admission guarantee.
Full-suite and independent-review receipts are recorded in the private lane.

The full suite passes 5,804/5,804 with no failures, cancellations or skips. A
separate read-only headless reviewer approved the product and signed-runtime
proof after closing its initial evidence/packaging gaps. Its test notes led to
strict assertions for accepted-plus-withheld MCP counts and the bounded live
fixture's reserved headroom; all four live cases still pass. Product source and
the full-suite tests are unchanged since that complete run. Unsupported pipeline
failures or unbounded model output still rely on the final hard guard; the
admission promise does not cover those paths.

## Butler read log for the person: "what it has read" (2026-11-11, renderer only, behind the closed entry)

Scope: a read-only dialog that shows the butler's read log to the person, reached
from the butler entry by one more action. The entry stays closed in every
ordinary launch, so nothing offers the dialog in this version. It uses only the
existing person-only call `butlerReview('reads', …)`; no main, preload, daemon or
core file changed, and no new call was added. Files: `app/butler-reads-view.js`
(pure view), `app/renderer/butler-reads.js` (dialog), five lines in
`app/renderer/butler-entry.js`, page markup, bundle list, styles and 35 catalog
keys per language.

What it shows is what a log record holds and nothing else: time, kind of lookup
(list of spaces, queue, delivery records with the time window asked for), the
space (the log stores an id; a name is the window's own, an id it cannot name is
shown shortened with the whole id as the tooltip), how many records came back and
whether more were left, and which designation asked. Session, native, runner ids
and record references are never drawn. Above the list: pages read and left in
the current counting day and when the count restarts. The core counts per UTC
day; every time on the screen is local and each day header gives its local span.

Prototype and stand-in review before implementation: every record in the
prototype was written and read back by the real `ButlerReadAudit`. An independent
session looking as the person returned `APPROVE_WITH_CHANGES` twice. First look,
seven required changes, all applied: rows lost their date when scrolled (day
header now pinned); nothing showed that more rows were below (scrollbar, fade and
a line saying how much of the log is listed); the note about unreadable earlier
records pointed the wrong way; the unreadable state lacked the rule and a next
step; UTC times read as local (now local throughout); a "page" was never
explained; refused reads after the limit are not listed and the screen did not
say so. Second look, one required change, applied here: "today" no longer
matched the person's day once times were local, so the summary names the span.
Private evidence: `.local/evidence/butler-reads-20261111/standin/`.

Found while implementing, and now said on the screen: a log found damaged stays
unreadable in the running app even after the file is repaired, until NAW is
reopened (a unit test shows this with the real module). A lock left behind does
not stick, so the sentence says to reopen NAW only if the log still cannot be
read after it was looked at. Two edge cases are
handled rather than papered over: when the newest record is not on screen the
dialog claims neither today's count nor "the newest N"; a log that reports
records and returns none is shown as unreadable, not as empty.

Author-run evidence, no model call: the read log's two test files and the
entry's pass 46 of 46 together with the entry view's; the full suite passes with
zero failures or skips (count in the commit message); 52 deliberate faults in
the view, the dialog and the entry change are each caught. Hidden real-Electron
check `scripts/test-butler-reads.cjs`: with the entry closed the dialog is in the
page, shut and invisible; a real 64-page log over two UTC days, written into the
isolated profile by the real module, is read through the window's real
`workspace.butlerReview` and drawn by the product's module, stylesheet and
catalog in both languages at 1280 and 860 wide (newest fifty, earlier on
request, day header pinned, nothing clipped, only the list scrolls); a damaged
log is said to be unreadable and stays so after the file is put back. Private
evidence: `.local/evidence/butler-reads-20261111/impl/`.

Limits of that evidence: the dialog in the Electron check is mounted beside the
product's hidden one, because nothing can open the product's own while the entry
is closed; the product's mapping of space ids to names is covered by a source
check and a unit test of the lookup, not on screen; the dark theme was not
looked at.

Required before the butler is switched on (not part of this delivery):
- A safe way to make room in a full log. None exists: nothing is rotated or
  pruned. Removing the file with NAW closed starts an empty log, so the record
  of what was read is gone and the day's count starts again; once the running
  NAW has read or written the log, removing, shrinking or replacing the file
  leaves the log unreadable until NAW is reopened.
  The dialog says there is no way to clear it yet and tells the person not to
  delete the file. By the module's own limits the worst case is about three
  days to the core's prewarning and four to the cap. Owner: butler outcome

- The person's decision on whether refused or failed reads are recorded at all.
- Known interaction, as the core already works: the person's read takes the

  A butler page arriving during that moment is withheld as busy, and an

## B6 integration handoff: the engine's faults in the person's overview — 2026-11-11

**Why.** The dispatcher keeps the last fault of the engine's own step (it could not be built, or a pass failed) and tells the person once. That notice is sent at most once: it is marked as told before it is shown, so one that fails to show while the app starts is never repeated, and nothing in the main process read the kept fault. The integrator's reviewer asked that it be readable in the person's overview before the switch is opened.

**What changed.** The overview the person's `handoff` entry returns now carries `engineFault`, a copy of the dispatcher's kept fault (its message, when, how often, and since when it is over once a later step went through), beside `fault`, the last fault the record raised on one of the person's own actions. When the switch is open but the engine could not be built there is no record: looking then returns that the handoffs did not start, with the fault; every action is refused as "failed to start" instead of "not enabled"; nothing is created. With the switch closed, or with no dispatcher at all, the entry answers "not enabled" as before. An agent's call is still refused in the entry's first line.

**Checks.** One unit test on the real entry and overview from `main.cjs`: a kept pass fault is shown as a copy and looking announces nothing; with no record and a kept build fault, looking says why and each action is refused in the new words; an agent is refused first; no dispatcher at all is "not enabled". Eight deliberate breakages each turned tests red. The real-window journey passes on the changed code; the full unit suite passes on the delivered head (the count is in the delivery note).

**Independent review (passed).** It asked that a fault which is over be told apart from one that still happens; the kept fault now carries the time a later step went through. The author lane's own reviewer (headless session 980f8974); its result is in the delivery note.

**Left open.** No screen shows the overview yet; the prototype for it is with the person.

## Butler entry: what a person window is answered with (2026-11-11, behind the closed entry)

Requested outcome (the integrator's dispatch, after the person-only controls
`7347c1c` reached main): the isolated switch, the adapter from the core's person
view to the entry the window draws, and the window asking for its state on
demand, without a second handler; and one alignment from the identity review of
those controls: the window sent a third argument with `designate` that the main
process refuses, and the core's `open`/`close` names are not actions of the
call. It serves the approved form of the butler: visible, can be turned off,

What changed:
- `app/butler-entry-host.cjs` (new, pure): the core's person view becomes the
  entry of `app/butler-entry-view.js`, by copying named fields only. The same
  `butler` handler in `app/main.cjs` answers `status` and `recheck` with it and
  cuts the result of the other actions down to plain facts. The session
  identity, runner and backend references, batch ids and stop targets no longer

- The entry is not in the window state. The window asks once as it starts, when

- The entry gained three fields: `unavailable` (the designation record cannot

  own). With nothing designated and no designation accepted, the dialog says

- Alignment: the main process is the authority. The window now sends the
  action and the revision only; one table of call shapes in the window's
  module is put through the real handler by a test, and the old three-argument
  shape is pinned as refused. A designation the core answers with "blocked" is
  said in the dialog.

Decision recorded for the owner of the controls: the adapter sits in the
handler, as its contract asked, which changes what `status` and `recheck`
return. The existing IPC tests keep every assertion on the core's view: each
makes the same call through the real handler and then reads the view from the
same real core object.

Checks (author-run, no model, no native program): the eight related test
files pass; full unit suite 5890 pass, 0 fail (an earlier run of it had one
failure, a timing test in `claude-mod-check.test.cjs` that this change does
not touch and that passes alone, three runs). The deliberate faults in the
adapter, the handler lines, the view and the window's module are all caught
(count in the verdict lines below). Three hidden-window checks pass:
`scripts/test-butler-entry-open.cjs` (new) drives the product's own row and

designation written by the core's own record store, a stale revoke refused in
words, revoke, the read log, an unreadable record, with no identity on the

`scripts/test-butler-reads.cjs`.

Not verified, and limits:

## The row under the single-session input: whole labels in the Chinese interface (T-163, 2026-11-11)

Requested outcome, in the person's words of 2026-11-04: the UI is not compact enough, not refined enough and its blocks are not well divided; lines and blocks should be clear and economical, without overdoing it. This is one place on the single-session page: the row at the bottom of the input card, which holds a hint and one or two controls. While a session worked, the labels broke in the middle (中断回 / 复, 发送 / ↑). In a small window the same happened to the take-over control in a read-only window and to both controls while waiting for a confirmation. The reviewer of the previous change to this page had called it the most visible flaw left on it.

Cause: the hint and the controls gave way together, each in proportion to its full width, so a full-sentence hint claimed most of a short row and each control lost a few pixels; a Chinese label breaks as soon as its control loses one.

Change, in `app/renderer/styles.css`: in the Chinese interface and in an input card of 320px or more, the hint asks for 16em instead of its whole sentence, and takes what is left once the labels are on one line. When 16em and the whole labels do not fit, everything gives way in proportion as before. The controls' own rules are not touched. In English and in a narrower card the row is sized exactly as it was. The input area becomes a size container so that the card's width can be asked; that changes no size.

Measured, with the program laying itself out again after each switch of styles: in Chinese at 1240x850, 1000x700 and 850x600 the working card goes from 153.2 to 136.7px, the height it has when idle, and both labels are on one line; at 850x600 the same holds for the read-only and waiting states, and the input area, which used to exceed its limit and scroll inside itself while working, now fits. Idle is unchanged. English is unchanged in every case, including its broken labels at 1240 and 1000 wide.

Why it carries two conditions. The rule gives nothing a new minimum, but that alone does not make it safe: a hint shorter than 16em stops giving way sooner than it used to. So it was measured: all 13 labels the send control can carry beside all 27 hints in the message catalog, with and without the interrupt control (702 combinations), at card widths from 150 to 600px in 5px steps, each against the earlier sizing; 63,882 comparisons per language. In English nothing differs. Under 320px nothing differs in either language. In Chinese from 320px no control is further out of the card, there is no more sideways scroll, no label is in more lines and no row is taller, in all 63,882; rows with every label on one line go from 19,570 to 35,448. Among the 52 label-and-hint pairs the program can actually show (the 26 pairs of `soloAction` and the two hints that can replace any of them), 5,928 comparisons from 320px: 2,018 rows shorter, none taller. Without the language condition 718 of 3,172 English comparisons had a taller row, by up to 52px, because English hints are long. With the width condition at 300px, three Chinese rows were 2.5px taller at 300 to 310px; hence 320px.

How it got here. Prototype first, as the task requires, reviewed by an independent agent in the person's place, in one session. Five earlier candidates failed. Keeping the controls whole unconditionally squeezed the English hint to five lines in a small window and cut its last line. Giving the hint a hard 16em minimum was the first candidate reviewed: the reviewer worked out from the source that with the divider at its 20% stop the minimum pushes controls out of the card, and the prototype then reproduced a 62px sideways scroll. Switching that rule off under a 355px card was the second: the reviewer pointed out that the width had been worked out for one pair of labels and that longer English ones ("Add instructions ↑", "Awaiting native receipt") still overflow at 360px; it also corrected the author's 135px to the measured 137px. An ordering that gave the hint its 16em first squeezed controls to one character per line in narrow cards. The present rule without conditions made rows taller in English and in narrow cards. The reviewer accepted the present form with notes, all three taken: the two hints that can replace any other were added to the real pairs and the measurement repeated; the comment in the stylesheet says measured, not impossible; and the check asserts that the rule is on in Chinese and off in English, so that a change to the language selector cannot switch it off unnoticed. That assertion caught the author's own first build: the rule was written against `:root`, which never matches because the build nests the stylesheet inside the application's root element; it now uses the nesting selector the stylesheet already uses. The same reviewer then checked the build and approved it with one change to the check, made in this commit: the send control's labels are read from the renderer's own function that chooses them, not from a typed list, so that a label added later is measured too.

The language is read from the state of the language selector in the setup dialog, as that dialog's own rules already do, because the page's `lang` attribute is fixed at `zh-CN` and does not follow the interface language. ## B6 integration handoff: the session that holds an open handoff gets no queue work — 2026-11-11

**What could go wrong.** The integrator's answer is everything it writes after the handoff message. An integrator is in no space, so the queue never sends it anything. But the person can put it into a space while a handoff is open. The queue's planner runs before the engine in every pass, so the moment the integrator went idle the planner could send it a queued task, before the handoff was settled; what it then wrote for that task would be read as the handoff's answer (a reply that begins "needs your decision" would even be taken as the handoff's question). It could also be rotated into a new session, and the answer lost.

**What changed.** The engine names the session that an open handoff was sent to (sent or waiting for the person; nobody when the record cannot be read). The dispatcher passes that to the queue's planner, where the session starts out busy: it is given no queued item, also not one assigned to it by name, and it is not rotated; an item it was sent before is still settled. When the handoff is closed (settled, or dealt with by the person) the queue treats the session like any other member again. With the switch closed nothing is passed, and the planner's one changed line builds the same empty set as before.

**Checks.** A planner test (an engaged session gets no item and no rotation; the item goes to another member or waits; an earlier item is settled; nothing named, or something that is not a list, plans as before) and a test on the real dispatcher and record (the integrator is put into the space with a task queued for it by name; it answers the handoff with a question; nothing but the handoff was sent to it; after the person deals with the handoff the task goes out; an unreadable record names nobody). Six deliberate breakages each turned tests red. The full unit suite and the two real-window journeys (the handoff with the switch open, the daily queue with it closed) pass on the delivered head; the counts are in the delivery note.

**Independent review (passed).** The author lane's own reviewer (headless session 980f8974). It confirmed that the planner is unchanged when nobody is named, that the busy set is read wherever a session could be given an item or be rotated while earlier items are still settled, that a rotation in progress and an open handoff cannot coexist for one session, and that within one pass no queue item can reach the holder before the handoff is settled. It asked that the commit wait for the daily queue journey in the real window, and added the last two points below.

**Left open.**
- The second half: a handoff whose integrator is found in a space should wait for the person instead of being read, because messages can reach a member in other ways than the queue (a space exchange, say).
- The vacancy list that the butler reads still showed such a session as free. (Changed: see "the vacancy list leaves out the holder".)
- When the record cannot be read, or the engine could not be built over a record that still holds an open handoff from an earlier run, nobody is named and the queue can send that session work; once the record is read again, what it wrote would count as the handoff's answer.
- Messages from outside the queue (an agent's wake, a continuation after a limit, a space exchange) can still reach the holder. The reviewer's proposal for the second half: end the answer at the first automatic message after the handoff, instead of only waiting when the integrator is found in a space.

## Butler cooperative lock crash recovery — 2026-11-11

The integrator's pre-activation list identified that the old empty O_EXCL lock
survives a writer crash and keeps person revoke busy forever. This checkpoint
changes only future protocol writers on Darwin. A private, already-fsynced
marker is atomically linked to the existing lock name while its stage descriptor
holds `O_EXLOCK|O_NONBLOCK`. The marker contains only the fixed protocol and a
UUID stage basename, no PID, person name, session data or credential. No empty
published-file window is introduced. The normal caller removes its own lock
name before closing the descriptor.

Recovery requires a recognized bounded private regular file, a kernel lock that
is actually available, a stable inode and matching named path. nlink2 is allowed
only for the exact marker-declared stage and canonical name on that same inode;
all ordinary selection files retain nlink1. The recovery removes those names
while holding the descriptor, then atomically competes for the name one more
time. It refuses if an old O_EXCL writer wins. Empty legacy/unknown bytes,
malformed fields, links, unsafe metadata and live holders remain busy. This is
advisory/cooperative exclusion, not PID death, arbitrary same-user path attack
protection or authority to remove unknown files. Unpublished orphan stages are
retained rather than enumerated for cleanup. Non-Darwin keeps the old protocol.

Primary local SDK facts: sys/fcntl.h:113/120 defines O_NONBLOCK=4/O_EXLOCK=32;
open.2 describes flock during open, link.2:63/75 the link-count change and
link.2:209 EEXIST atomic contention; flock.2:41/53/73 describes cooperative
advisory locking. The author read these actual SDK files. Existing host Node
26.12.1 evidence verifies contention and same-inode release after holder exit.
The new actual-host child cases verify both published two-link and one-link
crashes, and a live holder that is killed/reaped before recovery.

The test author's first three children missed the fault hook through a temporary
path alias; that fixture output is retained separately and is not crash evidence.
After canonicalizing fixtures, the old Role has 19 tests: 13 pass, 6 fail. Three
failures are actual empty locks left by two exited children and one killed/reaped
holder; three are new-protocol expectation failures, not observed old-code
namespace races. Current exact same tests pass 19/19, with three owned children
reaped and no skips. The first combined strict run has 228 pass/1 fail because
the prior close-fault hook looked up the lock after the correct new unlink-before-
close order. It now remembers the target inode once seen; selection write/fsync
fault hooks also track only the actual record replacement, so marker writes
cannot hide those checks. The corrected combined strict checks pass 229/229,
with no failures, cancellations or skips. Existing person/identity controls,
revision checks, read refusal and record-only action semantics remain unchanged.

One separately bounded owned noindex Electron executable invocation with
RUN_AS_NODE and constructed empty credential environment ends SIGTRAP with no
packet or stderr. Its scripted fixture was not created before the only child
spawn point, and no remaining mapping of that exact owned executable is found.
The parent is reaped, the owned copy's strict signature remains valid and its
LaunchServices registration remains false. No policy relaxation or retry is
attempted. This is UNKNOWN, not embedded-Node locking, Main startup, Session or

## Butler read log: the activation notes in the dialog's own files (2026-11-11, behind the closed entry)

Source: the integration review of the read log approved it with notes, none
blocking, and listed what has to be done before the butler is switched on. The
notes that are in the dialog's own files are done here. The others belong to
the log's and the host's owners and are listed at the end.

What changed:
- Two silences are said. When the day's count cannot be told, the line is no
  longer left out: it says so and why (the newest record is not understood by
  this version, or the newest records were not reached this time). When the
  answer carries no report of how full the file is, or one that does not add
  up, the dialog says it cannot tell how full the file is, and that a full
  file stops the butler whatever the day's count shows. A day's header gives
  its page count as "at least" when it cannot be told that the day's last
  record is on screen: the newest day without the log's newest record; an
  earlier day when the record after its last shown one is missing, since that
  record could belong to either day; a day that shows up again further on
  because the clock went back. So it does not contradict the line above it.
- One opening or refresh reads the log at most twice (once when the log fits
  one page): one read to learn where it ends and one for its tail. Pages
  written between the two are no longer chased with up to two more reads; they
  show as "newer ones were not reached", and Refresh reads again.
- The window starts without a butler part that cannot be set up. The read
  log's and the entry's setup in `app/renderer/renderer.js` each fall back to
  a stand-in, and the failure is written to the console. Before, a module
  missing from the page stopped the whole window. A read log that was not set
  up, asked for from an entry that was, tells the person it cannot be read.
- Without the entry on screen the read log does not stay open (the record
  table's existing rule, for the read log).

Measured, for the cost of the person's read (the real log module in one
process, a synthetic log, no application, no model): with records of a usual
size (about 660 bytes) one read takes about 12 ms per MiB of log from 8 MiB
up, about 0.38 s at the 32 MiB cap; with records of about 33,000 bytes about
0.12 s at the cap. Every read
goes through the whole file in the main process. One opening therefore went
from up to four such reads to at most two. The rest is not the dialog's: a
read that seeks the tail, or an index the log keeps, would remove it.

Checks (author-run, no model, no native program): the full unit suite passes
with no failure and every deliberate fault in these changes is caught (counts
in the verdict lines below); the hidden window checks pass: the read log with
the new sentences in both languages
(`scripts/test-butler-reads.cjs`), the entry with its switch open, and the
entry's drawn states.

Not verified:
- A window with a module really missing: the test runs the renderer's own two
  setup statements where the module is absent or its setup fails.
- The read log closing with the entry is tested on the renderer's own two
  lines, not driven in a window: in this version an entry that has appeared
  does not go away while the application runs.
- The new sentences were not shown to the stand-in reviewer.
- A file larger than its cap would be reported as "cannot tell how full"

## B6 integration handoff: what the integrator writes after someone else's message — 2026-11-11

**What could go wrong.** The answer to a handoff was read from everything the integrator wrote after the handoff message. Other automatic messages can reach its session while the handoff is open: another agent's wake or control message, a space exchange, a rotation request (a queue item no longer can, see the section before). What the integrator writes for such a message was read like its answer to the handoff; a reply that begins "needs your decision" would have made the handoff wait for the person with a question that belongs to something else.

**What changed.** When the handoff is settled, the integrator's messages are told apart by whether they came before or after the first automatic message from someone else. Before it, everything is read as it always was, and an answer found there stands. Only when nothing before it reads like an answer is a later message used, and then only by its result lines for this handoff's own deliveries: those lines name the delivery by its commit, and a merge is checked with git anyway. A question for the person in such a message is not the handoff's question, and lines it has for other commits do not make it the answer. If that leaves no result at all, each delivery is handed once more by itself, as any delivery without a result line is. A continuation after a model limit is not a message from someone else: it resumes the same work, and what follows it is read in full. "Automatic" is judged as the queue's reply reader judges it (the message's origin, or NAW's marker on a native row without one).

**Also changed: the handoff's own message is never the person's typing.** Where a native record takes the place of NAW's copy of the handoff message and carries no origin, the queue's reader does not know the handoff marker and counted that row as the person's typing, so the handoff would have waited as "you typed in the integrator's session". The handoff's settlement now judges the person's typing itself, by the same rule, except that this handoff's own message is skipped: a row that begins with the handoff marker and this handoff's id. A row that only quotes them is still the person's. The queue's reader is unchanged.

**Checks.** One test on the record's plan and settlement. For each kind of automatic message from someone else (four origins, two markers): an answer before it is read and a "question" after it is not; only a question after it gives no result and each delivery is handed once more; result lines for this handoff's deliveries after it are read and the merge is checked; a closing remark after those lines loses nothing; lines for other commits after it leave the earlier answer standing; its own answer, or its own question, is not replaced by lines written after the other message; an empty row is not counted. A continuation: a question after it is the handoff's, an unreadable answer after it is still the answer. Unchanged: no other message, a silent integrator, the person's typing before or after the other message, an unknown native row or another handoff's message, a message from before the handoff, a tool row. The handoff's own native row, with or without an origin, is neither typing nor someone else's message; a row that only quotes the handoff's header is typing. One test on the real dispatcher: an agent's wake during a handoff, a "question" written for it, a second handoff by itself, its answer read and the merge checked; the person is asked nothing. Nineteen deliberate breakages each turned the plan test red. The full unit suite and the real-window journey pass on the delivered head; the counts are in the delivery note.

**Independent review (first round blocked, then changed).** The first version cut the answer at the first automatic message of any kind and read nothing after it. The author lane's own reviewer (headless session 980f8974) blocked it: a continuation after a limit would have been taken for someone else's message, the real MERGED line after it would not have been read, and the same merge reported again in the next handoff cannot be confirmed (its commit is no longer new), so the person would have been told that a real merge could not be verified. The rule above replaces the cut. The second round passed and added two points, both taken (a third, short round passed them): the integrator's own answer comes first (a line restated for someone else could otherwise have hidden it), and the handoff's own row must begin with its header (a person who quotes the header while typing natively would otherwise have been missed).

**Left open.**
- (The rule of this section was changed again, see "the settlement after someone else's message, corrected" and then "four points from the review of the notice and the settlement".)
- Result lines are read from one message. Lines spread over a message before and a message after someone else's are not added together.
- An integrator that asked the person a question, was then sent someone else's message and settled the matter by itself still has its handoff waiting on that question. If it merged in the meantime and the person then chooses "hand out again", the merge it reports a second time cannot be confirmed (its commit is no longer new); reading its session and ending the handoff without handing out again avoids that.
- A wake that leaves only a question behind costs one more round.
- The queue's own settlement of a member's item still reads everything after the item, and its reader still does not know the handoff marker.
- Not exercised with a real provider: whether a native record really replaces NAW's copy of the handoff message, and with which origin.

## B6 integration handoff: a space is told that its member is kept out of the queue — 2026-11-11

**Why.** A session that holds an open handoff gets no queue work. When that session is a member of a space (the person put the integrator there while its handoff was open), the space's queue silently skips it, and nothing told the person why. This is worst when the handoff waits because the person typed into the integrator's session: that wait is deliberately not announced by a system notice, so the member could stay out of the queue with no word anywhere. The integrator's reviewer asked that the person be told.

**What changed.** In its telling step the engine looks whether the holder of the open handoff is a member of any space, and has one line written into that space's shared record: that the member is working on an integration handoff, and that until it is finished this space gives it no new tasks and tasks for it wait; or, when the handoff waits for the person, that it waits for them, with the same about its tasks. Each is written once per handoff and member; the windows are told that the record changed. A space that is being updated at that moment is told on a later pass, and that is not a fault of the engine; any other failure to write is kept and told once like other faults of the engine's step. An archived space is told nothing. An integrator in no space has no queue to be kept out of, and nothing is written. All of it is in the engine and in the function of the main process that builds it, which run only with the switch open; the dispatcher's file is not changed (another lane's fix to it was waiting to be merged). The dispatcher tells the windows as it does for the engine's other records.

**Checks.** One test on the real dispatcher and the real space record: nothing is said for an integrator in no space; put into the space while it works, the space is told once, after a pass in which the space was being updated (nothing written, no fault) and passes in which the writer failed otherwise (a fault, told once); the person types into its session, the handoff waits, no system notice is sent and the space is told the second sentence; repeats, a space that does not exist and a fact without its parts write nothing; after the person deals with the handoff nothing more is said; a later handoff is told for itself; a missing name falls back to the session's id; an archived space is told nothing; both sentences exist in both languages; an unreadable record names nobody; the main process gives the engine the writer and the names. Nineteen deliberate breakages each turned it red. In the real window (isolated run, switch open): the integrator is put into the space through the session menu while its handoff is open, and the first sentence appears in the space's shared record; the journey then finishes as usual. The full unit suite passes on the delivered head; the counts are in the delivery note.

**Independent review (passed).** It asked for three changes, all made: only "the space is being updated" is passed over in silence, so a bug cannot hide the line for ever; archived spaces are skipped; and the sentences say that tasks for the member wait, which "sends it no work" could have been read as dropping them. The author lane's own reviewer (headless session 980f8974); its result is in the delivery note.

**Left open.**
- The sentences are new words for the person and have not been seen by the person.
- The line is written when the engine's step runs; a space the member joins between two passes is told on the next one.
- The queue panel does not show it; that belongs to the screen whose prototype is with the person.
- When writing the line fails for a reason other than "the space is being updated", the fault is kept and told once, but that pass does not tell the windows about what else it changed; they catch up at the next announcement. Mending this means a change in the dispatcher's file, which is not to be touched for now.

## B6 integration handoff: the settlement after someone else's message, corrected — 2026-11-11

**What was wrong with the rule before.** The integrator's reviewer found two ways in which a real answer was not settled (neither could record a wrong merge; both ended as "no result", held and told):
1. A question for the person written after another agent's message was not taken as the handoff's question. The handoff settled with no results, the deliveries were handed once more and then held as "no result", and the person never saw the question.
2. An earlier message of the integrator's own with anything like a result line (a provisional HELD, or template lines copied from the handoff's own text) came first and hid the real answer written after the other message.

**The rule now.** The integrator's answer is again its last message that reads like one, wherever it stands: it begins with a question for the person, or it has result lines for this handoff's own deliveries. So a question is put to the person with its text and the handoff waits, and the later, real answer wins over an earlier provisional line. One thing stays from the rule before: after an automatic message from someone else (a queue item, another agent's wake or control message, a rotation request), result-shaped lines that cannot be read do not make a message the answer, because they may be about something else and would hide the answer given before. Before such a message, and after a continuation following a limit, an unreadable answer is still the answer, as it always was.

**Decided here: RETURNED and HELD lines after someone else's message settle the handoff without the person.** MERGED is checked with git; these two are not. They are accepted because each names this handoff's delivery by its own commit, which makes it the integrator's statement about that delivery wherever it is written; a held delivery goes to the person anyway, and a returned one goes back with its reason in the space's record, where the person sees it. Text inside a code block is read like any other line (backticks are removed), so a line the integrator only quotes would count. If that is judged too loose, the stricter rule is: after someone else's message only MERGED lines settle, and anything else makes the handoff wait for the person. This is for the integrator or the person to overrule.

**A message through a space makes the handoff wait for the person.** A message that reaches the integrator through a space carries the origin "room" and was counted as automatic, so the person writing to the integrator in a space did not make the handoff wait, while typing in its session did. Such a message comes from the person or from another member (a reply routed in a running exchange, a member's outbox), and its origin does not say which. It now counts like the person's typing either way: the handoff waits for the person, nothing is read from the reply, and (with the section before) the space is told that the member's handoff waits for them.

**Checks.** The plan test is rewritten. For each kind of automatic message from someone else (three origins, two markers): a question after it is asked, with its text, also when an answer stood before it; the real answer after it wins over a provisional line and over copied template lines, and its merge is checked; result lines after it are read when a closing remark follows; unreadable lines after it leave the earlier answer standing, and before it they are still the answer; an empty row is not counted; only words for the other message give no result and the deliveries are handed once more. A continuation, no other message, a silent integrator, the person's typing, a message through a space, a row that quotes the header, an unknown native row, the handoff's own native row, a message from before the handoff and a tool row are each pinned. The test on the real dispatcher: an agent's wake, then a question; the handoff waits with the question and the person is told once; after they deal with it the delivery goes out again and its merge is checked. Nineteen deliberate breakages each turned the plan test red. The full unit suite and the real-window journey pass on the delivered head; the counts are in the delivery note.

**Independent review (passed).** The author lane's own reviewer (headless session 980f8974) confirmed that without a message from someone else the rule is the one from before the previous change, that both cases above now settle or ask, and that the queue's own reader is unchanged. It agreed with the decision on RETURNED and HELD lines and with giving up "the integrator's own answer first", which it had proposed itself. It corrected one thing, taken in above: a message through a space is not always the person's.

**Left open.**
- A message written for someone else that begins with "needs your decision" makes the handoff wait with a question that may not be about it. The person is asked rather than left with "no result".
- A line restated for someone else after the integrator's own full answer becomes the answer; deliveries it does not name are handed once more.
- The sentence for the person's own step says "you typed in the integrator's session" also when the message came through a space, and also when another member sent it there: the handoff waits rightly, but the reason it gives is not the real one.
- The list of automatic origins is exported from the dispatcher's file and could be changed by a module that imports it; freezing it waits until that file may be changed again.

## Butler read log: what a line shows and what it does not (2026-11-11, text only, behind the closed entry)

Requested (the integrator's dispatch, from the log author's own note): two
honest statements on the read log dialog. A line is a page NAW approved, not
proof that the other side received it; and the log is not a tamper-proof
ledger against programs of the same user or a changed clock. The wording was
to go through the stand-in reviewer first, and only the dialog's text changes.

What is on the page now, as a second quiet paragraph under the introduction,
in every state of the dialog: a line means NAW approved giving the page to the
butler (every page is logged before it is given) and does not show that the
model service received it; the log is not tamper-proof: any program running
under the person's account can delete or change it, and deleting it or
changing the system clock gets around the limit of 64 pages a day.

Stand-in review (a fresh read-only session standing in for the person, on
screenshots of the product's own dialog with two placements, always visible
and one line that opens): `APPROVE_WITH_CHANGES`, always visible. Its three
required changes are applied as given. The draft said "while NAW is not
running", which named a smaller risk than the source shows: a program of the
same user can add well-formed lines while NAW runs. Deletion gets around the
daily limit as well as the clock does. "Approved" stays, never "gave". Two of
its suggestions are taken ("the model service", and that every page is logged
before it is given); one is not, for length: that a changed clock also makes
the logged times wrong.

One layout rule changed with it, because the added text (and a sentence added
to the introduction meanwhile on main) left no record in sight in the smallest
window with the long warning of a file at its limit, in English. The list now
keeps room for about two records. It still gives way first; when that is not
enough, the explanation at the top gives way too and scrolls in its own box,
so the count, the warning, the records and the actions stay in sight. The
hidden-window check now fails when no whole record is in sight, when the
explanation is cut in an ordinary state, or when it is out of sight; the
earlier check passed with no record in sight.

Each claim is tested on the real modules, not only as text: the 65th page of a
day is refused; a well-formed line appended by another program is read as the
log's own; the clock moved to another day gives a fresh allowance; a log
deleted while the application is closed is empty at the next start with a
fresh allowance; and the page is returned only after its line is written.

Checks (author-run, no model): the full unit suite passes with no failure and
every deliberate fault in the read log's activation changes, this paragraph
and its layout rule is caught (counts in the commit message); the three
hidden-window checks pass, the read log's in both languages and at both
widths. No independent code review of this commit: it adds one paragraph of
text whose claims the stand-in checked against the source, tests that run
those claims, and a layout rule the window check now enforces.

## The terminal pane's header: one row where its controls fit (T-163, 2026-11-11)

Requested outcome, in the person's words of 2026-11-04: the UI is not compact enough, not refined enough and its blocks are not well divided. On the single-session page the terminal pane's header wrapped: in Chinese at 850 wide a lone close button sat on a second row, in English at the default size "more, maximise, close" did, and the header was 64px instead of 33px, so its bottom rule did not meet the rule under the conversation pane's toolbar. The reviewer of the first change to this page had named it as the cause of that step between the two rules.

Cause: the hint with copy and paste was one item of the row and the three buttons after it were three more items, so a short row dropped whole buttons to a second row one by one. A first attempt with styles alone was dropped in the prototype: with the three buttons outside the group there is no way to say that they travel with it, and it made English at 850 wide worse.

Change: in `app/renderer/index.html`, one wrapper element, `.native-pane-actions`, around the hint-and-buttons group and the three buttons; in `app/renderer/styles.css`, the rules for it and one widened selector. In the compact session layout, in a header of 300px or more, the group sits on the right of the title in whatever room the title leaves. Inside it the hint gives way first, wrapping onto a second line and breaking only at spaces; the buttons do not shrink or wrap. When even that does not fit, the group moves to a second row as a whole. The group cannot wrap inside itself, so it is formed only where it fits on a row of its own (it needs 249px in Chinese and 261px in English): in a narrower header, and in the layout that is not compact, the wrapper lays out nothing and its children are items of the row as they always were. The first build did not have that condition, and two existing checks caught it: with the terminal pane dragged to its narrowest, maximise and close left the pane and could not be clicked (`test-terminal-selection`, `test-terminal-layout`). The prototype had not tried a narrow pane. The renderer reaches these controls by id (`terminal-controls`, `terminal-more`, `terminal-maximize`, `close-native-terminal`), not by their place in the row, and no script or style addressed them as direct children of the header except the one selector that was widened; without that the three buttons would have gone back to their larger size.

Measured in the prototype against the earlier markup, six cases, and asserted on the build by the check below: the header goes from 64 to 33px and one row in Chinese at 850x600 and in English at 1240x850 and 1000x700, the two header rules meet there, and the terminal gains 31px; Chinese at 1240x850 and 1000x700 and English at 850x600 (51px, two rows) are unchanged. No text is cut and no control changes size, order, name or Tab stop.

Prototype first, as the task requires: reviewed by an independent agent in the person's place, which required one line (the hint must not break inside a word: in Chinese at 850 wide 右键菜单 was split across the two lines) and asked that the check assert it; both are in this change. It accepted the rest and noted that in English at 1000 wide the second line starts with the slash, which it judged readable.

Owner: the author of this change. Evidence: `scripts/test-session-split-density.cjs`, hidden, synthetic backend, no model, thirteen steps. New in it: the four controls are laid out as one group inside the header; every part of the header stays inside it; the five buttons keep their order and their 26px height; one 33px row in Chinese at 1240x850, 1000x700 and 850x600 and in English at 1240x850 and 1000x700, two rows no higher than 52px in English at 850x600; the hint's line count in each; the hint does not break inside a word (右键菜单 in Chinese; Option, select, context and menu in English); the two header rules meet in Chinese at 850x600 and in English at 1240x850 and 1000x700; and the divider dragged through eight positions from the terminal pane's narrowest to its widest, in Chinese and English at 1240 and 1000 wide, where at each position every part of the header stays inside it and the window, the five controls are shown, the header is never taller than with the earlier layout (64 to 33 or 53px in Chinese and 82 or 64 to 51 or 33px in English where it changes), and under 300px the wrapper lays out nothing and the header is exactly as high as before. It fails on the earlier markup at the first of these. A second independent agent then reviewed the build, the condition added after the first build and the check: approved with notes, nothing required. Its three recommended guards are in the check: the words the hint must not break are looked for by name, so a hint whose wording changes fails instead of passing unmeasured; the group's narrowest one-row width is asserted to fit a 300px header, so a longer label fails the check instead of overflowing; and with the compact class taken off the session view, as it is when a member of a space is opened, the wrapper is asserted to lay out nothing. It also noted that under 300px the comparison with the earlier layout cannot fail, because both sides then apply the same styles; the evidence for narrow headers is the two existing checks that caught the first build and pass now. Seventeen other hidden checks that use this header, this page or the member-column input pass on the change, among them the two that caught the first build. An eighteenth, `test-dialog-lifecycle`, fails on the list of dialogs it expects, which does not yet name the three steward dialogs added to the page earlier the same day; it fails the same way without this change. Not covered: the header with the hint-and-buttons group hidden (a terminal that cannot be used), the non-compact layout, the same header when a member of a space is opened, a dark theme, physical keys and a screen reader.
## B2 trust recovery: record fault isolation, items 1–2 — 2026-11-11

Requested outcome: a malformed trust record or one failed cleanup must not stop queue dispatch and ordinary rotations in other spaces. Directory migration remains disabled. This checkpoint covers the first two pre-opening repairs only; unknown cleanup completion, adopted successors, native stop proof and flapping limits remain subsequent checkpoints. The integration engine and its methods are unchanged.

The prior loader threw on malformed trust fields, preventing construction of the entire dispatcher. It also discarded all successor identities when its JSON could not be read. Successor identities now have a separate safety record in existing root room metadata, retained across history clear/trim and omitted from the renderer projection. A bad primary row is preserved and fenced individually using that saved identity; unrelated members can receive queued work and ordinary same-directory joining continues. A corrupted or missing primary file does not release its indexed successors. A rejected row without an independent identity, or an unreadable safety record, holds all unproven admissions instead of guessing the target from corrupt fields. A damaged primary with no prior safety record retains the legacy ordinary-dispatch behavior; it does not prove a migration ever existed. Simultaneous loss of all identity evidence cannot be distinguished from an installation without migration history. A saved unknown state is re-evaluated at restart when a valid nonempty primary containing moved-successor identities is restored and every retained hold agrees; an empty rewritten primary does not lift it. Re-evaluation can also succeed on the next restart without a manual restore if the primary was already valid: identities are reconstructed from it, the known successor stays held and unrelated work resumes. This is now asserted explicitly. The primary format cannot prove backup completeness; a valid older backup that omits a later hold is a remaining two-source-loss risk. The person can ask for a verified complete backup to be restored; no in-app recovery control is introduced. No new service, timer or permission is added.

Cleanup exceptions are caught per record. Their successor stays held, the original can receive queue work, and automatic retries of that fault stop. Failure to save fault/notice metadata cannot poison an unrelated same-directory save; a new trust operation still cannot proceed before its own successor hold is saved. Unreadable primary bytes are retained before replacement, and an observed file changing meanwhile is not replaced. A valid matching saved confirmation can finish releasing its hold after a crash.

A decision notice is attempted through the existing space/system channels. Saved attempts are at most once, not guaranteed delivery: a crash between saving and sending may lose that notice. With the safety store unwritable, the running app warns once in memory; restart deduplication cannot be promised until persistence works. No failure grants native stop, membership or trust-answer authority. The shared send boundary also refuses held/unknown targets for other automatic senders. Its sole exception is the matching active rotation's own handoff at the created step; the integration engine and its callback are unchanged.

First review requested changes: a damaged primary with no trust history latched a permanent global hold. The fix preserves the ordinary fallback and adds restart re-evaluation from restored identity evidence, with regression tests. Other pre-opening notes remain: a moved successor failing before the trust-wait path can retain an orphaned hold; missing identity on a failing cleanup still requires recovery evidence; a shared-room write failure can suppress later space notices (the system notice is still attempted); recovery cannot overwrite a primary whose identity changed while observed. The held-successor handoff exception also has a direct regression: another automatic message is refused before writing, while its own exact created-stage rotation handoff succeeds. Validation and the same reviewer's final delta result are recorded after the runs finish. Native windows, real providers, real configuration and daily data are outside this checkpoint; the pending Claude window still requires the person's permission.

Validation for this checkpoint: `node --test --test-concurrency=2 app/tests/*.test.cjs` passed 5,838/5,838, with zero failures or skips; the final test-only additions passed a separate 7/7 targeted run (the added held-handoff case is outside the full-run count). Production code did not change between those runs. The corrected base-source replay failed all 14 original fault regressions. Codex3's separate headless Claude Fable reviewer for this record-isolation checkpoint, whose session id and raw transcript are held privately, first requested B1, then approved its delta conditionally, and finally returned APPROVE_WITH_NOTES for items 1–2 after reading the final evidence. These are author-run test results, not reviewer reruns; this is not the integrator's separate review. The review process verified Read/Grep/Glob only and left HEAD, index and worktree unchanged. Local delivery only; integration, daily installation and opening migration remain separate.
