## B2 isolation: shared-file damage is not migration evidence — 2026-11-11

The integrator's separate review accepted local adoption of the record-isolation patch but required a default-path correction before installation. A shared-room read warning alone must not manufacture unknown directory-trust state for every session. The warning now causes that global hold only when the rotation data contains a trust/moved-successor record (including rejected rows) or the rotation store itself cannot be read for a reason other than a missing file. A readable ordinary/empty store or a fresh missing store retains its ordinary behavior. No migration switch or native permission is enabled.

There is a separate pre-existing limitation: RoomState.assertAvailable rejects dispatch when shared metadata is unreadable because that file also owns global session archives. The same check is present before the isolation patch. Synthetic comparison against the earlier source shows ordinary rotation requests continue while dispatch is rejected; the isolation patch had newly stopped both, and the narrowed condition restores the former behavior. Bypassing the archive check is not part of this correction and requires a reliable archive-state design, not a silent exception. The integrator confirmed the scope: restore that baseline only (dispatch remains refused by the existing archive check, while rotation requests resume). Broader dispatch recovery is deferred until actual shared-file damage occurs or the person requests it; no archive protection is relaxed.

Additional pre-opening findings from the integrator are retained as open:

- Recovery in save applies even to ordinary rotations. A vanished/replaced/unowned primary, or a first read without a captured identity, can make saves keep throwing. Advance occurs before planning, so an ordinary rotation failure can stop all queue passes until restart. This is broader than an earlier author note that described only rotation saves; it is confirmed in source and is not narrowed by the shared-warning correction.
- Rejected rows are retained indefinitely. Automatic unknown-state re-evaluation currently requires zero rejected rows, so it cannot clear after a retained rejection without repair. Claims of automatic recovery apply only with a clean, rejection-free primary.
- A faulted original can still receive its own queued work but is barred from another automatic rotation. There is no in-app fault resolution. Unknown cleanup without a thrown fault still forces full passes, and a fault with no successor identity still holds unproven sessions. These are not closed by this correction.
- The integration view still consumes the unfiltered rotation dictionary behind the engine's closed switch. A shared-room write failure can stop the rotation-event loop before notices reach other spaces. Both remain open before activation.
- If a prior hold survives only in shared metadata and that file becomes unreadable while the primary is missing or contains only ordinary rows, the identity cannot be recovered by this fallback and may no longer be fenced. This loss-of-evidence case remains a pre-opening risk; the ordinary-path correction does not claim complete quarantine recovery.

The integrator's eight-condition status remains partial for malformed trust state and unknown cleanup, closed only for known-successor thrown cleanup failures, and open for adopted-recipient handling, inactive proof, flapping, downgrade and real native/Chat qualification. Subsequent code checkpoints have not been adopted by this record.

Validation for this additive correction: the six ordinary-path regressions pass against the earlier source and fail against the isolation delivery at the missing rotation request; all seven current regressions pass, including the unreadable-primary counterexample. Related tests pass 245/245; `node --test --test-concurrency=2 app/tests/*.test.cjs` passes 6,056/6,056, with zero failures, cancellations or skips. These are author-run synthetic checks. Codex3's same separate headless Claude reviewer returned APPROVE_WITH_NOTES for the incremental correction, conditional on those test results and the pre-commit scan; the production diff is unchanged. This is not the integrator's review. The migration gate remains closed.

## A backend's own program locations are taken out when it starts (2026-11-10)

**Status: the person agreed on 2026-11-11. Until then it was built, tested and reviewed on its lane and kept out of main; it takes effect for a backend the first time that backend starts on a version that has it.**

The one question left open by the earlier entry "A backend's own program locations no longer leave it silently unable to run a provider": should a backend's own entry for an older version that still exists also go when the backend starts? The author's conclusion page marked it as the person's to decide, with "take it out" as the recommendation. The person had asked 「为啥不把 agent 更新到最新」 and 「那么多更新应该自动更新才对」, and was away. The integrator first decided yes for them and asked that it be reversible (「清掉的内容照旧记进 runtime-locations.removed.json」); an independent review then pointed out that this overrode the author's mark, and the integrator withdrew the decision: the code was delivered as usual and stayed out of main and out of any installed version until the person confirmed. On 2026-11-11 the integrator put the question to the person with the recommendation to merge, and the person answered 「其他的貌似可以按你推荐的来」 (task board record; the original message was not checked for this document). It replaces the behaviour of 2026-10-29, under which an existing backend kept and reused its own paths at every bootstrap, and the narrower behaviour of the earlier entry (only entries whose program is gone are taken out).

Built. With a Settings file known, every entry of a backend's own `runtime-locations.json` is taken out at its start, whether or not its program exists (`backendLocations` in `app/runtime-locations.cjs`). The entries are first added to the record beside the file, each with its path and whether its program still existed; only then is the file rewritten empty, and the backend reads the shared Settings file. If the record or the file cannot be written, nothing is taken out and the file is used as it is. A record that is there but cannot be read is moved aside under a dated name, never written over. Unchanged: an unreadable own file still stops the start and names itself; the shared Settings file is never touched, and is now recognised by the file itself and not by the spelling of its path; a service started by hand with no Settings file keeps its own file; a running backend is not touched, so a backend still on an earlier build keeps its paths until it next starts on this one. The check before an update lists the entries a start will take out and no longer counts them. The existing bootstrap test that expected a backend to keep its paths now expects them in the record and the shared file in use.

Author-run, no native program and no model: unit tests with fake programs and a real start of NAW's own backend service; 21 single-line mutations each caught (a first run let three through: the write order, a record that is not a file, and a guard made redundant by the identity check, which was removed); full suite 4791/0. The hidden GUI check of the alert was not rerun: it uses the root backend, whose path is unchanged. No real-CLI test script writes a locations file under a `backends/` folder, so none loses its fixture wrapper.

Independent read-only review (one session: two rounds on the code, then three on the rebase below; the CLI reported the model as claude-opus-5-5): CHANGES (a record that could not be read was started again, which lost the earlier removals it alone held), then PASS on `1db20cd` (`555d56d` after the rebase onto `3adba67`). Also taken: recognising the Settings file by identity; the script header's missing fallback; where a damaged record goes, in the guide. Noted, not changed: an own file that is a link to the Settings file now starts on Settings where it used to be refused (no gate is loosened: the backend still reads the shared file through the same checks); the record can list entries still in the file after a failed file write; moved-aside records keep their mode and are not counted.

Rebased on 2026-11-11 onto main `1268f61`, 179 commits after the base it was reviewed on, with no change to its code: `app/service-client.cjs` and `app/tests/service-reuse.test.cjs` also took main's changes, without conflict, and the other files are as reviewed. On the new base `backendLocations` is still called only at the two reviewed places, and every test script that writes a locations file writes the shared one, none inside a backend's folder. Author-run on that base, no model: the four related test files, 40 pass; full suite 6134 pass, 0 fail. The same reviewer session read the rebase. Its first verdict was `APPROVE_WITH_CHANGES`: the diff the author gave it had been made against a main that had already moved on, so it showed other people's work reversed (the branch itself changed only its own eight files, which a second diff from the merge base shows), and a sentence here pointed to lines that did not exist. Its verdict on the second delta: `APPROVE`, except for the text of this section, which it had not read; a further read of the section asked for two sentences to be corrected, which were then corrected.
## B6 integration handoff: main is read only in the repository the person chose — 2026-11-11

**The decision.** The person decided (2026-11-11, relayed by the integrator and recorded on the task board): when a reported merge is checked, only the main checkout they have chosen counts; the working folder of the integrator's session is not read. Reviews stay off, and the switch stays closed.

**What was wrong.** The engine read "main" in the folder the designated integrator's session works in. If that is a separate clone or a linked working tree, its "main" is another one, and a merge that never reached the real main could be recorded as merged.

**What changed.**
- A small record, `integration-repository.json`, names one folder. Only the person sets or clears it, through two new actions of their own `handoff` entry ("see the repository", "choose the repository"); an agent's call is refused in the entry's first line, as for every other action there.
- The folder must be the top of a repository's main working tree: a folder inside the repository and a linked working tree are refused, although each of them has a "main". The repository must not reach outside itself (included configuration, borrowed objects, a path through a link, a partial clone): these are the worktree helper's own checks, now exported, and they are made when the folder is chosen and again before every use, since a repository can change afterwards. When it is chosen it must also have a main branch.
- The main process reads git only there. The builder no longer looks at any session's working folder.
- With no repository that can be read (none chosen, the chosen one fails a check, or its record cannot be read) nothing is handed out and git is not asked. The person is told once, like "nobody is designated": a new standing condition in the handoff record. It is asked after the questions about who merges. It ends when the person chooses a repository (so a later loss is asked about again) or when a handoff goes out, and what waited for the choice is tried at once. It keeps no passes going.
- A settlement takes one checked look at the repository and puts every one of its git questions to that look. If the repository cannot be read at that moment, the answer waits the bounded while that an unreadable main head gets and is then settled as "main could not be read", instead of the merge being judged as naming a commit that does not exist.
- Only an explicit "none" clears the choice; a call without a folder is refused.
- The overview shows the chosen folder and, when it cannot be read now, why.
- The refusals have sentences of their own. The helper's sentences speak of "automatic copies", which would mislead here; its reason is kept with the error for the record.

**Checks.** Unit tests on real temporary repositories made with git: the top of a main working tree is recorded (a private file, written whole), read back by a new instance and checked again before use; a change to the repository afterwards leaves the choice standing but unreadable; a folder inside, a linked working tree, a folder in no repository, a path through a link, relative and malformed values, included configuration and borrowed objects are each refused and record nothing; a record that is damaged, wrongly protected or a link is an error and never "none", and the next choice repairs it; a save that fails is not taken as made. The record's plan: asked once, after the questions about the integrator, whether or not the integrator is ready; not a reason a delivery can be held under; over when a handoff opens. The engine: every form of "no" (null, false, nothing, a throw) asks once and reads neither git nor the sessions again. The real dispatcher: the delivery waits, one notice, no open work, then the handoff after the person's choice. The entry, with the real choice object taken from `main.cjs` and the real git reader: choose, see, clear; a repository without a main branch, a folder inside one and a folder in none are refused; looking announces nothing; an agent is refused; closed switch. The packaging list names the new module. Twenty-six deliberate breakages each turned tests red. One checked look per settlement: its reader and head are the only ones asked; no look, a failed check and an unreadable head each wait and then settle as "main could not be read". Nine more breakages for these later points each turned tests red. In the real window the journey keeps main in a repository of its own, beside the session folders; the integrator's session folder holds no repository. The person is asked, is refused a folder inside the repository and the integrator's own folder, chooses the repository, and the merge that then checks out can only have been read there. The full unit suite passes on the delivered head (counts in the delivery note).

**Independent review (passed, with four points, all taken).** The author lane's own reviewer (headless session 980f8974) confirmed that no other path reads git, that nothing which is not the top of a main working tree passes, that the record is as safe as the integrator's, and that nothing new loads with the switch closed. Its points: the question about a missing repository ended only when a handoff went out, so losing the repository again before that was never told, and the handoff went out up to a minute after the choice; a call without a folder cleared the choice; the checks ran before every single git question, so a check failing in the middle of a settlement made a real merge look like an unknown commit; and the journey kept main in the integrator's own session folder, so it could not show which folder was read. A first run of the changed journey failed on an assertion of its own (the window's refusal arrives as an object, not as the sentence) and was corrected. A short second round passed the four changes and corrected one sentence of these notes, which claimed more than the code does (see the last two open points).

**Left open.**
- No screen has a control for choosing the repository; the journey chooses it through the window's entry. It belongs to the queue panel's handoff section.
- The sentence that asks the person covers "none chosen", "the chosen one fails its checks" and "its record cannot be read" in one; the overview says which.
- Between the check and the git call (milliseconds) a local process with write access to the repository could still change it; the reader's own settings keep programs from running.
- git itself failing in the middle of a settlement, after main's head was read (a timeout, the repository moved away, output over the limit), still reads as "no such commit", and a real merge is then held as not verified. Telling "git could not answer" apart from "no such commit" in the reader would mend it.
- A pass that is in the middle of handing out when the person chooses the repository can set its "only the person can change this" mark after the choice cleared it: the person may then be told once more that no repository can be read, and the handoff goes out with the next pass that runs for another reason.
- A repository on a path that goes through a link cannot be chosen, also when the link is harmless (the system's temporary folder is one).
- Only a branch called "main" is read.

## A creation grant follows the session that replaced its holder (B5 prerequisite, third step, 2026-11-11)

Status: built and independently reviewed; agreed by the person on 2026-11-11 in the narrower form described next. Whether a grant should follow a replacement at all was the person's decision; until now it did not. The integrator recommended merging it once narrowed as its own review had suggested, and the person answered that the recommendations could be followed (「其他的貌似可以按你推荐的来」).

The narrowing (2026-11-11). The per-session permission to use the agent control interface goes on only together with a grant in force. A holder that has the interface on and no grant, or only revoked or expired ones, is not followed at all: it is not listed for a decision, the desktop does not read the rotation log for it, its successor gets no setting, nothing is saved in the journal and nothing is written in any space. The journal checks again when it is asked to carry or to refuse, because a grant can be revoked or run out after the holder was listed; it then answers that there is no grant and saves nothing. The old session keeps the setting the person gave it. The grant in force must be one the holder already had when it was replaced, that is, given no later than the time the replacement was logged. A holder that is given a grant only after it was replaced is not followed either: it is listed, because the list does not know when it was replaced; the desktop reads the log and asks once for that state of the log; the journal answers that there is no grant; nothing moves, nothing is saved, nothing is said, and the grant stays with the session the person gave it to. A line in the log with no time can only be refused, which moves nothing; there any grant in force counts, and the person is told that the grant stayed. With at least one such grant in force the replacement is followed as described below, and what goes on is what the holder had when it was replaced: every grant that names it and was given no later than the replacement was logged, revoked and expired ones included, as they are. A grant the person gave the old session after that, in the time before the desktop's step, stays in the old session's name (closed on 2026-11-11, see the review below). Nothing new can be started under it while the old session's interface is off, and that session has ended; the person can revoke it from the old session's menu. Two things follow from rules that were already there: an open the person approved for the old session after the replacement was logged and before the step, the only thing that can already have started under such a grant, continues as it did before; and if the person turns the old session on again and brings it back, it holds that grant. The entry in the space counts only the grants in force that went on.

What the person was told before deciding (asked for by the integrator's own independent review of this change, a separate read-only session, which found nothing blocking), as it stands after the narrowing:

- More than the grant moves. The per-session permission to use the agent control interface moves with it. As first built it moved for every ended session whose interface the person had turned on, whether or not it held a grant; that is what was narrowed. The successor, a session the person may never have looked at, can then do what that permission allows: read the basic facts of every session of its backend that is not archived; read the task text and the latest report (up to 8,000 characters) of the requests made under the grants that came with it; and ask the person for a new grant.
- Revoking the holder's last grant in force stops it, as turning the interface off does: nothing moves and nothing is written. (As first built, revoking did not stop the permission from going on.) A grant revoked after it went on stays revoked where it is; if that happens before the entry in the space could be written, the entry says that only the interface permission went on and that no grant is in force. With the interface off for the old session, or for everyone, nothing moves and nothing is written.
- "No agent can forge a replacement" holds as long as no agent can write the desktop's data folder. Only the desktop writes the rotation log, and a log that others can write is not read. But a session running as the same system user could append a line to that private file; once a holder has ended, such a line would move its grant to a Claude session of the same backend that has no interface setting and is not archived. This is the exposure the secretary designation and the grant journal itself already have, not a new kind; what it would yield here is a grant to open sessions.
- Files changed: `app/operator-control.cjs` (the list of ended holders, `succession()`, the saved-record checks, and how turning a session off or revoking reaches a grant that has gone on), `app/main.cjs` (`carryGrants`, and the refusal from an agent's context), `app/workspace.cjs` (the desktop-only action; revoke from an earlier holder's card), `app/workspace-client.cjs`, `app/queue-secretary.cjs` (`follow()`, beside the unchanged `successor()`), `app/room-state.cjs` (`recordCarried`), `app/renderer/renderer.js` (the holder line on the card; the old session's menu revoke), `app/ui-messages.js`, and the tests and the hidden scenario.

Requested outcome: the person's session-creation grant should not be lost when NAW itself replaces the session that holds it. Until now the grant, and the per-session permission to use the agent control interface, were bound to a session id and native id; after a replacement the successor had neither, and nothing told the person. Now, once a replacement is finished, both go with the successor, one finished replacement at a time. The backend lists holders whose session has ended. The desktop, in a person's window only, looks in the rotation log for the one unambiguous successor, by the rule the secretary, integrator and steward designations already follow, and names it to the backend that owns the journal. That backend checks what it can see itself: the old session has ended and held the interface, the successor is a Claude session of the same backend with the native id the log names, and the person has made no setting for it. Then it re-binds the setting and the grants, and the old session no longer holds the interface.

It is the same grant. Quotas are counted per grant, so the daily and concurrent counts continue across the holders. Its expiry and the space it names are unchanged. Beside a grant in force, a revoked or expired grant is carried as it is, and a revoke reaches the grant wherever it has gone: from the card of any session that held it, from the old session's menu, or by turning any of them off. Each open still checks the holder's permission posture at that moment. With the interface off for everyone, or off for the old session, nothing is carried. What the old holder had already started under the grant (a report from a session it opened, a session waiting to join the grant's space) still counts under it until the person turns it off.

Anything ambiguous leaves the grant where it was: an old session still in use, two successors, a successor that replaced two sessions, a native id that does not match, a line in the log with no time, a successor in another backend, archived, or already given a setting by the person. A replacement logged before the person turned the holder's interface on is not a replacement of that holder at all: nothing is decided and nothing is said, as for a holder the person simply stopped. The outcome, carried or not, is saved once in the journal and is final: a grant that stayed is never moved later behind a notice that said it stayed, and the person turning the old session on again afterwards decides nothing anew. The holder stays listed until a space holds one entry saying what happened (that the permission and the grants went on; that only the permission did, when the grants that went with it were revoked or ran out before the entry was written; or that nothing did): the successor's spaces; failing that, where the replacement was recorded; and the default space when there is none, or when none of them could take the entry twice in a row. So a notice that could not be written is written later. The card of a carried grant says which session holds it now. From an agent's context the desktop refuses the step before any confirmation is shown, and no agent tool reaches it.

Independent review, three rounds in one session; the first two asked for changes. First round, two blocking findings. The old session's menu item that revokes its creation grants did nothing after a carry and still said it had; it now reaches a grant that has gone on from that session, as does turning that session off. And the notice in the space could be missing, or could say the grant stayed when it later moved; the outcome is now decided once in the journal and is final, and the holder stays listed until a space holds the entry. From its notes: reports and pending placements of what the old holder had started were being cut off and now continue under the grant; a chain is walked one step at a time, so a setting the person made for a session in between stops it; and a replacement logged before the holder's interface was turned on is not followed. Second round, one blocking finding: after a carry, the person turning the old session on again made the journal decide a second time and added a notice that the grant had not been carried, while the successor held it; a decision now survives the person's toggles, and a replacement older than the turning on is no replacement of that holder, so nothing is decided or said. Third round: passed, no blocking finding. Its most important missing test (what the old holder started must also end when the person turns the old session off after a carry) was added afterwards and passes. Left as noted: when a session turned on again is later really replaced, the log holds two replacements of it and the entry saying that the grant stayed does not say which period it covers; the time stamped on older settings at load is saved only with the next change to the journal.

Independent review of the narrowing and of the two rebases onto main (2026-11-11): a fresh read-only session, `claude-opus-5-5`, that had not seen the change before. APPROVE_WITH_NOTES, nothing blocking. It found no path that gives a successor the interface without a grant in force; refusals with a grant in force and notices owed for earlier outcomes are untouched; both rebases changed only context; and main's new unfinished outcomes (`trustStateInvalid`, `trustStateUnknown`) are never written to the rotation log, so they cannot look like a finished replacement. Its one note was a path the narrowing itself had opened: a holder with the interface on and no grant is replaced and nothing is decided; if the person later gives that ended session a grant, the grant and the interface would have followed the earlier replacement. Before the narrowing that could not happen, because the interface had already moved and the old session could no longer be given a grant. The reviewer left it to the person and asked for it to be recorded. The author closed it instead, since the decision reads as being about the time of the replacement and the other reading moves a permission further than was decided: only a grant the holder had when it was replaced counts. Whether such a late grant should go on is left to the person, below. The same session then reviewed that increment: APPROVE_WITH_NOTES, nothing blocking, the path closed for a carry and for a refusal, and nothing that should go on is stopped (a grant given while the hand-over was still in progress, a grant already carried once, a successor's own later grant, a grant given in the same millisecond). Two notes, both recorded and neither changed in the code. First, the window that was left as it was does the same kind of thing: when the holder also had an earlier grant in force, a grant given between the replacement and the step goes on with it. That window is usually seconds, but the step runs only while a window of the person's is open, so it can be longer; it was in the design reviewed before and is added to the question for the person. Second, the two times are wall-clock times of the same machine: if the clock is set back between a grant and the replacement, an earlier grant can fail to count (nothing moves and nothing is said), and if it is set back after the replacement, a later grant can count. The integrator's own reviewer then read the delivered version (APPROVE_WITH_NOTES, nothing blocking, no code change needed before installing) and named a small way to close the first note: in the step, move only the grants given no later than the replacement was logged. The integrator asked for that ahead of the person's answer, as the cautious side, to be opened again if the person chooses otherwise. It is built as its own commit. Building it showed one more place that had to follow: when a holder is decided in the same pass, the desktop counts the grants for the entry from the state taken before the carry, and would have counted a grant that stayed; it now counts by the same rule. The independent session that had raised the note reviewed this increment: APPROVE_WITH_NOTES, nothing blocking; a late grant cannot end up naming the successor or be counted or announced as having gone on, by the loop, the audit line, the entry written in the same pass or later, or a second carry; nothing new can start under the grant that stayed; a journal in that state loads; and nothing that should go on now stays. Its two notes: the wording about who can use the grant that stayed, corrected above; and a corner it judged unreachable in practice and that is left as it is: if a state taken before a carry were processed after it and the desktop's step were then a refusal, the journal would answer with the earlier outcome and the desktop would count the grants for the entry against the wrong time, possibly writing that only the interface went on.

Owner: the author of this change. Evidence: 29 unit tests in `app/tests/grant-succession.test.cjs` with a real backend journal and space store, the real log rule and the step from the main process, and one on the card in `app/tests/operator-ui.test.cjs`. The narrowing has its own test: four holders with no grant in force (never given one; the only one revoked; the only one run out; one revoked and one run out), for each of which the holder is not listed, the desktop asks nothing and does not read the log, the journal is byte for byte unchanged, the successor has no setting and cannot use the interface, nothing is written in any space, and a direct request to carry or to refuse is answered with no grant and saves nothing; a grant that runs out between the list and the step; and the control case, where a grant in force goes on with the interface. Five earlier tests that described the interface going on alone were rewritten for the narrower rule. Removing the check from the step turns one test red, removing it from the list three, removing both four. The rule about when the grant was given has its own test: a holder with the interface on and no grant, replaced an hour ago and given a grant only now (listed, asked once, journal byte for byte unchanged, the grant still with the old session, the successor without a setting and unable to use the interface, nothing written in any space, carry and refuse both answered with no grant); a grant given in the same millisecond as the replacement was logged, which counts; a holder whose earlier grant was revoked and whose grant in force was given afterwards; a grant with no time of its own, which does not count; a line with no time, refused and announced as before; and the control case, a holder with three earlier grants (one in force, one run out, one revoked) and two more that it was given after it was replaced or that have no time of their own: the three go on as they are and are the ones named in the audit line, the two stay in the old session's name and are not marked as having gone on, the entry counts one grant, the successor opens under the grant that went on, a request of the successor that names the grant that stayed creates nothing and waits for the person, and the person's revoke from the old session reaches the grant that stayed. Four deliberate breakages of the rule for following (the step ignoring the time, strictly-before instead of no-later-than, a grant without a time counting, a line without a time counting nothing) and five of the rule for what goes on (the step moving every grant that names the old session, the desktop counting every such grant, strictly-before, a grant without a time moving, a grant without a time counted by the desktop) each turn a test red. Before the narrowing: 46 deliberate breakages of the new code and three of the card change, each turning the tests red; full unit checks pass with no failures; in a hidden window with synthetic members and no model, the main-process dispatcher really replaced a member that held a grant, the grant was with the new member as soon as the old one had ended, the space said so in Chinese and English, the new member opened a session under the same grant without a new approval, the third open of the day stopped, the old member's card named the new holder, and a real click on the old member's menu revoked the grant (that step fails with the earlier menu code); the full queue journey, the open scenario and the operator journeys still pass. After the narrowing, the rule about when the grant was given, and the rebase onto main `db7846c`: the full unit suite passes, 6209 tests, none failed or skipped; and the same hidden journeys pass again, six runs with synthetic members and no model (the dispatcher really replacing a member that holds a grant, in Chinese and in English; the open scenario; the full queue journey; the operator journey with a space and without). Two of those runs were first started without the notification fixture, which the script refuses, so nothing ran; they were started again with it. With the last step (only what the holder had when it was replaced goes on): the full unit suite passes again, 6209 tests, none failed or skipped, and four of the hidden journeys pass again (the dispatcher replacing a member that holds a grant, in Chinese and in English; the open scenario; the operator journey with a space).

Decided by the person on 2026-11-11: a grant follows a replacement, and the interface permission goes on only when the holder has at least one grant in force (the narrower rule suggested by the integrator's review). For the person to decide, with the cautious answer built: whether a grant given to a session after it was already replaced should go on to its successor. As built it does not; it stays with the old session, which has ended and cannot use it, and nothing is said. The likely case is a request the old session made before it was replaced and the person approved afterwards; the person can give the successor a grant of its own. The same holds when the old session also had an earlier grant in force: a grant given after the replacement and before the desktop's step stays with the old session too (as first built and reviewed it went on with the earlier one; that was closed on the integrator's instruction until the person answers, and is to be opened again if the person wants late grants to go on). The entry in the space does not mention a grant that stayed. Not carried: pending or unfinished opens of the old session. Known: a successor in another backend never receives the grant, because the journal and its counts live in the old backend. A holder whose interface was turned on before this change has no recorded time for it; it gets the time the journal is next loaded, and only a replacement logged after that is followed. The rotation log is a private file of the desktop; a process that can write it as the person can equally write the grant journal itself, which is the boundary the designations already have. What is refused is a line that does not match what is there: a holder still running, a successor with another native id, a log that others can write.

## B6 integration handoff: four points from the review of the notice and the settlement — 2026-11-11

The integrator's reviewer passed the last two changes (the line that tells a space its member is held, and the corrected settlement) and named four things to mend before the switch may be opened. All are in code that runs only with the switch open, except one constant of the dispatcher that is now frozen.

**1. The line in the space had no ending.** A space that had been told "this member's handoff waits for you; no new tasks for it" went on saying so after the handoff was over. When the handoff a space was told about is over (or another one has taken its place), the space is now told once that it is finished and that the member gets tasks again. The engine remembers which spaces it told, per space and handoff; after a restart it reads from the spaces' records which lines are still open (again on the next pass if they cannot be read then), so a handoff that ended while the app was down still gets its ending. An ending is written only where the handoff was said to be open, and nothing is ended while the handoff record cannot be read.

**2. A later reply could replace a real answer.** With "the last message that reads like an answer wins", an answer written before another agent's message could be replaced by the integrator's reply to that message: an unrelated "needs your decision" made the handoff wait on it and dropped the real results, and a RETURNED or HELD line could replace an earlier MERGED, although only merges are checked. Now:
- With no answer before someone else's message, a later one is the answer, as before: a question is put to the person, a merge is checked, a returned or held delivery is named by its commit.
- With an answer before it, that answer stands. A merge that a later message reports in a line that can be read is laid over it, since git decides that merge; this is how a real answer written after a provisional line still wins. A later line that only repeats what the earlier answer said about a delivery changes nothing. Anything else in a later message (a question, another result for a delivery, a merge line that cannot be read) cannot be told from words meant for someone else: the earlier results are recorded, later merges are checked, and the handoff waits for the person. The question shown is the integrator's own earlier one if it asked one (a later question may be its reply to the other message), else the later message's, else none (the person is pointed to the integrator's session).
- An earlier message with nothing but lines that cannot be read (a stray note, lines copied from the handoff's own text) is no answer to protect: the later message is then the answer, and the count of unreadable lines is kept.

**3. A member's message through a space was taken for the person's.** A message through a space with a sender's name is another member's (it comes from that member's outbox) and now counts as a message from someone else, like another agent's wake. Without a name it is the person's own message in the space or a turn of an exchange they started, and makes the handoff wait as their own step, as before.

**4. What the reviewer could not verify, checked in the source.**
- The person's own message through a space and the routed turns of a running exchange both arrive with the origin "room" and no sender's name (`app/workspace.cjs`, the general send path: "room" when there is a route, "human" otherwise; an agent's operation overwrites the origin with "agent-control"). A member's outbox message arrives as "room" with the member's name.
- A space's events are not capped; only the person's "clear the shared record" empties them. Recognising a line that was already written by finding it among the events therefore holds; after such a clear an open handoff is told once more, which is right.
- The phone page does not read space events at all, so the new lines are not shown there.
- The step that tells the spaces reads the space records from memory; nothing is read from disk in each pass.

**Two smaller things in the dispatcher's file, now that it may be changed again.** The list of automatic origins, which the handoff reads, is frozen, so no module that reads it can change it for the queue. A pass of the engine that ends in a fault after it has changed something (a handoff settled, a record written) now still tells the windows; before, they caught up at the next announcement.

**Checks.** The plan test covers, for each kind of message from someone else (four origins, among them a member's message through a space, and two markers): a question after it with and without an earlier answer; later merges laid over a provisional line, over copied template lines and over an earlier RETURNED; a later RETURNED or HELD that leaves the earlier MERGED standing and asks, with the record taking that settlement; a later line that only repeats the earlier result; a later merge line that cannot be read; the integrator's own question standing when merges or another question follow; an earlier message of unreadable lines only; unreadable later lines; an empty row; only words. The person's message through a space, with no name or a blank one, still makes the handoff wait. The dispatcher test covers the ending (once, with its sentence; not where nothing was open; nothing while the record is unreadable, in the pass and in the telling step itself; after a restart from the spaces' records, also when they cannot be read on the first pass), a pass that settles a handoff while the space's writer is broken (the windows are told, the fault is kept, the ending is written later) and the frozen list. Twenty-six and thirteen deliberate breakages each turned tests red. In the real window the probe shows the first line and then the ending in the space's shared record; the full unit suite and both journeys pass on the delivered head (counts in the delivery note).

**Independent review (passed, with two fixes and four suggestions, all taken).** The author lane's own reviewer (headless session 980f8974) went through every combination of an earlier and a later message, confirmed that a sender's name is a reliable sign of another member, that an ending cannot be written while the handoff is open, and that the dispatcher's daily path changes only by the frozen constant. Its fixes: a later MERGED line that could not be read replaced the earlier result and left a real merge stuck as not verified; and when both messages asked something, the earlier question, the one about this handoff, was hidden. Its suggestions: a repeated line is agreement; an earlier message of unreadable lines only is no answer; read the spaces again if that fails at the start; remember by space and handoff.

**Left open.**
- When the handoff waits because of point 2 with no question of its own, the person is told "the integrator met a conflict and asks you to decide", the sentence of every waiting handoff with a decision; a sentence of its own would say it better.
- A routed turn of a running exchange carries another member's words but no name, and still counts as the person's step, because the person started the exchange.
- An ending is not written into an archived space, and the member's name in it is the one the space was first told.
- An ending that could not be written because the space was being updated is written by the next pass that runs for another reason; it keeps no passes going by itself.
- git failing in the middle of a settlement still reads as "no such commit" (see the section on the main repository).

## B6 integration handoff: what the queue panel will read — where each delivered task stands, and giving a returned task back — 2026-11-11

The person agreed (task board, 11-11) that deliveries on hold are shown in the space's queue panel, prototype first. The prototype pictures are with the person. This is the part behind the screen and changes nothing they see: two more actions of the person's own handoff entry, behind the closed switch like the rest of the handoff.

**Where each delivery stands.** For one space the entry gives the overview and, by queue item (in an object without a prototype, so that any item name is only a key), the delivery that task led to: it waits to be handed out, the integrator has it, it is inside a handoff that waits for the person, it is on hold (with the reason), merged (as which main commit, with the test count), or returned (with the integrator's words, and whether its task was given back). A delivery that a newer one of the same branch replaced is left out. A returned or held line that gave no reason carries no words, not the record's own "unspecified". Looking changes and announces nothing.

**Giving a returned task back.** The person may put the task of a returned delivery back into the space's queue. The new task is the old one as it was written (the delivery's short label when the queue no longer has the task, the branch when there is no label), followed by the branch and the integrator's reason; a long task is cut so that the reason still fits, and not between the two units of one code point. It goes to the member who did it while that member is in the space, not archived and not ended; otherwise to no one in particular, so that any free member takes it, and the answer says which. The delivery is then marked, so that it is not offered again; the mark is valid only on a returned delivery and is kept across a restart. Like every action of this entry it is the person's alone.

**Once.** After the list of sessions was read, the check of the delivery, the new task and the mark are one step, so two presses, or two windows, add one task. When the task cannot be added (the queue is full, the space is gone, archived or being updated), nothing is marked and the queue's own refusal is shown. When the mark cannot be saved, the task that was just added is cancelled again, the windows are told (the space's record changed) and the record's fault is shown; if the task cannot be cancelled either, the person is told that it is still in the queue and not to press again.

**Checks.** The record test covers the state of each delivery by queue item (waiting, with the integrator, inside a waiting handoff, on hold with its reason, merged with commit and tests, returned with the integrator's words), another space, a replaced delivery, that what is handed out is a copy, the mark (only on a returned delivery, once, kept across a restart) and a saved record that carries the mark elsewhere. The entry tests run the real entry on a real record and a real space record: the view for one space and for another, values that are no space; the task given back with its full text, branch and reason, to its member, announced once; a second press and two presses at once (one task); a line with no reason; who gets the task (in the space, left, ended, membership unreadable, not listed, delivery without a member, archived but listed in the space again); the short label and the branch as names; a task of the greatest length, one that just fits and one cut at a two-unit character; a full queue (refused, nothing marked, works once there is room); a space that is gone; sessions that cannot be read; a mark that cannot be saved (the task is cancelled, the windows told, the fault said, the delivery still to be given back) and a task that then cannot be cancelled either (said as still in the queue, the fault kept); a queue item named like a property every object has. An agent's call, the closed switch and an engine that did not start refuse both actions like the others. Thirty-eight deliberate breakages each turned a test red. The full unit suite and the handoff journey in the real window pass on the delivered head (counts in the delivery note).

Not taken: writing the delivery's key on the new queue task so that the record could refuse while such a task is open. It would close the two ways left to a second task (below), but it adds a field to saved queue items, which an older version of the app, after a rollback, may refuse to read.

**Left open.**

- Nothing is on screen yet; the panel that reads this is the next step.

Requested (the integrator's dispatch): when the read log page cannot be bound,
the window shows nothing, and the person takes that for "no records". Show the
failure and its reason on the page, never as "no records", and make this
page's window check catch it. The entry's switch stays closed; only the read
log page and its checks change.

Reproduced first, in the product's own hidden window with the entry's test
switch on and the page's program kept out of the window: the window started,
and choosing "what it has read" from the entry showed a notice for a few
seconds saying the log could not be read right now, and no page. That sentence
is the one used when the log file itself cannot be read, so it also blamed the
wrong thing. A second silent case was found on the way: a page that was set up
and then threw as it was asked for showed nothing at all.

What happens now:
- A page that could not be set up opens, when asked for, as a page in the read
  log's own place with one sentence that says which of three things happened
  (its program is not in this window; its place in the page is missing;
  setting it up failed), that this is a fault of the interface, that it does
  not mean the butler read nothing, and what to do. If the page has no place
  in the window, one is made for it.
- A page that was set up and fails as it is asked for, at the call or later,
  is torn down and replaced by the same view with a fourth reason.
- A failure while drawing what was read says that the log was read and the
  page could not show it. It used to say the log could not be read.
- If the failure view itself cannot be shown, a notice says it is the page
  that failed. Nothing in any of these reads as an empty or unreadable log,
  and no error text reaches the screen; the error goes to the console.

The sentences first said "the log file has not been touched". The window
cannot know that, so it now says what the code supports: this page only
displays the log, so its failing to open does not change the log file. That
rests on three facts, each tested: the page's program makes one kind of call,
the read; the main process answers it with the log's read and nothing else;
and that read leaves the file byte for byte as it was, with no lock left.

Checks (author-run, no model):
- Unit tests run the window's own setup lines with each part missing, and
  with pages that fail at the call, later, and at teardown. 49 deliberate
  faults in the changed lines and sentences; a first run let one through (the
  test's stand-in for a dialog accepted being shown twice) and showed that a
  teardown that throws had no test. Both are fixed; all are caught.

- Counts for the full suite and the three hidden-window checks are in the
  commit message.

Not verified, or known:
- Two of the four reasons are reached only in unit tests. In this window the
  page is built and set up in one step, so the check cannot take the page's
  place away before the setup, and a setup that throws with both parts present
  has no way to be provoked from outside.
- The entry's own setup failure is unchanged: the row is then absent, and
  nothing says why. The dispatch limited this change to the read log page.
- The sentences are new text the person has not seen. They are on the
  screenshots kept with the private evidence.
- A failure while drawing "reading", "cannot be read" or the drawing-failure

Independent read-only review (one fresh session, the code as rebased onto

## B6 integration handoff: the queue panel says where each delivered task stands and what waits for the person — 2026-11-11

The person agreed (task board, 11-11) that deliveries on hold are shown in the space's queue panel, prototype first. The prototype's third round was accepted by a stand-in reviewer in the person's place and its pictures are with the person. This is that screen in the product. It is drawn only where the window's state says that handoffs are enabled, and the state says so only with the switch open (also when, with the switch open, the engine could not start: the panel then says that it did not start, and why). With the switch closed, as in the daily app, the state carries no such word, the page asks the main process nothing about handoffs, and the panel is as it was.

**What the panel shows.**
- On the row of each delivered task, in place of the queue's own status: where its delivery stands, with the member's name. Delivered and no integrator yet; goes to the integrator when it is free; in line until the integrator is done, or until the person has dealt with what it waits for; delivered while handoffs are paused; with the integrator; with the integrator and waiting for the person's answer (or for the person, when it did not ask anything); merged into main; on hold; returned; given back to redo. The integrator is called by its session's name.
- A row on hold says why in one short sentence (the causes the space's record already tells apart, without the task's text; a cause with no sentence of its own shows the integrator's words, or that none were given) and has "Send again". A returned row shows the integrator's reason and "Give back to" the member who did it, or "Put back in the queue" when that member can no longer take a task.
- Rows that wait for the person, and rows that a handoff waiting for the person is about, come first when the panel opens. While it stays open no row changes place and a row that appears later goes to the end; the places are those of the first view whose reading began after the opening, also when that view has nothing to say about this space yet. A row that waits for the person stays in the list although its task is older than the ten finished tasks the panel shows, and also when the queue no longer has the task.
- A block on top: who the integrator is, and how many of this space's deliveries it has or are in line; with nobody designated, how to designate one; once there is an integrator, the project folder where merges are checked (its last two parts, the whole path on hover; or that none is chosen, which folder to choose and that finished work is not handed over until then; or why the chosen one cannot be read now) with a button that opens the system's folder dialog; that handoffs are paused while the designated integrator is inside a space; a fault of the handoff step or of its record. When a handoff waits for the person and is about a delivery of this space: what the integrator asks (or that it did not answer, or that the person wrote in its session), which deliveries of this space it is about, a button that opens the integrator's session, "Done, send again" (or "Send again"), "Hold for now", and a line that says what the two do. When it is about another space's deliveries and this space's are in line behind it: the same words, the name of that space, and the button that opens the integrator's session; the two steps are offered in the space whose deliveries they act on. A space with nothing in line is not told about another space's handoff.
- The button that opens the panel says how many things in this space wait for the person: rows on hold; returned rows not yet given back; a waiting handoff, as far as the block above shows it here; and, while a delivery of this space is in line or with the integrator, a main repository that is missing or cannot be read and an integrator inside a space. A space whose deliveries are all settled shows the repository's folder without weight and counts nothing for it.
- A step that is refused says so inside the panel: for a folder that will not do, first that it was not chosen and to choose another, then the cause in smaller words.
- On screen the folder is called the project folder throughout; the five older sentences that said "main repository" (four refusals and the system notice) now say the same.

**Behind it.**
- The main process tells the window that handoffs are enabled (read from the dispatcher, which the state already reads), gives each delivery on hold the words for its row (from the table that already groups the reasons), and has one more action of the person's own entry: choosing the main repository in the system's folder dialog, opened for the person's window. The folder goes through the same checks as one that is named; the page names no path.
- The rules of the display are a module of their own without the page (`app/renderer/handoff-queue.js`): from the view, the queue and the sessions it gives the rows, the block, the count and the order.
- The page reads the view for the space on screen when that space's record or the integrator changes, and with every state while the panel is open: one read at a time, at most a few a second.

**Found in the real window while building.**
- A refusal shown in the general notice at the foot of the window lies behind an open panel, blurred and out of reach. The panel's new buttons therefore say a refusal in a line of their own. The queue's older buttons (cancel, dealt with, add) still use the general notice.
- A row that began to wait for the person while the panel was open jumped to the top when the view read after opening had shown nothing new. The places are now kept from that first read on; with that line taken out again the real-window script fails.
- A long folder path broke its line after two characters; the words and the button are now two columns.

The state function now reads only the dispatcher, the row builder is as it was (the delivery's state is added where the rows are drawn), and the new dialog's options sit after the last of their kind.

**Different from the prototype's third round.** Taken from the stand-in's last remarks: "Hold for now" with a line that says it lets the others go first; the integrator's name in the statuses; the path "hold, send again, asked again, done, returned" run as a test. New, because the prototype was drawn before them: the main repository's line; "handoffs are paused" on rows; a waiting handoff that is not a question; the refusal line. Reworded: "goes to the integrator when it is free" instead of "about to go". As decided there, "main can be installed" is not in this panel.

It blocked on two display rules: a handoff that waits for the person was shown and counted in every space that had any delivery, with the steps offered away from the deliveries they act on; and an engine that had not started was reported as "cannot be read right now", because the panel's own question to the main process was refused where the overview's was answered. Both are mended as described above, the second with a test that goes through the real entry. Also taken: a view counts as read after the opening only if its reading began after it; the places are kept from a view without rows too; a refresh that fails no longer hides what came of the step; the view after a step is one read after it; a held row offers no "send again" while nobody is designated; a member without a name is still named on the button the way the main process treats it; a holder whose session is gone is not called by the designated one's name; "Hand over again" and "Send again" are two different English labels; the count in English no longer needs a plural; the hint quotes the menu item in full; a wait in the script that could not fail is now a check after the step. On the increment it passed and suggested six more things; five are taken: a handoff about this and other spaces names the others and says that the two steps act on all its deliveries; when no other space's panel can be opened the steps are offered here; the places are not kept from a view that could not be read; a failing draw inside a read no longer hides what came of a step; each space's name is quoted on its own.
