## B6 integration handoff: git that does not answer is not "no such commit" — 2026-11-11

One of the things to mend before the switch may be opened (listed under the main repository's section and again under the review follow-ups). Behind the closed switch like the rest.

**What was wrong.** A reported merge is checked by asking git six things. The reader answered "null" both when git said no (there is no such commit) and when git said nothing at all: it failed, timed out, was killed for too much output, or the repository had gone away after its head was read. So trouble with git during the check made a real merge look like a claim that failed: the delivery was held as "not found in main", and the queue panel now shows that cause to the person on the task's own row.

**Now.**
- The reader tells the two apart: null (or false) is git's answer "no"; undefined means git did not answer. A name that could never be a commit is still refused before git is asked.
- The check of a merge gives a verdict of its own for an unanswered question. A "no" that git did answer stands, whatever went unanswered beside or after it.
- The engine treats an unanswered question like a head that cannot be read: nothing is settled on that pass, the handoff keeps its place, and the answer is checked again on later passes, for the same bounded while (ten minutes from the first time, kept with the handoff, so a restart does not begin it again). If git answers within that time the merge is recorded as usual.
- After that the answer is settled, and a merge whose check went unanswered is held as "could not be checked" (the reason the record already has for a head that cannot be read), never as a merge that was not found. A merge line that cannot be read at all stays an unverified claim, as before.
- The three sentences for that reason (the row in the panel, the space's record, the system notice) now say that NAW could not read the project folder, which is true for both causes; the row adds that this does not mean the work was not merged.

**Independent review (blocked once, then passed).** A reviewer that had seen none of this (headless session 8f6e7280) found no caller of the reader that treats the new answer differently, that the wait cannot go on without end, that a merge is never recorded from an unanswered check and that a line that cannot be read stays an unverified claim. It blocked on one order: with nothing delivered (or a range too large) on one side and no answer on the other, the verdict was "no answer", against the rule that an answered "no" stands. That pair is now decided like the pair of commits, with tests for each side. Its other remarks are under "Left open".

**Checks.** The reader on a real repository: a folder that is gone and a folder that is no repository give no answer to any of the three questions, a commit the repository does not have is "no" for the commit and no answer for ancestry and changes, refused names stay refused. The verdict: each of the six questions unanswered, alone and together; an answered "no" beside an unanswered question; a repository that is gone and a starting commit that is no longer there, against real git. The record: one line unanswered, one answered "no", one confirmed and one unreadable in the same answer; a verdict made for another handoff does not count. The engine: each question unanswered, the wait kept and bounded, nothing written or read afresh while it waits, the hold after it; git answering again within the wait; one unanswered merge beside a confirmed one; an answered "no" does not wait. Twenty-four deliberate breakages each turned a test red. Two lines of the reader have no test that makes them fail on their own: the patch text or the patch ids failing after the list of commits was read.

**Left open.**
- A delivery held as "could not be checked" had no way back to "merged": sent again, the integrator reports the same merge, which is then no longer new for the later handoff, so whenever the merge really landed the retry ended as not verified. Mended in the next section (the claim is kept and can be checked again).
- Patch text over the reader's own limit (64 MB) or a git run over its fifteen seconds also count as "no answer": they are NAW's fixed limits, so waiting does not help, each pass runs the heavy command again, and the person is then told the folder could not be read. A range of more than five hundred commits is still "not found". The two limits want a verdict of their own.
- A full commit id that the repository does not have is "no answer" for ancestry and changes (git ends with the same code as for its own trouble). In the check this can only be the main commit the handoff began on; it then waits and is held as "could not be checked".
- The wait shares its clock with the wait for main's head: a handoff that already waited for the head waits correspondingly less for an unanswered question.

## B6 integration handoff: a merge that could not be checked can be checked again — 2026-11-11

The follow-up to the section above, and one more thing to mend before the switch may be opened. Behind the closed switch.

**What was wrong.** A delivery held as "could not be checked" (main's head could not be read, or git did not answer a question about the merge) had one step: send it to the integrator again. For a merge that had in fact been made, that could not work: the integrator reports the same merge, the later handoff began on a main that already holds it, so it is "not new" and ends as "not verified". The row in the queue panel offered exactly that step.

**Now.**
- When a reported merge is held because git could not be read, what was reported is kept with the hold: the commit the line names, the test count, the review note if any, and the main commit the handoff began on. It belongs to that hold only: every way out (the person's retry of the delivery or of the reason, a newer delivery of the branch, the second check itself) drops it, and a saved record that carries it anywhere else, or in another shape, is not read.
- The person's "Check again" on such a row asks git about that claim once more, in one checked look at the project folder, against the main commit of the handoff it was merged in. So a merge made then is still judged as new, however far main has moved since.
  - Verified: the delivery is merged, with the tests that were reported, and the main commit of that moment may be installed (one question per main commit, as when a handoff is settled). The next pass tells the space and the person.
  - Git answers "no", the tests did not all pass, or the verdict is for another commit than the one named: the delivery stays on hold as an unverified claim, and from then on is sent again like any other hold.
  - Git still does not answer, or main's head still cannot be read: nothing changes, and the person is told that nothing was checked. The two are said differently: when the head was read but git said nothing about the merge, the folder is not named as the trouble.
  - An install question that was opened while the check was asking git is about a newer main, which holds this merge too: it stands, also when the person has answered it meanwhile, and the older main the check had read is not offered in its place. Nothing but an install question has that effect.
- In the panel a row with such a claim has "Check again", also while nobody is designated: it needs the folder, not an integrator. "Send to … again" stays beside it while there is an integrator, for a check that can never be answered (a change too large for the reader's limits, a starting commit the folder does not have). A hold of that kind from before this change has no claim and keeps the one button it had.
- A claim whose tests did not all pass is settled without asking git.

**Checks.** The record: what is kept (a short id, a review note, a failed test count), the copy handed out, each outcome of the second check, the install question asked once per main commit, a verdict for another commit, a missing main head, a changed claim refused, each of the three other ways out dropping the claim, an unreadable head keeping it and an unreadable line keeping none, six kinds of damage to a saved claim, a claim on a merged delivery, and a hold from before claims were kept. The engine: git answering after main has moved on (the two ancestry questions are asked with the handoff's own starting commit), done once, still silent, four kinds of unreadable head without git being asked, an answered "no", a failed test count without git or the head being read, the checked look asked once and the general reader never, a look that cannot be had, keys that are no such delivery. The person's entry, on the real record and engine: the row is told to the panel and drawn as "Check again" with and without an integrator; no answer said as that with nothing changed or announced; merged; done once; unverified and then offered as "send again"; a record that cannot be saved; a dispatcher without an engine; an agent, the closed switch and an engine that did not start refused. Forty-three deliberate breakages each turned a test red (two of them only after tests were added for the race: at the engine, and for a question of another kind opened meanwhile). The full unit suite and the real-window journeys pass on the delivered head (counts in the delivery note).

**Independent review (blocked once, then passed).** The reviewer of the section above (headless session 8f6e7280) went through every place a delivery's state or reason changes and found the claim dropped on each way out and written on each way in, a second press or a step taken meanwhile refused, and nothing accepted that a settlement would not accept. It blocked on a dead end this change had made: with "Check again" in place of "Send … again", a hold whose check can never be answered had no step at all, and its refusal blamed the folder. Both buttons are now there, and the refusal says which of the two kinds of silence it was. Its other point is taken too: a newer install question opened during the check is kept.

**Left open.**
- Not run in a real window: making git unreadable there takes the ten-minute wait. The row and its button are covered by the tests of the display rules and of the entry.
- Nothing checks a claim again by itself once the folder can be read; it is the person's step.
- A delivery held as "not verified" because git answered "no" has no second check: it is sent again, as before.

## B6 integration handoff: an integrator found inside a space is not read — 2026-11-11

The second half of "the integrator is put into a space while it holds a handoff", listed since the first half (the queue leaves such a session alone) went in. Behind the closed switch.

**The rule.** Once the session that holds an open handoff sits in a space, nothing it writes is read as that handoff's answer. The members of the space and the space's queue may be speaking to it, and a reply cannot be told from words meant for them. The handoff waits for the person instead: at once, whether the session is at work or idle and whatever it has written (results, a question, nothing).
- What is decided before the session is looked at stays as it was: a handoff not yet confirmed as sent, a designation taken away, a session that is gone.
- A membership record that cannot be read says neither yes nor no: nothing is settled from such a look, the first or the fresh one.
- Only the handoff's own native session counts; another one under the same id is "gone", as before.
- The person is told once by the system notice that already exists for "the designated integrator is inside a space" (its words now speak of deliveries that are paused, which fits those already handed too), each delivery's space says why it waits, and the holder's line in the space is the "waits for you" one. With the queue panel, the block on top says that the integrator is in a space, why its words are not read, and what to do: move it out (or designate another), then "Moved out, send again"; or "Hold for now". The general line about paused handoffs is not shown beside it.
- The person's steps are those of any waiting handoff. With a retry the deliveries may be handed again (to the same session only once it is out of every space; until then the person is asked about that, as before). Without, they are on hold under that reason, with a sentence of their own in the space and in the panel, and the person's retry brings them back. A later handoff does not take them along: until now nothing could be on hold under that reason, and opening a handoff let go of everything under it; it now only ends the question.
- Moving the session out again does not make the old answer count: a waiting handoff is the person's to end.

**What changed for the earlier half.** A handoff's holder found in a space used to be told to the space as "is working on a handoff"; now the handoff waits at once, so the space is told "waits for you". The other line remains for a handoff whose message is not yet confirmed as sent.

**Checks.** The record: five kinds of session all planned as that wait; without "in a space" each read as before; the earlier decisions unchanged; the settlement (the place kept, told once, each delivery's reason, no line and no question taken, kept across a restart, the count for the notice, the panel's view); a later look, in or out of the space, changing nothing; both ways of ending it and the retries; another reason still refused. The engine: settled without the answer, git or a fresh look being read; a session at work; the older single-space field; unreadable membership on the first look (with and without merges) and on the fresh one; put into a space while git is read; another native session under the id. The dispatcher's two tests of a holder in a space now describe this (the wait at once, the one notice, later words of the integrator and the person's typing changing nothing, the faulted pass that still tells the windows). The words: the two new space sentences, the row's, the notice's. The display rules: the block's kind, the general line left out, the count, the rows. Fifteen deliberate breakages each turned a test red. In the real window (one more stage of `scripts/test-handoff-panel.cjs`): a delivery is with the integrator, the person moves the integrator's session into the space, the handoff waits, the integrator writes words that would be a question and they are not taken for one; the panel says so; the person moves it out, presses "Moved out, send again", and the merge that follows counts.

**Independent review (blocked once, then passed).** The reviewer of the two sections above (headless session 8f6e7280) found no path on which such a holder's answer is still read, the wait safe also while the session works, and the reason told once. It blocked on the hold: deliveries the person had left on hold from such a handoff were let go by the next handoff that opened, without a step of theirs, against what the panel and the row say. That is mended as described under the person's steps, with a test.

**Left open.**
- A membership record that stays unreadable keeps the handoff as "sent" and is reported nowhere; the hand-out side already behaved so.
- After "Hold for now" while the session is still in the space, the notice that asks about it counts the deliveries just held, not those waiting to be handed.
- If the integrator did merge while it sat in the space, that merge is not read; sent again after it is moved out, it reports the same merge, which was then no longer new for the later handoff and ended as not verified. The same held for every handoff that is ended and sent again after a merge was made (no reply, the person's typing). The next section gives such a merge a step of its own.
- The holder's "waits for you" line that could not be written when the handoff began to wait is written by the next pass that runs for another reason (a waiting handoff is nothing the engine can move).
- The real-window stage waits four seconds before it looks, to give the engine time to read what it must not read.

## B6 integration handoff: a merge made before its handoff began waits for the person's confirmation — 2026-11-11

Listed as open in the three sections above, and one more thing to mend before the switch may be opened. Behind the closed switch.

**What was wrong.** A reported merge counts when three things hold: the named commit is on main now; it was not on main when the handoff began; and it holds all of the delivery's changes. A delivery that is handed again, after a handoff that waited (no reply, the person's own typing, the integrator inside a space) or after a hold the person ended, may already have been merged while the earlier handoff was open. The integrator then reports that merge, main already held it when the later handoff began, and the check calls it "not new": a real merge ended as "not verified". Sent again, the integrator reports the same merge again; no step could mend it.

**Tried first and dropped.** Judging "new" against the main commit of the delivery's first handoff, so that such a merge simply counts. The independent review refused it: the three questions are about main's history, and history says that the named commit came to main after the first handoff, not that its changes are still in effect. A merge made during the first handoff and reverted before the second would have been recorded as merged by NAW itself, and that main registered as one that may be installed.

**Now.** The automatic check is as strict as it was: new for the handoff at hand, or it does not count.
- Where main was when a delivery first reached an integrator is kept with the delivery (`firstHead`), through every later handoff. "Reached" is a send that was confirmed, and one that never was (the handoff then fails as unconfirmed, but the message may have arrived; a crash between opening the handoff and sending it ends the same way, with nothing sent, which can only lead to a hold that waits for the person). A send that was refused went nowhere and keeps nothing; so does a delivery that came in while the handoff was open. A newer delivery of a branch is another delivery and has none yet.
- When the strict answer is "already on main when this handoff began" (the named commit, or the delivery itself, was behind that main) and the delivery first reached an integrator on another main commit, the same three questions are asked once more against that first commit. If they hold, the verdict is `merged-earlier`. It is never "verified". What it establishes: the delivery's commits (by id, or by the id of their change) are in main's history in the named commit; they came to main after the delivery first reached an integrator, and the delivery was already in main's history when this handoff began (the named commit itself may be a later one, main's current head for instance). Not by whom, and not that it is still in effect.
- Such a delivery is held under a reason of its own, `merged-earlier`, with the merge that was reported kept beside it. Nothing says "merged", and no main commit is registered for installing. The space's record and the person's notice say that the delivery was already in main's history before the handoff began and is recorded as merged only once the person confirms it. The row in the queue panel says more: that NAW cannot tell whether it was undone since; and, because a person cannot look into main, that someone who is not sure should first ask the integrator in its session whether the change is still there, and which button follows from each answer. It also says that the row may come back after the delivery was merged anew, and that "Confirm merged" is then the step: when the first merge was a merge commit or a fast-forward that was reverted, the delivery's own commits are still in main's history, so the next handoff's strict check finds nothing new ("no changes") however the new merge is made, and the new merge is held the same way. A new merge counts by itself only if the delivery's own commits never came into main's history (the first merge, too, landed copies: a cherry-pick, a rebase). The confirmation then records the new merge. (The stand-in for the person refused the first wording, which told the person to confirm "if you know it is still in main" and otherwise to send it again: sent again while the merge is still there, the same row comes back, and the only way out would have been a confirmation pressed on a guess.)
- The row offers "Confirm merged" and, beside it, "Send to … again". "Confirm merged" is the person's step (an agent's call is refused, as for every step of this panel): the kept merge is asked of git against the first commit once more, and recorded as merged if that holds, with the commit and the test count that were reported; the main it was checked on is then registered for installing. If it no longer holds (main was moved back since), the delivery becomes a plain unverified claim; if git does not answer, nothing changes and the panel says so.
- "Confirm merged" and "Check again" are two steps, from the button to the record: each names the hold it is for, and a delivery held the other way is refused as stale. So a press on a "Check again" button that was drawn before the hold changed (another window, or a row not yet drawn anew) never confirms a merge, and a check that was under way when the delivery was sent again and came back as an earlier merge is refused when it returns, although commit and start are the same. The second round of the independent review found this: both buttons had gone through one action that acted on whatever hold it met.
- A merge that could not be checked at all (held as "could not be checked") and is checked again later may turn out to be such an earlier merge: that second check does not record it either; the hold becomes one that waits for the person's confirmation.
- A record from before the first commit was kept has none for its deliveries, and they are judged as before. A value that is no commit id is refused when the record is read. A `merged-earlier` verdict that names another commit than the reported one, or comes for a delivery with no first commit kept, is treated as an unverified claim, in the settlement and in the second check.

**Checks.** The record (`integrator-settle.test.cjs`): the first commit kept at the first confirmed send and at an unconfirmed one that failed, not before, not for a refused send, not for a delivery outside the handoff, unchanged by a later handoff, absent for a newer delivery; a merge made during the first handoff told apart from a delivery first handed out in the second (same commit named: one `merged-earlier`, one `not-new`); which main commits git is asked about; held, not merged, nothing to install, the claim kept against the first commit; the person's confirmation recording it; a delivery merged with a merge commit and reported under a later commit ("no changes" for this handoff) told apart the same way; four cases that are not an earlier merge (the first commit unanswered, the named commit behind it too, the changes not all there since, a merge new for this handoff that does not hold the delivery); verdicts that do not fit refused; an older record judged as before; an unchecked merge found to be an earlier one on its second check, and the claim as first asked for then stale; a claim asked for under the other reason refused, and a claim read under one reason refused under the other although commit and start are the same. The engine (`integrator-engine-settle.test.cjs`): the same through two real hand-outs, the space record and the person's notice saying "waits for you" and nothing registered for installing, the person's step asking git about the first commit, "check again" refused on such a hold without asking git, the person's step refused when main was moved back, an unchecked merge found late and a second "check again" on it refused. The entry (`integrator-actions.test.cjs`): `confirm` is the person's alone, refused with the switch closed and with no engine, refused for every delivery not held that way; `recheck` refused on a hold that waits for confirmation and `confirm` on one that could not be checked, nothing written; git silent said as that; confirmed, recorded, the windows told. The words in both languages and the panel's step (`integrator-words.test.cjs`, `handoff-queue.test.cjs`). 43 different deliberate breakages each turned a test red; two of them only after a test was added for them (a merge commit reported under a later commit; a delivery outside the handoff). One more changed nothing that can be observed (the claim's reason taken from the hold it had just been compared with). In the real window the last stage of `scripts/test-handoff-panel.cjs` is this case: while the integrator sits in the space it merges the delivery for real and says so, none of which is read; moved out and handed the delivery again it reports that merge; the row is held with the sentence above and the two buttons, the space's record does not say "merged"; the person presses "Confirm merged" and the row and the space's record say merged, with the commit and the test count.

**Left open.**
- The blind spot the review named is older than this step and is not closed by it: within a single handoff, a merge that is made and reverted before the reply is settled also passes the three questions, because they are about history. Closing it needs a fourth question (are the delivery's changes still in main's tree), which is a step of its own. Until then "merged" means: the delivery's commits, or the ids of their changes, came into main's history in the named commit during the handoff.
- "Confirm merged" asks git about history only, like the automatic check. That the merge was not undone is the person's word; the sentence on the row says so. Once confirmed, the row and the space's record read like any other merge: neither says that the person confirmed it. Both reviews suggest marking it, so that the person knows which row to doubt if the work later turns out to be missing.
- The row sends the person to the integrator's session. If another handoff is open at that moment, the person's typing there makes that handoff wait for them, as it does for any typing; the panel then says so and offers to send it again. The row has no button that opens the integrator's session (the question block has one).
- The row does not say that confirming may be followed by the notice that this main may be installed.
- If the second look against the first commit gets no answer from git, the strict verdict stands (not verified), and the confirmation is offered only after the delivery was sent again and the look answered.
- If main is rewritten so that the first commit is gone, that second look never gets an answer: every "Send … again" ends as not verified, as before this step. For a delivery already held as an earlier merge, "Confirm merged" then gets no answer and says so; "Send … again" stays beside it.
- A delivery that was returned and redone is a new delivery: nothing of the old one carries over.

## B6 integration handoff: one pass waits for git only so long — 2026-11-11

One of the things to mend before the switch may be opened ("the engine's pass gets a time budget or its own loop"). Behind the closed switch.

**What was wrong.** The engine's pass is the last step of the queue's pass, and the queue's next pass begins only when it is over. Each git command the engine asks may take fifteen seconds before the reader gives it up, and one settlement asks up to ten commands for each reported merge (seven more when the earlier look is needed), besides main's head. A repository that answers slowly (a cold disk, a very large change, a machine busy with something else) could keep the queue's next pass waiting for minutes, and members would get their tasks that much later, with nothing saying why.

**Now.** One pass may wait for git for fifteen seconds in all (`GIT_ALLOWANCE_MS`).
- Every question the pass asks of git goes through the pass's allowance: main's head when handing out; the look at the repository, main's head and each question about a merge when settling. A question that is not answered within what is left counts as not answered, exactly like a question git fails to answer. Once a question was given up, or the time is over, nothing more is asked in that pass. Git may go on working on a question that was given up; nobody waits for it, and its answer, or its failure, is dropped.
- Nothing else changes in what a pass does with an unanswered question. A settlement with an unanswered merge, or with main's head unread, waits the same bounded while (ten minutes) and is asked again by later passes, each with an allowance of its own; so a repository that was only slow for a moment settles by itself a pass later. After that while the merges still unanswered are held as "could not be checked" with what was reported kept, as before.
- The person's "Check again" and "Confirm merged" are no part of a pass and have no allowance: they wait for git as long as it takes, so a repository that stays slow is checked by the person's one press.
- When main's head is not answered in time while handing out, nothing opens and nothing is sent; the delivery waits for a later pass.
- One case needed a rule of its own (found by the independent review). The second look at a merge that is not new for its handoff (was it made earlier, against the delivery's first handoff?) falls back to the strict verdict when it gets no answer; that was decided for a first commit that is gone, where waiting can never help. When it is the pass's own allowance that cut the second look off, that fall-back would call a real earlier merge "not found in main" and leave it with no step. The verdict therefore says when its second look got no answer (`earlier: 'unanswered'`), and a pass whose allowance was used up treats such a verdict as unanswered: it is asked again, and in the end held as "could not be checked" with its claim, so that the person's check, which has all the time, finishes the look. When git itself says quickly that it cannot answer the second look, the strict verdict stands as before, in a pass whose allowance was not used up. (In a pass that did use it up, on another delivery's questions say, such a verdict is treated as unanswered too. That costs a wait and one press of "Check again", which then reaches the same strict verdict; nothing is recorded as merged.)
- The engine keeps no timer of its own (its test forbids it; it reaches the app only through what it is given): the main process gives it `within(answer, ms, late)`. Without it an asked question is waited for, and the allowance only stops further questions; the app always gives it. The engine takes a late failure of a question upon itself, whoever supplies the bound.
- The allowance is counted on time as it passes (`performance.now()`), not on the date that goes into the record.

**Tried first and dropped.** Settling at once when the allowance ran out (holding what was unanswered for the person straight away), because a later pass would wait as long again. The independent review pointed out what that costs: one slow moment, which before went through by itself, would make the person press "Check again" for every merge of that settlement. Waiting as before costs the queue at most the allowance per pass for ten minutes, and heals by itself when the slowness passes.

**Why not its own loop.** A pass of its own, beside the queue's, would let the engine read sessions and write space records while a queue pass is under way; every rule that now holds because the engine runs between two queue passes (what the session that holds a handoff is sent, which sessions NAW itself is busy with, one fresh look per decision) would have to be shown again for that interleaving. The allowance bounds the wait without changing the order of anything.

**Checks.** `integrator-engine-settle.test.cjs`, one test with readers that answer only when the test lets them, or never: a first question never answered (nothing settled, the second commit not asked; asked again by the next pass; held with the claim once the wait is over, and main's head then not asked for the delivery that arrived meanwhile, which the pass after hands out); the person's check on that hold still waiting after several allowances and recording the merge when git answers; one merge answered and one not; ancestry never answered; main's head not answered in time, through the engine's reader and through a checked look, with no question to the reader; handing out with main's head not answered; the second look cut off by the allowance (unanswered, then held with its claim, then found to be an earlier merge by the person's check) beside the same look unanswered by git itself (the strict verdict); git that says quickly it cannot answer; an answer that fails after it was given up, with the app's bound and with a bound that never looks at the answer; an engine without a bound; nothing asked after a question was given up although the clock says a moment is left; a direct call without allowance. `integrator-settle.test.cjs`: the verdict says when its second look got no answer, and the record treats it as the strict verdict. `integrator-dispatch.test.cjs`: the main process gives the engine the bound, and that function gives the answer, gives up a late one, passes a failure on, and leaves no timer running. 27 deliberate breakages each turned a test red (two only after a test was added: ancestry waited for without bound; time that was over before the second look was asked not noted as used up). Several are caught by the test's own twenty-second limit, because a pass that waits for git after all never ends there.

**Left open.**
- While git stays too slow, every pass waits up to the allowance for it: for up to ten minutes for an open handoff, and for as long as deliveries wait to be handed out and main's head is not read in time (before this step: up to thirty seconds a pass for the head, and without bound for a settlement). A pause between such attempts is not built; nothing has shown the need.
- A settlement that needs more than the allowance in all never finishes in a pass, although each of its questions would be answered: each pass starts from the beginning. It ends as "could not be checked" after ten minutes and is finished by the person's "Check again". Keeping git's answers from one pass to the next would mend that; it needs a way to know that the repository is still the same one. Not built.
- A question that was given up leaves its git process running until the reader's own fifteen seconds are over: at most one for each pass.
- The slow send is not bounded here: it is the queue's own send, with the queue's limit of sixty seconds.
- In the person's own check a second look that git does not answer still ends as the strict verdict (unverified, the claim dropped), as decided for a first commit that is gone. The verdict now says when that happened, so the check could leave the hold as it is instead and let the person try again; not done.
- The telling at the end of a pass (space records, notices) has no bound of its own.

## B6 integration handoff: deliveries that wait long are said once — 2026-11-11

One of the things to mend before the switch may be opened ("an integrator that stays unable to take a message for a long time … is not reported yet"). Behind the closed switch.

**What was wrong.** Finished work is handed to the integrator only when its session can take a message. While it cannot (it works on something else for hours, it has ended, its backend needs an update, automatic messages are off), deliveries simply wait, and nothing tells the person; they see it only if they open a space's queue panel and read the rows. The record could list what waited more than four hours, and nothing read that list.

**Now.** Each pass, after it handed out what it could, looks at what still waits to be handed out. If something has waited more than four hours since it arrived, the person is told once, as a condition of its own (`waited-long`). The notice says first what happened (work finished that long ago still waits to be handed over, and how many deliveries wait now), then where to look first (the integrator's session: still busy, or ended; automatic messages may also be off), and last that another integrator can be designated. It names the integrator's session as the person knows it, when that session is in the engine's view; otherwise it says "the integrator". The name goes into a system notice, so characters that are not shown but can change how the rest of the line is laid out (controls, formatting marks such as the right-to-left override, line separators) are taken out of it, it is cut at eighty characters, and a "name" that is only the session's id (a session with neither a label nor a name) is not used. The other notices still carry counts only. (The stand-in for the person refused the first wording: it gave causes and one drastic step, no first step, no name, and was long enough to be cut off in a system banner.)
- It begins only when nothing else already tells the person why nothing is handed out: they were not asked about the integrator or the repository (nobody designated, the designated session gone, the integrator inside a space, no repository that can be read), and no handoff waits for them (that notice already says that everything behind it waits).
- It is over when nothing waits that long any more, and not before: it is not said again each time one of those other things comes and goes. A later delivery that waits that long is said again.
- Only what waits to be handed out counts. What the integrator has, and what is on hold, have their own records and notices.
- It holds nothing and changes nothing about dispatch or handoffs. The person's "retry" on it does nothing (it is a condition, like "reviews are off").

**Checks.** The record (`integrator-handoff.test.cjs`): nothing said and nothing written before four hours, at exactly four hours, or with nothing waiting; said once after that, with the count, also across a restart; over when handed out; said again for a later delivery behind a handoff that is being worked on; lasting while a handoff begins to wait, through the person's retry and new arrivals; not begun while the person is asked about the integrator (four kinds) or a handoff waits for them, and begun when that is over and the delivery still waits; handed and held deliveries not counted. The engine (`integrator-engine-settle.test.cjs`): an integrator at work the whole time, the pass four hours later tells the person once in that same pass, with the session's name, later passes say nothing, and the pass that hands the delivery out ends the condition; no name for a session without one, with a name of blanks, of invisible marks only, or one that is no text, for the session's id standing in for a name, for another native session under that id, for a designation that cannot be read; marks taken out of a name and a long name cut; no name on a notice for another reason. The words in both languages (`integrator-words.test.cjs`). 32 deliberate breakages each turned a test red (two only after a test was added or corrected: the name of another native session under the same id; a line separator inside a name). One check was taken out instead, because the failure it guarded against already ends the same way.

**Left open.**
- The notice names the usual causes; it does not say which one holds now (the record does not keep why the last hand-out did not open). Causes it does not name: the session paused for the person, a backend that needs an update, main's head that cannot be read (for that one the advice to designate another integrator does not help).
- The queue panel shows nothing of it: the rows that wait say "waits until the integrator is free", as before.
- The notice does not name the space, and a click on it only brings the app to the front, as for every notice. Deliveries of several spaces may be waiting.
- The look happens in a pass. While only the person can lift what blocks the hand-out (automatic messages off, the session paused), the engine asks for no passes of its own, so the notice comes with the next pass that runs for another reason (queue work, a window's own check). Listed above as "with no window open".
- The four hours count from when a delivery first arrived. One that was handed out or held and came back (the person's retry, a handoff that waited, a refused send, the one re-send after no result) can therefore be "long" as soon as it waits again; the sentence says "finished more than four hours ago", which stays true.
- Four hours is the record's existing figure; nobody chose it for this notice.

## Native programs no longer carry the session that started NAW — 2026-11-11

Found by the integrator on the installed alpha.234 (variable names only were read, never values): the app and its backends had been started from a Claude session's command tool, and the four Claude processes NAW had started carried that session's `CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET`, `CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN` and `CLAUDE_PID`, three of them its `CLAUDE_JOB_DIR` as well. The person's instruction for findings of this kind: fix them and let development go on.

**What was wrong.** `nativeEnvironment()` in `app/platform.cjs` says that a NAW started from an agent's command tool must not pass that agent's session identity on, and removed four Claude names and four Codex names. Claude Code sets more than those for the commands it runs. Read on the installed backend and on one Claude process it had started, the ones passed on were the inbox socket and its token, the launcher's process id, its background job's folder, its effort level, its "attended" flag, the path of its executable, and its agent marker. While the launching session lives, every Claude session in NAW holds the address and the token of its inbox. Two of the others are read by a starting Claude: the "attended" flag (the new session records that an attended session spawned it) and the job folder (the session writes its exit cause there, and the documentation says writes there are not asked about).

**Which launches use this function** (read in the source). Every launch of a native program: the native Claude and Codex terminals (through `Terminal` and `pty_host.py`, which adds only the terminal type, the working directory and what the adapter passes for that launch), the Codex app server, the legacy dedicated-service runner, and the `claude agents --json` question before a take-over. The others give a fixed or filtered environment of their own (the steward's host and server, the computer-use server and the outbox view, the plugin and Codex qualification checks), except git, which gets the backend's environment without the `GIT_*` names, and the system tools (`ps`, `top`, `sysctl`, `plutil`), which inherit it whole. Git is not changed here.

**Now.** One list, `LAUNCHER_SESSION`, holds the names an agent program sets to describe its own session, and all of them are removed:
- as before: `CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT`, `CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION`, `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, `CODEX_SESSION_ID`, `CODEX_TOOL_CALL_ID`, `CODEX_CI`;
- new, each documented by Claude Code as set by itself for the commands it runs: `CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET` and `CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN` ("Set by Claude Code, not by you … never one inherited from a parent session"), `CLAUDE_PID`, `CLAUDE_JOB_DIR`, `CLAUDE_EFFORT` ("Set automatically in Bash tool subprocesses and hook commands"; the setting a person makes is `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL`, which is kept), `CLAUDE_CODE_BRIDGE_SESSION_ID`;
- new, not documented, taken from the installed Claude Code 2.1.322: `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED` (in its child-environment function), and `CLAUDE_CODE_EXECPATH` and `CLAUDE_CODE_INVOKED_SKILLS` (two names it sets together for the commands it runs, so that a `claude` started there is the same program and knows the skills already invoked).

`AI_AGENT` is removed only when its value begins with `claude-code_` or `claude-code/`. That is the marker Claude Code writes, and the condition is the one Claude Code itself uses before replacing the value; any other value is someone's own and stays.

NAW's own per-session values are a second case of the same thing, found while checking this with a launch from a NAW session's command tool. That shell carries the session's `NAW_HOOK_TOKEN`, `NAW_HOOK_SOCKET` and `NAW_SUBMIT_SOCKET`: the token and the sockets through which its hooks and its bridge speak to the backend as that session. A NAW started from there keeps them in its backend's environment. A native Claude is given its own three with its launch, and those replaced the inherited ones; a native Codex terminal, the Codex app server and the `claude agents --json` question are given none, and received the launching session's. The function now takes these three names out of what it inherits before it adds what the adapter passes for the launch. Nothing in NAW puts them into a process's own environment (the adapter's launch is the only place that sets them), so an inherited one can only be a launching session's. For every other name the order is as it was: what the adapter passes replaces what is inherited. `NAW_OUTBOX_DESCRIPTOR` is not part of this: the app sets it in its own environment on purpose, after deleting an inherited one, and native programs are meant to inherit it.

What a person configures stays: `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`, `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL`, `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR`, `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, the `ANTHROPIC_*` model names, `CODEX_HOME`, keys, and whatever else is not on the list. What remains after the removal is the environment NAW gives when it is started from the Finder, where none of these names exist; no new state is introduced.

**Checks.** `native-environment.test.cjs`, five new tests. On the unchanged function the first four fail.
- The function: every name of the list is gone, eight settings a person makes are kept with their values, what the adapter passes for the launch is still passed.
- `AI_AGENT`: both forms Claude Code writes are removed, another value is kept.
- The whole path of a native terminal: the real `Terminal` and the real PTY host start a stand-in program, which writes the names it was given (and the values of the made-up settings only); none of the launcher's names reach it, the settings and the adapter's values do.
- The `claude agents --json` question, with a stand-in for `claude`: the same.
- NAW's own values (one more test, failing before the second change): given nothing, the function passes none of the three on; given its own three, exactly those; given one, the other two do not fall back to the launching session's; any other name is inherited when nothing is given and replaced by what is given; the outbox descriptor is still inherited; and the real terminal path, started the way a Codex terminal is, hands none of the three to the started program.
- The full unit suite, author-run three times as the change grew: all 6250 tests passed on the second commit. On the first and on the third one test of another change failed, the same one both times (`integrator-engine-settle.test.cjs`, the pass that waits for git only so long, which runs on an allowance of 40 ms); run alone sixteen times, that file failed once. It fails by timing, and it loads neither `platform.cjs` nor a native program, so this change does not touch what it tests.
- Author-run, from a real Claude command tool and without made-up values: the same stand-in started through the real path. With main's function eight of that session's names reach the started program (inbox socket and token, process id, job folder, effort, attended flag, executable path, agent marker); with this change none, and the five settings from the person's own settings file are still there. That command tool belongs to a NAW session, and its hook and submit sockets no longer reach the started program either. No provider program was run and no value was read or printed.

**Left open.**
- Listed and left alone because it is not clear whose they are: `CLAUDE_CODE_HOST_SHORT_TEMP_DIRS` (present on the installed backend; a host's switch that a starting Claude reads, neither identity nor credential); `TRACEPARENT` (in Claude Code's list for the commands it runs, not seen on the backend; a general name other tools use too); `CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE` and `CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_ID` (cloud sessions only); Codex's `CODEX_SANDBOX` and `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED` (if NAW really was started inside that sandbox its children are inside it too, so they are true); Codex's `CODEX_NETWORK_PROXY_*` (state of its managed network proxy, tied to the general proxy variables, not seen).
- Conveniences Claude Code sets for the commands it runs also reach native programs and are not identity: `GIT_EDITOR=true` was on the installed backend, so a `git commit` without a message inside a native program gets an empty one. A person may set the same names, and the two cannot be told apart from the value alone. Not changed.
- The rest of Claude Code's own list for the commands it runs is made of general names a person or the system sets too, and is left alone: `SHELL`, `TMPDIR`, `TEMP`, `TMP`, `TMPPREFIX`, `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR`, `BUN_OPTIONS`, `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS` (and `GIT_EDITOR`, above). Of these only `SHELL`, `TMPDIR` and `GIT_EDITOR` were on the installed backend. `BUN_OPTIONS` would matter most if it ever appeared, because a native Claude's runtime reads it.
- Names that an editor's integrated terminal sets for a Claude started inside it were not looked at; NAW has not been started from one.
- Codex: the per-thread and per-call names were read in the 0.167.1 program's text. No Codex command tool was run for this, so what such a shell really carries beyond them (pager overrides, for one) was not observed. `CODEX_INTERNAL_ORIGINATOR_OVERRIDE` stands beside the sandbox names in that text; it reads as a host's override, not a session's identity, and is left alone.
- The PTY host adds what the adapter passed for the launch once more after this function. A name of the list passed that way would therefore reach the program; no caller passes one.
- Git commands the backend runs itself get its environment without the `GIT_*` names, so with the names above.
- The list follows Claude Code 2.1.322 and Codex 0.167.1. A later version may set more; nothing here notices that.

**Independent review.** A fresh read-only session (`bd2888f2`, claude-opus-5-5; Read, Grep and Glob only) read the diffs, the function's callers, the PTY host, every process start in `app/` outside the bundled DSH client (whose processes start from an allow-list) and the evidence: APPROVE_WITH_NOTES, nothing blocking. It confirmed the table of launches, that each new name is supported by the evidence, that removing `CLAUDE_EFFORT` is right although the integrator's message had named it as a setting (the integrator should say so when taking the delivery), that nothing sets or relies on an inherited hook token or socket, and that the result for every name is what a start from the Finder gives. It could not compare the quoted documentation and program text with their sources. Taken from its notes: `CLAUDE_CODE_INVOKED_SKILLS` joined the list (same evidence as `CLAUDE_CODE_EXECPATH`; the tests failed on it first); an assertion that the outbox descriptor stays inherited; the wording about git; the names now listed under "Left open"; and two of the made-up settings in the test were swapped for other documented ones. Its advice on the second case: merge it with the first. The same session then read that delta: APPROVE_WITH_NOTES again, nothing blocking; its two notes (how far its own search of process starts went, and one more Codex name to list) are in this record as it stands.
